alex-philips-1881-06.A1:
RESISTING ARREST.
FATAL RESULT.
Last Sunday afternoon an unfortunate affair occurred on Dr. Huguet's plantation, on the Highlands below this city. Capt. J. W. Bates, as will be seen below, discovered that one Allen Philips, colored, a prisoner who was sentenced by our District Court for burglary and larceny and who had escaped with other jail birds from the parish jail in 1876, while Mr. O. H. Foreman was sheriff, had returned to his "native roost" in this parish.

During the forenoon of Sunday Allen Philips was at the stope of Mr. John Wax in the southern limits of the town, and getting under the influence of liquor, allowed his dangerous passions to get the better of his judgment. He began to flourish his pistol and make the most dire threats. To prevent a disturbance, Mr. Wax, unabashed by the invections hurled at him and others, snatched his trusty repeater from a drawer, and disarming Allen, started him in the direction of his home.

These facts coming to the ears of Chief T. B. Hillen, with others, he was convinced of the identity of the negro, and informed Sheriff Bates of the circumstances, who took immediate steps to effect an arrest. Deputy Sheriff Skolfield, with Mr. Dennis Daigre as assistant, and Mr. Henry Adams as identifier, was despatched to execute the warrant of arrest. These precautions were taken at the instance of several parties who were cognizant of the desperate character of Allen Philips and his brother Alex, both of whom were an annoyance and terror to the colored people of the neighborhood.

Upon reaching the house of Alex Philips, the officers found both of them seated near the house in evident conversation. They at once resisted arrest. Alex, brother of the prisoner, caught up a hoe, and rushing upon Mr. Skolfield, was in the act of crushing him to the earth, when Mr. Daigre shot him down. Instantaneously, Allen seized a butcher-knife from the hands of a little child present and rushed upon Mr. Skolfield in an effort to get into the house. Mr. Skolfield stood his ground, and, seeing the negro was bent on the commission of some desperate deed to effect his escape, shot him in close proximity. Mr. Daigre fired simultaneously, and both balls taking effect, the negro fell.

The wounds of the two men are not considered fatal by Dr. Duchein who visited them in company with Sheriff Bates yesterday, if they receive the proper care and attention, and the sheriff has already taken steps to this end.

Since the above occurrence sheriff Bates has ascertained the fact that Allen Philips, the prisoner came near beating a white man to death at Plaquimine, some months ago, and made his escape. Also, at Musson station, some time ago, Albert Philips, threatened, with drawn pistol, to kill a clerk, in a store there, when he was driven away. Altogether, the officers were fully justified in what they did; at least a feeling of relief pervades the coloured community which has been annoyed by these desperadoes.
alex-philips-1881-06.A2: From our account of the affray in which the man Allen Philips participated, it might be inferred that he became intoxicated at the store of Mr. John J. Wax, who desires it known that it was because of his refusal to sell him liquor that Philips misbehaved in his establishment.

Our New Orleans Letter. The reality of the "business boom
the usual time for the annual higera in search of health and pleasure is at hand, and yet Canal is gorgerus with the kaleidoscopic tints of fashion's fancy, and our fair ones seem to linger lovingly along their favorite boulevard, before bidding adieu for the long summer month; many of these people go away alone for custom's sake and to do servile deference to the silly requirements of "society"; not that they would obtain more comfort or pleasure elsewhere, and quite a respectable minority of even the uppercrust is taking issue with the custom, and declaring upon experience that New Orleans is fast becoming a desirable summer residence! Expunge yellow fever from our programme, and the incoming season promises a round of entertainments, equal if not superior to the over-lauded summer watering places our fashionable people patronize—with excursions in all directions, at the most moderate prices, and our two splendid lake resorts, a third of which will soon be added at the "old lake end," while our balay atmosphere and delicious breezes modify the semitropical sun to a comfortable coolness—all makes our situation quite endurable! It rains nearly every day in summer here, and such rain! that it has been necessary in the ages gone, to originate a certain provincialism to suit the case. The universal expression "it pours" fitly expresses it—no other would describe our rains—therefore our strictly creole population substitute the term in all its various moods and tenses for the milder verb "to rain." Yes; when clouds gather over a New Orleans sky, they do not say, "I think it will probably rain," but "It's going to pour," and it always does. Your partial, variable, intermittent shower is unknown here, for it always "pours." In the cotton belt, the summer clouds so often wander irresolute across the sky, and even after gathering all the paraphernalia of the thunder storm, at last retreat in tantalizing obstinacy, as if they only came to curtain sunset with their gorgeous drapery! Our clouds never do thus—never deceive—but always come dancing to the earth, in big, rattling, generous drops, making a first class "pour."

But here I am, flying off at tangent on something I did not start to say. This letter was not to discuss clouds, rain, or other meteorologic phenomena, though it is ever so tempting to describe the great interest exhibited in the gratuitous celestial performance, of a few nights since. It would be pleasant also to furnish an extended line of evidence that "fair luna" was, as heretofore the sworn ally of love-sick swain, and romantic damsels, in thus furnishing them a reasonable excuse to while away the dewy hours of a moonlight night in each other's company, though on this occasion, strictly for scientific investigation. I must ignore all this at present for this letter is to say that the hearts of all true women are with THE BEACON in its brave stand, for the unlimited extension of woman's mental culture. vision of woman's mental culture. Have studied the subject carefully, I have long felt that the enlargement of female education was a great need, and one that was pressing its claims upon the thinking minds of this generation. I have also believed that in "God's good time" your sex would be willing and eager to invite our daughters, as well as our sons, into higher and broader fields of literature, and open to them generously, not grudgingly, all the possibilities for which their mental organism is fitted. Regardless of the ill-timed ridicule of those who pretend to confound the coeducation of the sexes with the claims of so-called "woman's rights"; in spite of all their hideous pictures of "the impending doom" a thorough education would bring on woman kind, there are enough true hearted men to defend the cause, and we need not speak a word. Fortunately the experiment of education has been tried, in both the Colleges of Europe and America, and while woman's brain is known to be inferior in weight, its deminished bulk has not proven it to be entirely useless. We don't expect the universities to manufacture brains, but to cultivate what we have regardless of sex, making sex no barrier to advancement.

Speaking of the barriers that hem in the diverse industries of man and woman, did you ever study the statistics for information as to the infringements of one upon the other, in our great cities? The revelation would be novel, and would certainly mitigate the aggressiveness of working women who have ungracefully stepped into unfeminine employments. W. J. Moran, traveling advertising painter from New York, while walking in his sleep, fell from the Pacific Hotel gallery at Shreveport last Monday night and was fatally hurt.

A woman at Cape Girardeau, Mo., who has suffered from a husband's neglect, traced him to a barroom, where he was playing cards with several companions. Setting a covered dish she held in her hands down upon the table, she said: "Presuming, husband, that you were too busy to come home to dinner, I have brought you yours," and departed. With a forced laugh he invited his friends to dine with him, but on removing the cover from the dish found only a slip of paper, on which was written: "I hope you will enjoy your meal; it is the same your family have at home."

Among our State Exchauges.

The Natchitoches Vindicator is out again in full dress, and really improved in appearance since it was burned out.

That paper of June 18th says: Carpenters have more work in this locality than they can well do. A good sign that the spirit of enterprise and progress is "king of the walk" in these parts.

Green apples are in vogue now and so are cases of choice. Green fruit is not over healthy as a diet and should be avoided.

The editor of the Vienna Sentinel is feasting on the fat of the land, in the form of garden vegetables and fruit presented to him by his admiring friends.

Lake Providence Herald: Sheriff Powell returned from Greenville, Miss., on Monday last bringing with him a negro man, who, we learn, is charged with murder, but as to who he killed or where the dead was committed, we did not learn. The prisoner was placed in jail, where he will remain until the July term of District Court.

The case of the State vs. T. J. Stephens charged with the killing of a man named Clark, three weeks since, took place on Tuesday last. Judge J. W. Montgomery presiding. After hearing all the testimony in the case the Judge discharged the prisoner, the evidence going to show that the killing was purely accidental. We congratulate Mr. Stephens upon his delivery from prison life, and especially on his good fortune of being able to prove that the shooting was purely accidental.

One evening last week whilst the steamer D. Stein, was discharging freight at the Point, three of her deck hands died very suddenly, it is supposed from overheat. The evening was intensely hot, and the laborers imprudently drank freely of ice-water which, doubtless, produced congestion. People cannot be too careful during this blood-heat weather.—Morthouse Clarion.

It is charged that a pair of brass-knuckles, in the hands of the mate, had more to do with their death than ice-water or the hot sun.

The Clarion and Cotton Plant are still hammering at each other. Don't get excited brethren, it is too hot for that.

Last week the sheriff of East Baton Rogue went with a posse to arrest Allen Philips (col. ored). He and his brother Alex, both resisted the officers, and were shot and dangerously wo

The mourning emblems with which the interior of the market house wae so tastefully decorated following the death of the late President Garfield, were removed yesterday, having been continued in place for ninety days.

Frank Carr, the crank, who was arrested Sunday night armed to the teeth with revolvers and other weapons, was up yesterday, and as doubts of his sanity were entertained, he was recommended to the county physician for an examination.

The committee on public buildings of the council held a meeting yesterday afternoon, to arrange for the placing of the new chairs in the Market house hall. After some discussion the matter was delegated to the chairman with power to act.

August Johnson was altogether as drunk as a boiled owl. He lushed on the terrible tangle-foot and while crazy drunk he insulted two ladies whom he insisted on following. He was up yesterday and paid the court $25 of his good coin to get out of the scrape.

J. W. Taylor, a bell boy at the Metropolitan hotel swore out a warrant yesterday for the arrest of another bell boy, named Chas. Ford, on the charge of stealing a valise containing promissory notes to the value of $500. The grip was taken from his room two weeks ago.

George Hausen, a toney youth, appeared at the police court yesterday with a swelled head and his left eye draped in mourning. Sunday night he and two chums started out for a time. They got drunk and when ordered to keep quiet they pitched into Officer Molarity and took his club from him. Hausen was run in and the others got away. The spree cost him $25 bills.

The two Rundell boys, from Austin, Texas, who arrived in St. Paul Saturday night, and not meeting with their father as expected, applied at police headquarters for aid, were last evening sent to Fergus Falls, where, as appears, the father had arranged the meeting. The father resides at Pelican Rapids, Otter Tail county. The tickets, as he supposed, were bought from Austin, Texas, to Fergus Falls, where he had made arrangements to receive and care for them.

Arrangements have been made for the transfer to the city next week of the mechanics employed by the St. Paul, Minneapolis & Omaha railroad at Shakopee. They will take possession of the company's new shops near the city hospital, where it is proposed to employ 500 men this winter. In this connection enterprising residents of the locality should make more ample arrangements for their accommodation, and the Fort street line of street cars should be extended at once.

Parties who delight in tripping the "light fantastic" can be accommodated to their heart's content this evening—that is if they are among the elect—as both the Brotherhood of Telegraphers, and the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, receive their friends, the first named organization at Sherman hall, and the latter at Market hall. Both have made extensive preparations, and both entertainments will be largely attended and prove to be among the most enjoyable affairs of the season.

It was reported yesterday that sneak thieves had been at work on Sunday and that they had reaped a rich harvest of overcoats. The police were on the "lay" for the thieves, and last night two of the gentry were run in by Capt. Clark and Detective O'Connor, who arrested a couple of tough looking duffers at the corner of Fourth and Jackson streets. They were identified as having sold three coats to some colored men, and when arrested they carried a lady's muff, a pair of pants and a picture frame in blue setting, containing the photo of a lady, all having no doubt been stolen.
Twenty-seven years ago Frederick Banholzer, a resident of St. Paul for twenty-six years, took out his first naturalization papers, at Freeport, Ill., which he subsequently lost. For a dozen years Mr. Banholzer has been trying by letter to get a transcript of the issuance from the Freeport officials, but without success. Finally he gave the matter in charge of Col. Keifer, clerk of the district court, who yesterday received the proper official certificate, upon which he promptly made out and delivered to Mr. Banholzer his second papers, who can now, after being a resident of St. Paul for more than a quarter of a century, consider himself a full-fledged American citizen.

About as abject a looking creature as even a reporter is often called upon to meet in his daily rounds for police happenings, appeared at the municipal court yesterday afternoon, in the person of the fire bug Alonzo Garner, arrested for setting fire to several buildings near the Post Siding, Sunday night. He was ragged to the verge of nakedness, unkempt, whisky soaked, and bloody, and his appearances indicated a most desperate spree. A witness named Bender testified that the prisoner had stated that he was going to burn up the town. Several witnesses testified to having seen him in the neighborhood of the fires just before the alarm, and to the arrest, after which he was almost lynched by the populace. Defendant stated that he had the tremens, and didn't know what he was doing. He was held to the grand jury.

THE JANUARY TERM.
Opening of the District Court—The Call of the Callendar—The Criminal Calendar. The January term of the district court
Opening of the District Court—The Call of the Callender—The Criminal Calendar.

The January term of the district court opened at 10 o'clock yesterday morning, Judge Brill presiding.

The court room was filled with members of the bar from St. Paul and the state, and the business of the court was expedited in a prompt and spirited manner.

The grand jury was first called, the members answering to their names as follows:

J. N, Bond, E. A, Hemenway, Chas. S. Rogers, D. D. Merrill, F. V. Heyderstead, Ed. Sealey, Michael O'Brien, Edmund Rice, Peter Mueller, Channing Seabury, F. S. Swisher, J. E. Miller, Geo. W. Lawson, J. A. Sabin, H. Hechman, L. E. Reed, J. J. O'Leary, D. Schutte, Christian Stahlman, Herman Greve. For cause shown, Messrs. Curtis, Sabin and Stahlman were excused.

Mr. John E. Miller was appointed foreman.

After the usual statutory charge by the court they retired, and shortly afterwards adjourned until this morning.

CITY GLOBULES
Last evening Officer Shields arrested a man named Donahue for raising a disturbance on Rice street.

The only applications under the new law for permission to carry concealed weapons were made by a clergyman and a journalist.

Maxfield & Co. on yesterday commenced suit and wore out an attachment against F. Ericson, to secure an innebtedness of $5,000.

The management of "Hearts of Oak" decided not to give the usual Wednesday matinee, which will be regretted especially by the ladies.

The funeral of Frederick Smith, for many years a carpet weaver on Washington street, took place from his late residence yesterday afternoon.

Judge Simons filed an order yesterday opening the garnishee disclosure in the case of Schaber & Passavant vs. J. L. Pollock and J. C. McCarthy, garnishee.

Mr. Albert Scheffer received yesterday from a gentleman in Stillwater a buck fawn which attracted a good deal of attention as it stood in its box on Third street, in front of Dawson & Co.'s bank.

Monday afternoon a lady called at Hammer's store on Third street and asked permission to leave a satchel for a few minutes, which was granted. She did not return and the grip was taken to the city hall.

N. Smith was before Judge Burr yesterday charge with selling liquor without a license. The offense took place at Cook's old stand which was closed some time ago. The case continued to the 28th inst.

Frank Loomis was up yesterday charged with disorderly conduct. Officer Patterson visited his house a few days since to abate a nuisance and was given the grand bounce being, so to speak, himself abated. Defendant was fined $5.

The jury in the case of the state against W. D. Smith, indicted for blowing the safe of Breen & Young and tried last Monday, returned a verdict of guilty. The trial of Hamilton, his pal, will take place in a few days. Proceedings in the case of Smith were stayed for twenty days.

Most of the buildings that were destroyed by fire on Eighth street, between Cedar and Minnesota streets, about three weeks ago, have been rebuilt in an enlarged form, and are nearly ready for business. The smoke stack of the box factory was being raised and put in position yesterday.

Edward Nacey was before the court yesterday for getting drunk and beating his helpless little children. He is an old timer and his misfortune and brutality is all owing to whisky. He was required to give bonds in the sum of $150, and not having the savors he was committed.

He bore the illustrious name of John Adams and he was before hizzonor yesterday for frescoing the bugle of a man named Loveland. It was shown that the latter had threatened to shoot defendant and he was fined only $5. Not haying the dust he went to quay for five days.

Articles of incorporation of the Winona Plow company were filed with the secretary of state yesterday. The corporation has a capital stock of $100,000. The incorporators are J. M. Bell, J. K. Palmer, D. L. Kerr and Fred. J. Bell, Winona, who constitute the board of directors and officers of the association.

J. S. Sprague commenced an action in the district court yesterday against Francis Martin and others to enforce payment of $5,000. An injunction was also prayed for in the same suit to restrain the sheriff of Hennepin county from interfering with real estate involved in the suit. An order for the injunction was issued by Judge Simons.

Complaint was made by the society for the prevention of cruelly to children and animals, yesterday, against George Herman, a resident of the sixth ward, charged with beating his step daughter, and Mrs. Frank Kaufman, residing near Seven Corners, who is charged with having locked a blind child in a room and deserted it until it almost perished from cold.

Yesterday morning the district court took up the case of the State against Alonzo Garner, indicted for setting fire to several buildings near Seventh street bridge. There being four counts of the same nature he was tried for attempting to burn the store of Chas Jabuke. The jury were out a short time and returned a verdict of guilty. He was remanded.

About 3:30 o'clock yesterday afternoon a team attached to a wagon while proceeding along St. Peter street near Ninth street became frightened at a street car and started to runaway. The team and wagon was driven by Mr. John Bigelow, of Park avenue, containing in addition that gentleman's wife and child. When opposite No.1 engine house the tongue of the wagon fortunately broke, thus releasing the horses, which were caught by one of the firemen, and what bid fair to be a terrible accident was avoided. No great damage was done.

Yesterday forenoon the dwelling of Mrs. Hanks on Mississippi street was entered by a sneak thief who secured two watches. A young man answering to the description of the thief was arrested by Capt. Clark and Detective O'Conor at the Union depot last night. On the way to the station they took the prisoner into a hallway to search him and the watches were found on his clothing. As they were passing out the prisoner broke away and ran up Sibley street, chase being given by Detective O'Conor who fired two photographs at him.
A long time ago when the birds were singing in the morning and the hawthorn and the myrtle were in bloom, George Rierson met and loved a bonnie damsel named Miss McFeegan. A cloud came over their young dream in the form of a relentless papa and big brother, who swore that they would have none of Rierson's in theirs, if the court knew itself, and she thought she did. By and by the McFeegan's gave a party and Rierson was not invited. This was gall and wormwood and he made up his mind to take in the party anyway. He went, and on being refused admission he knocked in the door. The big brother tackled him with a chair and there was a regular picnic. Rierson was arrested and yesterday he was fined $10 and put under bonds to keep the peace.

Leadville Lawlessness.
Denver, Col., Dec. 3.—The Tribune's Leadville special says: The Gold Park mining camp is in a furore of excitement. Four days ago Harry Weston, foreman of the Gold Park mining company, was shot and killed by Bagley, a discharged blacksmith. Bagley also made an unsuccessful attempt to shoot Superintendent Turney, and then fortified himself in a cabin, which was immediately surrounded by a mob. The cabin was besieged for eight hours without dislodging the occupant.

Finally a large quantity of giant powder was placed near the door and ignited; the explosion following tore the cabin to pieces, and Bagley was found with a bullet hole through his heart, having evidently committed suicide. Bagley has several sympathizers who have threatened Turney's life and a strong guard surrounds his cabin day and night. Jack White and Bagley's friends were ordered out of the camp by the vigilantes, and paraded the town all day with a pair of cocked revolvers looking for the committee, but left at night. Much trouble is anticipated.

A FATAL QUARREL IN A MINING CAMP.
DENVER, Col., Dec. 4.—A dispatch to THE TRIBUNE from Leadville says: "There is great excitement in the Gold Park mining camp. Four days ago H. Weston, foreman of the Gold Park Mining Company, was shot and killed by Bagley, a discharged blacksmith. Bagley also made an unsuccessful attempt to shoot Superintendent Turney. He then fortified himself in his cabin, which was immediately surrounded by a mob. The cabin was besieged for eight hours without success. Finally a large quantity of giant powder was placed near the door and ignited. The explosion following tore the cabin to pieces, and Bagley was found with a bullet-hole through his heart, having evidently committed suicide. Bagley has several friends who have threatened Turney's life, and a strong guard surrounds his cabin day and night. J. White and other friends of Bagley, who were ordered out of camp by the vigilants, paraded the town all day looking for the committee, but left the camp at night. Much trouble is anticipated.

Following are some of the most important sections: A bill to enforce a treaty of stipulations with the Chinese. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled:

SECTION 1. That all subjects, citizens of China, who are students, coming to the United States for purposes of education, merchants or tradesmen engaged in lawful commerce, travelers in and through the United States, from curiosity or upon lawful business, or officers of the Chinese Government, with their body and household servants, may lawfully enter, remain in, or pass through the United States, upon being identified as hereinafter provided. But the introduction, or coming into, or residence in the United States of any and all other Chinese, or natives of China, of whatever class or description, whether they come from China or elsewhere, except such Chinese as were residing in the United States on the 19th day of July, 1881, is hereby declared unlawful and are suspended and prohibited until otherwise provided by law.

Sec. 2. That in case any Chinese residing in the United States on the 19th day of July, 1881, shall depart therefrom, their re-entry and future residence therein shall be conditioned upon their having before their departure been duly registered at a custom-house in the United States, and producing to the Collector of the district at which they shall seek to re-enter the certificate of registration and consular certificate, hereinafter provided for, and any Chinese not residing in the United States at that date shall, as a condition of entry, produce to the Collector of the district in which he seeks to enter the permission of the Chinese Government and the consular certificate, hereinafter provided for.

Sec. 7. That no master of any vessel shall bring any Chinese within the jurisdiction of the United States, except the executive officers of the Government, unless said Chinese shall first produce to him the permission of the Chinese Government, attested to by the consular officer of the United States, as hereinbefore provided, or a certificate of registration duly issued by a Collector of Customs of a Collection District in the United States, with the identity of the holder similarly attached by consular authority; and any master of any vessel violating the provisions of this section shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor, and for each person brought by means of the vessel of which he is master will, in the jurisdiction of the United States, be fined in the sum of $5, and may be imprisoned for a term not exceeding one year; provided that this section shall not apply to any master of a vessel wrecked on the shores of the United States, or any vessel in actual distress.

SEC. 12. That any person who shall aid or abet the landing in the United States from any vessel of any Chinese not authorized by this Act to enter the United States shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor, and shall for each person so landed be fined in the sum of $500, and be imprisoned for a term not exceeding one year.

SEC. 13. That no Chinese subject shall be permitted to enter the United States without producing to the proper officer of customs the certificate herein required of Chinese seeking to land from a vessel, and in case of wrongful entry, or attempt to enter by land, the vehicle, car, animal, or other means of conveyance used for transporting such person into the United States.
A Young Bride Becomes Homesick.

New York, Dec. 5.—About two years ago the daughter of Amos Stillman of Brooklyn eloped with W. S. Guild. Miss Stillman was only about 16, while Guild was 70. After the private marriage ceremony they slipped away to Europe, without the knowledge of their relatives and friends. Things were not what the young bride thought they should be, and in four days she became homesick, and prevailed upon Guild to return. When they reached the wharf in New York he hired a coach and sent her home, while he got upon another steamer and set sail for California. For one year he remitted his young bride $18 per week, and then the remittances stopped. Now she sues him for a limited divorce on the ground of abandonment. It is understood that he claims that she abandoned him. On Saturday a motion was made by her counsel for a counsel fee and alimony. It was opposed by counsel for defendant, who said his client was in California, and would have to send affidavits to him. The case was postponed.

Foreman of a Mining Company Killed.

LEADVILLE, Dec. 5.—The Gold Park Mining Company is in a furore of excitement. Four days ago, Harry Weston, Foreman of the Gold Park Mining Co., was shot and killed by Bayley, the discharged blacksmith. Bayley also made an unsuccessful attempt to shoot Superintendent Turney. He then fortified himself in his cabin, which was immediately surrounded by a mob. The cabin was besieged for eight hours without dislodging its occupant. Finally a large quantity of giant powder was placed near the door and ignited. The explosion which followed tore the cabin to pieces, and Bayley was found with a bullet hole through his heart, having evidently committed suicide. Bayley has several sympathizers who have threatened Turney's life, and a strong guard surrounds his cabin night and day. Jack White and Bayley's other friends were ordered out of the camp by the vigilantes. The Bayleyites paraded the town all day with cocked revolvers; looking for the vigilantes, but left at night. Much trouble is anticipated.

The Liquor War in Nebraska Bringing Forth Assasins—The Murder of Col. Smith.

Omaha. Neb., Nov. 5.—All Omaha was startled this morning by the announcement in the morning papers that Watson B. Smith, Clerk of the United States Court, had been found murdered at about 2 o'clock this morning at his office door in the third story of the United States Court-House. Col. Smith not coming home last night at the usual hour, his mother became anxious concerning him, and called on Dr. Moore, a near neighbor, to go and look for him down-town. The Doctor telephoned to druggist Kuhn about 2 o'clock to go to Col. Smith's office and see if he was there, as he had been complaining of being sick. Kuhn did so, and found Col. Smith lying dead upon the floor in the hall, in a pool of blood, with a bullet-hole in his head.

THE ALARM WAS GIVEN, and investigation was begun. A revolver of a large calibre was found sticking in his left pantaloons-leg, near the foot, with the butt-end exposed. His key was still in his door, which he was about to shut up on departing. The door was partly open. Two letters which he had written, directed, and stamped were on the floor at his feet, as they had fallen from his hand. It was apparent that he intended to mail them down-stairs in the post-office as he should leave the building. His hat was on the back of his head, full of blood. He had turned out the gas in his office, and the murderer probably turned out the gas in the hall, and laid in wait for him, and, as he was about to close his door, put a revolver to his head and fired, striking above the left temple, the ball.

GOING CLEAR THROUGH THE HEAD and landing on the floor. The revolver that was found did not belong to Col. Smith, which explodes all theory of suicide. Everything shows that the deceased had no idea of the kind, but that he was preparing to go home. His own two revolvers were found at his home. At the Coroner's inquest today several threatening letters were produced. Col. Smith was a prominent temperance man, and had taken an active part to enforce the Sloeumb Liquor law, compelling saloons to pay $1,000 license. He also caused the saloons to close on Sunday. For some time past a bitter feeling has existed toward him on the part of some liquor men on this account. Letters containing threats came from that source, and are villainous productions. The Coroner's jury returned a verdict of murder.

AT A CITIZENS' MEETING
this afternoon indignation was expressed and $5,000 subscribed for a reward for the arrest and conviction of the murderers, to whom as yet no clew has been obtained. The affair remains a dark and painful mystery. Other rewards are offered, one of $500 by the Liquor-Dealers' Union, one of $200 by the Good Templars, and another of $200 by Gov. Nance. Great excitement prevails. Deceased was a prominent and respected citizen, a man of correct habits, a zealous member of the Baptist Church, and was widely known through Nebraska. He had been Clerk of the United States courts for over twelve years.

EXCITEMENT AT LINCOLN.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
LINCOLN, Neb., Nov. 5.—The news of the shooting at Omaha of Watson B. Smith, Clerk of the United States District Court, was brought into the District Court in this city this morning, and it caused a profound sensation. The Hon. T. Marquette addressed the court, and said that telegrams received from Omaha announced that Watson B. Smith had been murdered at the door of his office at Omaha. He suggested that there be a meeting of the bar of the United States Court this evening, and that his Honor preside. Mr. Marquette further remarked that Mr. Smith, in his office, had been a friend and helper of the attorneys who practiced in the United States Courts. For the past five months he had been actively engaged and endeavoring to enforce the laws in this city as well as in Omaha. Lawyers knew the necessity of enforcing the law, and the good which follows such enforcement. He hoped, therefore, every member of the bar would be present to honor the memory of one who had sacrificed his life in support of the laws of his country. In compliance with the suggestion of Mr. Marquette, a full representation of the bar of Lincoln is now in public meeting at the United States Court-House, and speeches are being made in relation to the sad affair. The people of Lincoln, and especially the legal fraternity, are horrified over the assassination. Every particular in relation to the same is eagerly caught up and discussed by our people, and the greatest sympathy is felt for the immediate friends and relatives of the deceased. Col. Smith was well known in this city, and bore the reputation of being an excellent citizen and a bold and outspoken friend of law and order.

THE GREENVILLE LYNCHING.
Details of the Crime and Execution of Bob Williams-Another Negro Narrowly Escapes the Same Fate.
Williamston Correspondence Charleston News and Courier, 4th.
About 7 o'clock this morning two of our best citizens drove into town and lodged in the guardhouse a negro whom they had arrested in Greenville county some time during last night. It was soon ascertained that the negro had, a few days ago, outraged a little nine-year-old child, the niece of one of the gentlemen who had him in charge. The little orphan girl was living with a Mr. Clark between Greenville and Macloy's factory, who, yesterday, as soon as he discovered what had been done, brought her to her uncle in a fearfully injured condition. That gentleman, who, though a preacher, is noted for his nerve and pluck, procured the aid of his nearest neighbor, and going very quietly to the home and bed of the fiend who committed the awful deed, tied him hard and fast. His first question was, "Are you going to kill me?" While coming to Williamston he begged his captors to stop and shoot him. He said his former master had often told him he would be hanged some day; that his time had come; he was guilty, and wanted to be shot.

At eight o'clock, about one hundred men assembled at the depot to do justice to the prisoner and justice to the poor little outraged orphan child. This crowd was made up of young, old and middle aged men, all anxious to learn the particulars and pursue whatever course the facts of the case might demand. After some consultation it was determined to take the criminal back into Greenville county and there mete out to him such punishment as in their judgment his conduct deserved. Though he had boldly contessed his guilt time after time, two of the crowd were appointed to take him to the little girl and have him identified. She did identify him, and while the demon stood in the presence of his innocent victim, he said, "Yes, that's the little girl." His doom was segled. He was marched across the bridge over the Saluda river, at Pelzer, just two miles from this place, and there on the hill opposite that beautiful and growing town, was hanged until he was "dead, dead, dead."

That is the closing chapter in the life of Bob Williams—a demon too flendish to be buried in the soil that contains the ashes of human beings. Our streets have been very quiet ever since the very orderly crowd marched the culprit away to the last scene of his life. I am informed this evening, however, that after things had quieted down this morning, and the laborers at Pelzer had returned to their work, a negro, whose name I did not ascertain, remarked that if the dead man had been anything to him he would not have suffered him to be killed for that offense. He was instantly seized by some of the same crowd that had hanged the other negro, and with a rope around his neck was being hurried off to the spot that was made memorable by the incidents of the hour before, when President Smythe and Mr. Caughfin interfered, and after begging hard for him, had him released, with the promise that he would never more be seen in Anderson county. When seen last he was making tracks towards parts unknown,

Tuesday's Elections.
Elections were held in several States Tuesday. The greatest interest was felt in Virginia and New York. The latest news we have is from the Charleston News and Courier of yesterday, which is to the effect that New York went Democratic by about 15,000; that Virginia is very close and that the Democrats have elected Daniel for Governor and a majority of the Legislature. Maryland and Mississippi go Democratic; Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and Wisconsin Republican. Full and reliable returns cannot be obtained for several days.

At Marion, Meridian County, Miss., the whites at the polls were fired on by negroes and four were killed and two wounded.

David R. Locke, ("Petroleum V. Nasby") has returned from Europe. His letters to the Toledo, O., Blade were exceedingly interesting and instructive. Mr. Locke before visiting Ireland and while in England was a bitter denunciator of the Irish, charging them with being lazy and thriftless. Their complaints and the agitation of the Land question he regarded as unfounded. After visiting Ireland his opinions on this subject underwent a complete change, and he is now one of the ablest champions the Irish have in this country. His descriptions of Irish suffering, of which he was an eye witness, are vivid and powerful. He characterizes the treatment of Ireland by the English government as brutal in the extreme and a disgrace to civilization.

The Star Route prosecutions drag along very leisurely and indifferently. Nothing has been done up to this time except to squabble over the indictments. It is said that Arthur does not desire a bona fide prosecution.

A negro named Robert Williams was lynched near Pelzer, Greenville County, the 4th instant, for a brutal outrage on a nine year old white girl. He was hanged by about one hundred men, in the daytime and publicly.

The present Executive is a politician pure and simple. He may be a shrewd politi- cian, in the sense of suiting means to ends, but in all his plans and pur- poses he will never rise above the thought of party success. This much is clearly foreshadowed both in his past record and in the first steps of his administration. One of the first acts of the new Executive was to bring the power and patronage of the Government to the aid of Mahone in the Virginia campaign solely for the purpose of gaining a small party ad- vantage, which must be of question- able value to say the least of it. It is beyond controversy or doubt that we are to have a Cabinet of Grant men and a return of Grant policies On the inside and outside the President's advisers are drawn from the Old Guard at Chicago—the famous 306—and the influences and connections surrounding his Administration will be of the same sort. Political trading and scheming to party ends and for the success of certain in dividuals will be the chief characteristic of the Administration. Even Mr. Blaine acknowledges this prospect and recognizes that he has no place in the crowd. It is not unlikely, therefore, that the relations of Democrats toward such an Administration will be very different from their feelings toward that of Gen. Garfield.

After all that has been said and done about the star route ring and its robberies the prospect now is that every one of the rascals will go scot free. No more doubt exists now of the guilt of the parties accused, or of the enormity of their stealings, than has existed at any time heretofore, but the difficulties surrounding the prosecution of the cases are coming to be better understood. There is a strong suspicion obtaining here, also, that the President is not in earnest in his expressed desire for a vigorous prosecution. This suspicion arises partly from his anxiety to throw all the responsibility upon the Garfield administration, and is strengthened by the stubborn determination of Attorney-General McVeagh to retire. It has been asserted in circles where McVeagh's purposes ought to be known that this is really his private view. Certainly he knows the value of the evidence that has been obtained and he asserts with the utmost positiveness that it is sufficient to convince any unbiased mind. This leaves only the one opinion that the Attorney-General has no faith in the professions of President Arthur against Dorsey, Brady and their associates, and therefore insists on retiring rather than be humiliated with a defeat his legal acumen could not avoid against the secret touches of Presidential influences.

Dorsey and Brady are the head and front of the offenders and the chief beneficiaries. In other words they pocketed most of the swag. Dorsey is Secretary of the Republican National Committee and knows all the secrets of that body. He was dined in New York for his success in bribery in Indiana and one of his entertainers was President Arthur, who looked upon his use of "soap" in the Indiana contest as a good joke. The accomplished Dorsey is therefore perfectly unconcerned. He knows he is safe. He has said to the party managers: 'I must be fully vindicated or when I fall I will pull down with me the pillars of the Republican temple. I can make an exposure that would shame the party out of existence, and will do it rather than be disgraced for saving the party.' He will not be punished, neither will Brady, and all this polling and hauling by Arthur and McVeagh, has this meaning. McVeagh does not want to be the scapegoat.

President Garfield was removed from Washington to Long Branch last Tuesday. He endured the trip admirably; the speed and motion of the car not discommoding him in the least. His sleep was peaceful the first night after his arrival and the physicians say he is improving and that every indication in his case points to a recovery. The latest news is that the President has begun to gain strength and his stomach is in a more healthful condition than at any time since he was shot.

FIVE persons—three white men and two Indians—were hung at Fort Smith las Friday.

The littls war between the Arkadelphia Standard and Columbia Banner has ended. The temple of Janus has closed for repairs.—[Arkansas Gazette.

From a perusal of the Standard of last week we suppose the repairs have been made and the doors opened again.

There has been a general overhauling and cleaning up at Mark Wyeough preparatory to his departure for purchasing new goods. He has had the clothing removed up-stairs, away from the dust.

United States Senator J. S. Williams, is a tobacco raiser. He has on hand—last year's crop—worth $25,000 and the crop for this year is estimated to be worth as much.

SOME of the Ohio penitentiary convicts have been engaged in coining nickles from babbitt metal, and with outside assistance has a great many of them in circulation.

THE Sheridan Spy greeted us last week, hailing from Sheridan, Grant county. with Hon. W. N. Cleveland in charge as editor. We welcome the Spy and hope that Bro. Cleveland may spy his way into safety and wealth; which is hoping a great deal for a newspaper nowadays-

JACKSONPORT with eight stores gives in $59,215 in merchandise. Newport with forty-one stores gives in $63,784, and twelve country stores in the county gives in $65,000. This is fuuny; wonderfully amusing. Will the merchants of Newport, or the editor of the News please rise and explain.

An attempt was made by a large mob last week to execute the three prisoners in the Yell county jail, at Danville, which was foiled by the prompt action of the sheriff in removing the prisoners beyond the reach of the mob.

DURING the season of 1880-'81, ending August 31, 1881, the cotton receipts at New Orleans reached 1,879., 593 bales, the value of which is estimated at $99,035,755. A large increase over any previous year.

SHORT crops are not confined to Arkansas. A subscriber of Ozark county, Mo., who is a physician, has seen much of the county crops writes us, August 5th, that hard times are ahead, on account of the severe drought. Cotton will not make over one-fourth of a crop and corn not over one-third; hay badly damaged and but little mast.

TEE Golden Epoch is the name of a semi-monthly six column folio newspaper published by Geo. H. W. Stewart, editor and proprietor, at Helena, Ark. The aim and object of the Golden Epoch is to benefit the social, moral, intellectual and religious elevation of the colored race. The salutatory is well timed and golden in tone and we wish the Epoch to be golden with success in its undertaking.

THE first of September edition of the New Orleans Democrat was an immense paper—sex tuple shee, twenty-four: pages of six columns to each page, making 144 columns; the largest paper ever issued in the south, and the best; giving the latest and most reliable news from all quarters. The issue of the 1st contains a statement of the trade, commerce, manufacturing, etc., of New Orleans; also a tabulated statement of the cotton receipts at that city from 1835 to 1880-'81; value of exports and imports; freight by water and by rail; in fact a concise review of all business appertaining to New Orleans. Saturday it has the latest crop telegrams from all points in the cotton belt regarding the cotton prospects.

THE continued endebtedness of many ef our towns and counties is due in a great measure to the tax assessments heretofore made. A change in this direction would bring cities, towns and counties out of debt: for instance, the city of Little Rock and county of Pulaski. We have not the figures before us but understand, from a reliable source that the assessment of Pulaski county, on personal property, for 1680 was only a little more than $4,000 over and above the assessed valuation in this county, on personal property. There is not a sane man in the state but knows that such assessment is at fanlt; erroniously so, for the real value of the personal property in the city of Little Rock cannot be far short of $5,000,000. A half truthful statement would show that the moneys, credits and effects, goods, wares and merchandise would reach that seemingly large figure. The fault of these false assesments is not in the law but in the officers of the law.

Jobe, the able junior editor of the Russellville DEMOCRAT, who spent several days of last week in our county on a visit to his father, was in Searcy Saturday and paid his respects to the Beacon. Accept thanks of the senior for the above complimentary notice and mention of our co-editor, and which we know to be duly appreciated by him.

If sent to the private address of either of the Editors, and they should be absent, their letters would remain in the Post office unopened, as was the case in the communication from Scrap, which should have appeared in last week's paper, and can be found in te-day's issue.

—Mrs. Virginia C. Moseley, with her son and daughter, Mr. C. B. and Miss Jennie Moseley, the mother, brother and sister of our worthy, enterprising and much esteemed fellow townsmen, Mess. J. A. and M. Moseley, we regret to say, left Russellville for Quitman since our last issue, with a view to making the latter place their temporary home. Another death sentence has been commuted by Gov. Churchill. This time it is Cal Emory, of Franklin county, who was convicted of murder at the September 1880 term of the Pope circuit court on a change of venue from Franklin county. An appeal has been pending since last December before the supreme court, and last Friday on petition from Franklin county and judge of the supreme court the governor commuted the sentence to twenty-one years in the penitentiary. At best this action is an outrage upon public decency and calls forth the loudest condemnation. Emory was convicted of murdering a woman, the details of which crime is of the most fiendish and revolting character. Emory is either guilty or innocent of this crime. If guilty he should have suffered the full penalty of the law; if innocent he should have been released. There should have been no compromise in this case. The spectacle of the supreme court of a state seeking concessions of this kind is a novel one in criminal jurisprudence.

The Little Rock, Ark., Gazette's Russellville, Ark., special says: Last night between twelve and one o'clock, an armed crowd of twenty-five men, thought to be from Franklin county, friends of the murdered woman, took possession of the Dover, Pope county jail and hung Cal. Emory, whose death sentence Governor Churchill, a few weeks ago commuted to twenty-one years imprisonment in the penitentiary.

Taylor, in Franklin county, nearly a year ago. Emory had been sentenced to be hanged for this horrible crime, but the Governor, on the recommendation of the Judges of the Supreme Court, of whom a new trial was asked, commuted his sentence to 21 years’ imprisonment. The case of the Chinaman and the white woman who married each other in Colorado and were indicted therefor in Cheyenne, Wyoming Territory, was decided yesterday by Chief Justice Sever, of the Territorial Court. He held that the marriage, being legal in Colorado, was also legal in Wyoming, under the statute, and ordered the defendants to be discharged. A curious result of the marriage is the social ostracism of the husband, Lee Chin, by his own countrymen, who says he has disgraced himself by marrying a white woman.

Yesterday noon, at the end of his seventeenth day of fasting, John Griscom weighed 172¼ pounds, a loss of ¾ of a pound during twenty-four hours. His pulse was 64, respiration 18, and temperature 98.3-5. It is said that his face thus rar produced little alteration in his appearance, and in conversation his voice is full and his actions animated.

Mr. Knapp, the present chief clerk of the Post-office Department, will retire on account of ill health, and be succeeded on the 1st of July by J. R. Van Wormer, the private secretary of Postmaster General James.

Two young men, named Estes and Globe, were drowned at Dallas, Texas, on Monday. Estes got beyond his depth while bathing, and Globe perished in trying to rescue the sinking man.

A boat, containing five young men was carried over a dam in the Iowa River, at Marshallton, Iowa, yesterday and two of them named Samuel S. Jones and Dell Kribbs, were drowned.

Information was received here last Friday from Dover, of an unsuccessful attempt that morning about 2 o'clock to lynch Cal Emory, the murderer, who is confined in jail at that place. The action of the governor in commuting the death sentence of Emory to twenty-one years in the penitentiary is generally condemned and the attempt above mentioned was not wholly unexpected here where the details of the fearful crime with which he is charged are so well known. The public, so far as our information extends, is of one opinion, and that unfavorable to the governor, for his utter disregrrd of the verdict of courts and juries as evidenced by his wholesale clemency to criminals of every class. Should this continue people will be forced, in self defence, to take the law into their own hands and such occurrences as was attempted at Dover last Friday night may be expected to become frequent in all parts of the state.

LATER.—Since the above was put in type the determined band of lynchers, after two intellectual attempts, made the third one and succeeded in their designs. On Monday night about 12 o'clock the jail was forced open and the guards overpowered. One of the lynchers attempted to descend into the cell where Emory was confined, but was beaten back by the prisoner who was rendered frantic with fright. Emory was then shot through the head and a fellow prisoner made to adjust a noose about his neck by which he was drawn up through the aperture and taken from the jail and hanged to a gallows. It is thought he was more dead than alive when hanged. The lynchers left the body hanging where it remained until the arrival of the coroner which was late Tuesday evening. The lynchers were from Franklin county and came to avenge the death of the woman murdered by Emory.

NEWS AND OTHER NOTINGS.
The Bedford Gazette wants an anti-cigarette law passed. Next?

Sebastian McKay, of Titusville, struck oil in his garden while digging for potatoes on Friday.

A wind and rain storm in Minnesota last Saturday and Sunday caused the loss of several lives and did considerable damage.

Three men were killed on Sunday by an explosion on the wrecking steamer B. & J. Baker off Cape Henry beach.

A. D. Robeson, a nephew of ex-Secretary Robeson, was killed by lightning on Sunday near Hunnewell, Kan.

Five persons living near Solomen City, Kan., were killed on Thursday by a cyclone, which also destroyed many buildings.

A stately woman walked solemnly down California street, San Francisco, dressed only in a night-gown. She was insane.

Mr. John Black, of Oliver township, Perry county, has a colt that is only two years and twenty-two days old that weighs 1,322.

Logs that escape from the boom at Williamsport are worth 25 cents a piece to the finder. One man made over $100 in this way on Thursday.

A hundred persons were killed and sixty injured by an earthquake which recently devastated a number of villages in the Pashalie of Van Armenia.

Jew boys are preferred to any others as office boys by numbers of Christians in New York. They are found to be exceptionally intelligent and trustworthy.

Charles Johnson, of Eau Claire, Wis., was killed in his doorway on Friday by Louis Carter, a married man, who had tried to elope with Mrs. Johnson.

Father Larocca, General of the Dominican Order for the entire world, accompanied by Lieutenant General Calberry, has arrived at New York from Europe.

Mrs. Harper, a colored woman, living in Rock Hill township, Bueks county, accidentally shot and killed her husband on Thursday while examining a gun.

An insane woman at Clinton, Ill., committed suicide recently in a most horrible manner. She saturated her clothing with kerosene and then set them on fire.

Daniel Moran and Henry Donsberger, two of the men who were scalded by the explosion at Pottsville on Saturday have died, and L. Blakenhorn is not expected to survive.

—Mr. Flanagan and Mr. McDermitt, of White Mills, were both drowned at Kimble on Saturday afternoon. They were in a row-boat on a pleasure trip going to Lackawaxen.

—A special from Little Rock, Ark., says that near Arkadelphia, on Saturday last, Pleasant Gray, aged thirteen, shot and killed a colored boy named Russell of about the same age.

—The oldest minister in the world is believed to be Rev. John F. Adams, of the New Hampshire Conference. Of the ninety-four years he has lived, sixty-nine have been spent in the ministry.

—John Smith, living in Plymouth township, Montgomery county, was attacked by highwaymen on Thursday, who shot him dangerously and then robbed him of clothing and $17 in money.

—Two Michigan girls in love with the same man induced him to go to Utah and marry them both. This is a slight improvement on the old method of shooting one and eloping with the other.

—A terrible boiler explosion occurred at Pottsville about noon on Friday, at Atkins Bros. Fishback rolling mill. Eight or ten men were badly scalded and of those it is thought three at least will die.

—The wife of an old colored man in the eastern part of Georgia recently presented him with the sixth pair of twins, the family having been previously endowed with two pairs of triplets—all flourishing.

—By the explosion of the boiler of the steamboat Hannah, at New Orleans, on Wednesday, of last week, one man was killed, and a number of others were fatally injured, five of whom have since died.

—On Tuesday night Cal. Emory, who murdered his wife, was taken from jail at Russellville, Ark., by a mob and hung. The Governor only a few weeks ago commuted his death sentence to imprisonment for twenty-one years.

—Michael Connally was killed, Patrick Burke seriously injured and John Hawkins had his leg broken on Monday at No. 2 mine of the Delaware and Hudson Coal Company, at Plymouth, Pa. The accident was caused by a premature blast.

—A chartor has been filed in Kansas for a co-operative society to colonize Old Mexico. It is for the purpose of buying lands in Mexico and settling colonies there on a capital stock of $200,000 divided into eight thousand shares of $25 each.

—Isaac Alfrey's dog bit Anderson Johnson's hog, at Owingsville, Ky. Then Johnson shot Alfrey's dog. Next, Alfrey shot Johnson's hog. Finally, Johnson shot Alfrey, killing him, and the latest report said that a mob had gone to hang the murderer.

A turkey gobble on the farm of W. C. Beates, of East Donegal township, Lancaster county, recently undertook to carry a full-grown chicken on its back. The chicken kept her balance nicely, and was carried for some time before the gobble tilted her off.

Diphtheria has become epidemic at Lerdington, Mich. One hundred and twenty children have died recently in a population of 4,000 people. The schools are closed, and special policemen have been stationed at the houses where sickness exists to prevent ingress and egress.

A man employed in an ice house in Wisconsin, Me., lost his footing and fell, involuntarily throwing his arms wildly in the air. His pick was thrown in such a manner that the back of his neck struck upon the sharp point, severing an artery, and he bled to death in five minutes.

George C. Gatling stabbed and killed his wife at the Atlantic Beer Gardens, San Francisco, on Thursday evening. He suspected her of infidelity and wrote her a decoy note, which she answered by going to the gardens. He met her in the room and stabbed her to the heart.

Reuben E. Brown, a farmer of Limestone township, four miles from Peoria, Ill., while crossing an iron bridge over the Kickapoo river in a wagon during a thunder storm on Saturday evening, was struck by lightning and instantly killed. His son, a lad of 12 years, who was with him, was not hurt.

One of the Protestant churches in Patchogue, L. I., has made a novel addition to its music by introducing into the church two dozen canary birds in cages. They sing with the choir and also when the choir is not singing, and their music is not complained of by either the minister or the congregation.

Dr. Harry Darling, of Atlanta, Ga., while visiting Niagara Falls week before last, was so smitten by the charms of a girl who sold relics in one of the museums—Anne Murphy, of St. Catharines,—that he proposed, was accepted and the next day they were married and started for the sunny South.

John Crabill and several members of his family were also badly hurt, several of whom will likely die.

JUDGE_LYNCH.
The Straight Story of the Lynching.
A Frantic Fight for Life by Emory.
Editor Little Rock Democrat.]
RUSSELLVILLE June
RUSSELLVILLE, June 14. — Last night about 12 o'clock a body of about twenty-five men overpowered the jailor at Dover, and after killing Cal Emory took him out and hung him to the gallows that was erected sometime since by Sheriff Hocins for his lawful execution. The jailer, who sleeps in the upper story of the jail, at first refused the mob admittance, but they undertook and succeeded in smoking him out, throwing a heavy blanket over him and seating two or three of their number on him they proceeded to get their man. Lowering a ladder one of them started down, but Emory being frantic with fear and excitement, broke one of the rounds from the ladder and so successsfully defended himself with it that the invader had to retreat up the ladder. Next they tried to force a negro prisoner to tie the rope around his neck, but Emory told the negro he would kill him if he laid his hands on him. Finding it impossible to get him out of the jail alive they shot at him three or four times, only one of which took effect, that being right in the top of his head. They then took him out and hung him to the gallows, a dead man. While the affair is one greatly to be deplored it was not unexpected here, as there was two former attempts made to lynch Emory, the man of whom it is said that "he violated the person of his afflianced and killed then her." That was what hewas tried for. A good jury found him guilty of the crime. It was the sentence of a just judge that condemned him to be hung, which was commuted by the governor to twenty-one years in the penitentiary. Guilty or innocent he paid the penalty with his life at the hands of a mob, and the stain rests upon the county of Pope. CITIZEN.

PRESS COMMENTS ON THE LYNCHING OF EMORY.
Below we present a few paragraphs selected at random from our exchanges, showing the spirit in which the lynching of Emory has been received by the press. It will be observed that the sentiments expressed indicate no disposition to ap prove mob violence, but a desire to mete out to criminals of every class a mode of punishment commensurate with the crimes committed by them. It will be interesting reading to Editor Blackburn and otner apologists for a slack method of administering justice by the powers that be.

Had the governor allowed the law to take its course the man would have been hung by the sheriff instead of a mob and met the fate he so richly merited.—Log Cabin.

We regret to hear that he was hung illegally. Mob law is always to be deplored. But it is what we expected to result from the injudicious use of the pardoning power.—Ozark Democrat.

The News has no comments to make condemnatory to the act, for while we think that law and order preserved in a legal way, yet we are willing to see all men who commit rapes, hung without judge or jury.—Atkins News.

Governor Churchill commuted his sentence to 21 years in the penitentiary, but an outraged people could stand no such an imposition upon them, and took the case into their own hands. We do not believe in mob law but if there ever were cases in which it is justifiable this is certainly one of them.—Van Buren Graphic.

Our people do not favor mob law but the general sentiment is that Emory got his just deserts. The friends of the poor woman he outraged and then murdered and to conceal his hellish crime threw her body in Mulberry creek to rot, are not alone in feeling that they could not allow this wretch to escape the death he deserved through executive clemency, after he had been lawfully tried and condemned. Mob law should be frowned down, but there is a point when popular feeling becomes outraged to such a degree that it demands life for life and the hand of justice cannot be stayed. A feeling is getting abroad that it is scarcely worth while to try criminals and burthen the counties with expense since the decisions of the court are set aside so constantly on small pretext. The courts must be respected more by the Governor if he would have the people respect order, otherwise Judge Lynch has only begun his work.—Independent Arkansian.

charles-stewart-bay-st-louis-1881-08-15.A1:
LYNCHING AT BAY ST. LOUIS.
Our Bay St. Louis correspondent has furnished us with an account of the lynching of the colored man Charles Stewart, at that place, last Monday night for the murder of his wife. Lynch law is a dangerous precedent, even where proof positive can be established, but much more so where the evidence is circumstantial, as we learn is the case in this instance. The man who was hung bore a very bad character, and it is asserted had killed a man sometime previously, but these facts do not justify the hanging of him without a fair and impartial trial, which he could have obtained before the circuit court at its next sitting.

If mob law is allowed to usurp the regular legal course of courts in a community there will be no security for law-abiding and peaceable citizens, for there would be no telling when any innocent man may be jerked up and swung into eternity; society will be demoralized, and good people will be forced to leave and never return. We learn that the best citizens of the Bay condemn this recent act of the lynchers, and will take steps to have the guilty ones indicted and punished, and will do all in their power to put down all such acts of violence. Certainly something ought to be done to put a stop to such illegal and revolutionary acts, and the sooner the people understand such proceedings will not be tolerated the better it will be for the community and society.

DIED. CAMPBELL—At Mississippi City, Miss. Thursday, August 11, 1881, William West- ley Campbell, aged 28 years 11 months, oldest child of Capt. Wm. and Johanna Campbell. MOBBED FOR MURDER. A Colored Man Hung at Bay St. Louis for the Supposed Murder of His Wife.
Charles Stewart, the negro who was jailed here on suspicion of killing his wife, was brought before Justice Sylvester on Monday and put under a bond of $1000 to appear at the circuit court for trial; failing to give such bond he was recommitted to prison, and placed under the protection of the officers of the law. The county prison is a sacred place, where the innocent and the guilty are under the protection of the laws, and when circumstances make it necessary it should be properly guarded.

During the investigation of this case before the Justice, it was shown that he was a man of intemperate habits and violent temper; that he had often whipped his wife, and perhaps had, on one occasion, threatened to kill her. It was evident that the witnesses were, in some instances, what the law books term "swift witnesses," and had made up their minds as to his guilt. There is a strong presumption that he really was guilty, but there was no positive proof, no eye witness of the bloody deed. Every one knows how deceptive circumstances are. God alone knows who committed the foul murder.

All day, 15th., a crowd of colored people was gathered in and around the courthouse, men and women, vowing vengeance. They took up a collection, bought a rope, and kept it on exhibition, declaring their intention to hang the prisoner. The only peace officer to be seen was Louis Paoli, constable. The day closed amidst this excitement. No guard was placed about the prison, and about midnight the mob hewed down the strong gates and doors of the jail, took the prisoner out and hung him. At a late hour on Tuesday his body still swings, a ghastly spectacle, to testify to the supremacy of MOB LAW at Bay St. Louis.

The same thing may occur again and again, unless sternly repressed by the next grand jury. Every man concerned, their aiders and abettors, is responsible for this man's life, to the laws of his country. Public opinion, here and elsewhere, demands a thorough investigation. Next time we shall hear of a white man being taken out of jail before trial, and hung by a negro or a white mob. Open the door for those violations of law and there is no longer security here for life and property.

A few weeks since a young white man shot a negro, as he claims, to save his own life. The friends of the wounded man were greatly excited, and openly proclaimed their intention, in case of his death, to lynch the assailant!

A difficulty occurred between two young Amherrian citizens and some Italians, in which the former got the worst. The Italians claimed to have acted in self defense and in defense of their employer, premises from a gross outrage, yet there was an organized excitement against them, no exertion of the law to protect them; and they have to fly for their lives.

How much such a state of thing will conduct to the prosperity of Bay St. Louis its citizens can determine for themselves.

PERSONAL AND GENERAL.
THE Boer Government has been formally proclaimed. It is to be known as the South African Republic.

MANY towns and villages in Western Prussia have recently suffered much from incendiary fires. The fact that the inhabitants are Jews leads to the conclusion that the incendiaries are Jew-haters. Anti-Jewish disturbances have again broken out in West Prussia and Pomerania.

THE Nebraska Supreme Court has rendered a decision that the high-license liquor law is constitutional in every particular. It compels saloon-keepers to pay $1,000 license, give bonds in the sum of $5,000, etc., in cities of over 10,000 people, and in cities of under 10,000 the license is $500.

THE large woolen-mills in Iowa belonging to the Amana Society, valued at $75,000, have been destroyed by fire.

THE Atlantic Flouring Mills at St. Louis were entirely destroyed by fire, caused by a lightning stroke, on the night of the 12th. The flames burst forth so quickly following the stroke, and spread so rapidly, that the men at work on the upper floors, a dozen or so in number, were completely hemmed in and were compelled to jump from the windows. All were severely burned and otherwise injured, and two of the unfortunates died during the night. It was feared that several perished in the flames. The mills were the largest in St. Louis, having a capacity of 1,200 barrels a day. They were owned by the Atlantic Milling Company, George Bain, President, and the total value of buildings, machinery and stock was estimated at about $250,000. Insurance from $75,000 to $100,000. The mills have been three times destroyed by fire. Considerable surrounding property was burned, the most important being the Future City Oil Works, valued at $25,000.

An express train on the Grand Trunk Railway was thrown from the track near Prescott, Ont., on the 13th, caused by the locomotive striking a cow. The locomotive and tender and express-car were overturned and completely demolished, and four passenger coaches were derailed. The engineer stuck to his locomotive and met a most horrible death. The fireman was pitched off by the concussion and badly injured. Two express messengers and a baggagemaster were buried beneath the debris of their car and rescued in an almost dying condition. Nine passengers were injured, six of them seriously.

THOMAS A. CRANDALL, a prominent Colorado stock dealer, fell from the top of a cattle train at St. Joseph, Mo., on the 13th, and was run over and killed.

E. M. MARKS, of Rome, Ga., and C. M. Creswell, of Mebanesville, N. C., students at Eastman's College, Poughkeepsie, N. Y., while boating on the Hudson River were run down by a steamer and both were drowned.

An emigrant train ran into a washout near Las Vegas, N. M., on the night of the 12th, killing engineer Townsend and fireman Patton.

By the sudden falling of an old building in one of the most frequented quarters of Vienna, on the 13th, twenty persons were killed and thirty injured.

CHARLES BOYNTON, a mill hand at Portland, Me., attempted to kill his wife, who had left him and gone to her mother's at Bar Mills. He fired at her with a revolver but missed, and she saved her life by jumping from a second story window. His wife's sister, Mrs. Waterhouse, then entered the room, when he fired two shots at her, one of which entered her breast inflicting a probably fatal wound. Boynton then shot himself through the pit of the stomach, expiring instantly.

MAXIMO JAREZ, the Minister from Nicaragua to the United States, died of apoplexy at Washington.

The drouth in Switzerland has continued for nearly two months. The grass is burned, and in the mountain pastures beasts are perishing from heat.

A band of cowboys recently attacked a caravan from Sonora on the way to Arizona, killed four of the party, and carried off $5,000 and the pack animals. The civil authorities in Arizona seem powerless, and the Mexicans hold the Americans responsible for the outrages.

Three negroes lay down on the railroad track near Tuscumbia, Ala., and fell asleep. A freight train came along and killed two of them and seriously injured the third.

JENNIE CRAMER, a beautiful New Haven (Conn.) girl, of poor and respectable parentage, recently came to her death in a mysterious manner, her body being found one morning on the beach near Kelsey's wharf. She was not drowned, as ascertained by the post mortem examination, and it is believed she was drugged. James Malley, son of a wealthy dry-goods merchant, was her frequent attendant, and was the last person seen in her company. He is under arrest.

JAMES NUTTER, a young farmer residing near Rushville, Ind., choked to death from a wheat-beard lodging in his throat.

At Newark, N. J., the other evening, a number of children were playing on the sidewalk, when the son of Leopold Graf, a wealthy shoe manufacturer, fired off a toy pistol. Stella Crane, aged eleven years, who stood near him, dropped to the sidewalk dead. Investigation showed a bullet hole in the corner of her right eye, the ball having penetrated her brain.

WILLIAM LEWELLEN, under arrest at North Vernon, Ind., charged with poisoning his wife, jumped from a second-story window while undergoing examination, and died of his injuries within three hours.

The excessive rainfall in Arizona has caused serious washouts on the Southern Pacific Railroad. The town of Maricopa is flooded.

A GREAT sensation has been caused at Lancaster, N. H., by the reported discovery that several deaths that occurred there last year, supposed to be from diptheria, were really caused by poison. Dr. Frank Bugbee and Mr. and Mrs. Towne, all well-known residents, were among the victims. Miss Nellie Webb, now Mrs. Mayo, lived with both families at the time the alarming mortality prevailed, and she is now under arrest. Mrs. Mayo has always borne

just arrived and report the presence of large numbers of savages there. Business is paralyzed and mining is in a great measure suspended.

Two men were instantly killed and two others badly mangled by a nitro-glycerine explosion at a mining camp 28 miles from Gunnison, Colorado.

The Apaches are reported to have swooped down upon a small Mexican village, eighteen miles from Rio Purca, a point on the Atlantic & Pacific Railroad, and murdered twenty-seven out of twenty-nine inhabitants. The two Mexicans who made good their escape were nearly exhausted when they reached the railroad, and had their horses shot under them before getting out of reach of the Indians.

INFORMATION has been received of a desperate duel fought in the Indian Nation between T. O. Carpenter, a Choctaw chief, and Col. Amos Price, a prominent citizen of the Creek Nation. Price was killed and Carpenter fatally wounded. Considerable feeling exists over the affair, as both were among the most prominent men in the Nation.

MRS. MORRIS EPLY, wife of a farmer near South Bend, Ind., aged 22, was bitten on the ankle by a rattlesnake while gathering corn. She received prompt medical attendance, notwithstanding which she only survived a few hours.

JOHN JENKINS, aged 60, a wealthy farmer residing near Mount Vernon, O., was set upon by an infuriated bull which he was leading to water, and so horribly gored that he lived but a few moments.

WILLIAM BROOKS, a well-to-do farmer residing near Shelby, N. C., attempted to shoot his wife, with whom he had quarreled, and not succeeding he went and hanged himself.

A PROMINENT physician of Cincinnati reports twenty well-defined cases of typhoid fever among the four hundred English colonists at Rugby, Tennessee. A corps of physicians and nurses have been dispatched to the afflicted settlement. Bad drinking water was the chief cause of the epidemic.

GOVERNOR PORTER declines to call an extra session of the Legislature of Indiana.

A BERLIN dispatch says it is feared Breslau will shortly be declared in a state of siege, because of the prevalence of social agitation there.

A farmer named D. Drue, living about eight miles from Nashville, Ill., was assassinated in his bed last Monday night.

A row between the whites and blacks of Morrilton, Ark., has led to several battles and a threat to burn the town.

Quite a number of citizens from Alabama have been out prospecting around Water Valley, during the past two or three weeks.

Meridian Homestead: The trial of the State vs. James M. Reason indicted for the murder of Lee Belk, which occurred in Dec. 1865, occupied three days of the present week. There were a great many witnesses for the State and the defence, and the prosecution was conducted by Hon. T. S. Ford, the District attorney, and the defense by Messrs Fewell, Evans, and Smith. The case was submitted to the jury late Wednesday evening, and a verdict of "not guilty", rendered Thursday morning.

The recent Bay St. Louis wife murder is, we learn, the second affair of the kind which has taken place there, as there was a similar case a year or two ago. A big black negro had a white wife, and murdered her, as was conclusively proved. He was jailed, and would have been hung; but his negro friends broke open the jail and helped him to escape.

Vicksburg Commercial: Rev. Dr. C. K. Marshall who sailed from New York on the sixth to attend the Ecumenical Conference of Methodism, which meets in London on September seventh, has arrived safely at Liverpool.
