Death of an Old Resident.
WATSONVILLE, August 25th.—Judge Thos. M. Davis, a resident of this vicinity for nearly thirty years, died here to-day. He was 71 years of age. For several years previous to this he held the office of Justice of the Peace of this township. He will be buried by the Masons and Odd Fellows. The latter Order he had been a member of for fifty years.

Narrow Escape of a Chinese Incendiary from Lynching.

STOCKTON, August 25th.—A Chinese boy, 11 years of age, was arranged in Court yesterday for setting fire to a stack of grain on the ranch of R. H. McCoy, on Roberts Island, last Tuesday. He was observed by a workman to place a piece of paper in the stack and then strike a match with which to light it. The match went out, and he tried another and met with better success. In an instant the flames ran up the side of the stack, and the boys struck out for the tules, where he hid himself. After much difficulty the fire was extinguished. The lad was captured and tied to the rack of a header-wagon by his cue, and had it not been for the interference of the women on the place he would have been strung up. His examination is set for Saturday.

cole-edwards-1881-08.A1: Deputy Sheriff Cornelius, of Issaquena county, while at Edwards on Tuesday with a warrant to arrest some fugitive negroes shot and killed a negro named Cole. Cornelius is in jail and the shooting is regarned as a great outrage.

RECORD OF CRIME.
James Mulligan, near St. Louis, stabbed and killed Wm. Hall, a negro.

Mrs. George W. Turner of St. Paul drowned herself last week. Insanity.

Dr. Thomas N. Cream, a noted abortionist in Chicago and other places, has been arrested.

Ruben A. Caidwell, a town pauper of Wilberham was killed by Morris Monahan. The murderer was arrested.

Last week Welch's feed windmill, at Marshall, Lyon county, was destroyed by fire, with a warehouse attached. Loss, $3,500: insurance, $2,000.

D. C. Cass, a carpenter of Witoka, Winona county, suicided by taking laudanum on Friday afternoon, his body being found in the barn of Mr. Beban, near Sugar Loaf.

A man named Hyde thought he had a mission to kill Governor Cornell of New York. He had an old unloaded gun on his shoulder and after avowing his intentions was arrested.

The store of P. C. Burke, at Garry Owen, sixteen miles from Dubuque, was broken into by burglars. The safe was blown open and a package containing $1,200 s'olen. Two horses were then stolen and the rascals rode to town.

W. R. Dickinson and Joel Van Arsdale, lawyers, of Philadelphia, were convicted of forging the will of R bert Whittaker, by which it was proposed to divert the estate, worth $800-000, to their own ends.

At Pittsburg, G. W. Nelson, land broker, D. L. South, stock broker, and a man named Miller were arrested recently for negotiating nearly $6,000 worth of stolen bonds, the property of William Connors of Catfish, Clarion county.

A special from Edwards, Miss., reports the killing of Henry Cole by Deputy Sheriff Cornelius of Isaquena county. Cornelius went to Edwards to arrest Cole and some other negroes for violating a contract with a planter up the Mississippi river.

Chas. Parker, a guide in the Adirondacks, while guiding Mrs. George Bull from Forked lake to Long lake, where she was to be the guest of ex-Senator Platt, made a dastardly assault on the woman. All the guides in the Adirondacks are hunting Parker, swearing to capture him dead or alive.

At Peoria, Ill., P. W. Crowe of infernal machine notoriety was arrested Monday by the United States authorities on an order from attorney General McVeagh. Crow disposed of his business here last week and was preparing to go through the country raising recruits for the Irish cause. Members of the leading Irish citizens gathered and bail to amount of $10,000 was tendered, the marehal simply replied to all inquiries that he could take no bail and that Crowe must go with him to Chicago. Crowe takes the affair very coolly.

Deputy United States Marshal-Garrins has brought into Denton, Texas under arrest James Tyler, charged with complicity in mail robberies committed by the notorious Sam Goss gang in 1878. He was arrested at Aloka, I. T. There are now but three of the Goss gang at large. Davis who was in the Union Pacific railroad robbery at Big Springs. Neb., and is now in New Orleans; Harry Underwood, the most desperate of the band, who is running a cattle ranch on the Pan Handle of Texas, and Frank Jackson, who is now in Arkansas.

At East Saginaw, Michigan, on Tuesday 19th, a fire caught and spread to Wylie Bros. mill premises, burning a barn, office and several hundred cords of wood, involving a loss of $8,000; partially insured. From there the fire spread to J. H. Pearson & Sons saw mill and Gault block, and in a short time the property consisting of saw mill, Harding house, store, seven tenement houses, 2,000 feet of tramway, 3,000 feet of docks and 4,500,000 feet of lumber thereon, were consumed. Total loss, $150,000; insurance about $75,000.

S. B. Jackson, sheriff of Woodbury county, Io., has gone to Sioux City in charge of a crook known as Capt. Jack, charge! with robbing the fur warehouse of O'Bern, Hosick & Co., at Sioux City, some four weeks ago. Sheriff Jackson has been on the fellow's track ever since the commission of the crime and overtook him at Fort Pierre several days ago, where he caused his arrest. Capt. Jack, the prisoner, has been operating in the west for ten years and is not unknown among Deadwood crooks. He is thirty. two years of age, short, dark complexion and weighs about 140 pounds.

INDEPENDENT candidates will have a hard road to travel in this county.

THE Meridan Homestead and Observer is soon to be issued tri-weekly.

THE Southern Humorist at Cor. intb, has been changed in form to a four-page six-column paper.

WILL the next legislature give our State good immigration laws. Such laws are necessary to the progress of the land.

WE have good quarantine laws, and there is little danger of yellow fever making its appearance upon the coast this season.

THE Augusta, Ga., Chronicle has discovered an obstinate Georgian who refuses to believe that President Garfield has been wounded, and says it is all a Yankee lie.

COL JOHN C. BURCH, secretary of the United States senate, died last Friday in Washington. His remains were taken to Nashville and interred in Mount Olivet cemetery.

DEPUTY SHERIFF CORNELIUS, who shot a negro at Edwards, Miss., a few days since, has been bound over in the sum of $1500 for his appearance before the circuit court of Hinds county.

NEXT Tuesday, the 9th, Gen. J. A. Smith, State superintendent of public education, will hold a teachers' institute at Mississippi City. All teachers in Harrison and adjoining counties are cordially invited to be present.

THE gauge of the Mississippi and Tennessee railroad running from Memphis to Grenada, one hundred miles, was changed last Saturday from five feet to four feet eight and one-half inches. The work was done in ten hours.

THE Wesson Telegram a sprightly six-column paper, published at Wesson, Miss., is a new candidate in the newspaper world. It is edited by Mr. E. T. Eaton, the well known newspaper correspondent whose nom de plume is "Pap." We wish the Telegraph success.

THE prohibition movement is spreading throughout our State. At the convention recently held in Jackson, it was decided, and very wisely too, not to bring politics into the matter, but let the question be made a separate issue.

THE New Orleans States of Wednesday says: " The subdivision of large plantations into small farms is progresing quite rapidly in some of the Southern States. In Mississippi there were 42,840 plantations in 1860, and the average number of acres in each was 370. Ten years later there were 68,023 farms, the average area of each being 193 acres. In 1830 the number of farms was 75,205, averaging 185 acres each.

LAST Monday Kentucky elected a state treasurer, nineteen senators and one hundred representatives, and in the Third district, composed of twenty-one counties, a judge of the court of appeals. The election, except in a few places, was a very quiet one, and a small vote was polled. Returns show immaterial republican gains in both senators and representatives. The last legislature stood; Senate, 34 democrats and 4 republicans; house, 80 democrats and 20 republicans and greenbackers. Exactly how the legislature elected Monday will stand it is impossible to say, but it will certainly be overwhelmingly democratic, and with a large majority favorable to the re-election of Mr. Beck to the United States senate.

A Colored Brute Fate.
ANTA. Dec. 18. On Monday.
A Colored Brute's Fate.
ATLANTA, Dec. 18.—On Monday night Dave Bumpers, colored, eighteen years old, entered the house of Mrs. Driscoll at Athens, Ga., during the absence of her husband, and assaulted her in a brutal manner. The miscreant was captured Friday night while asleep in a cotton house. He was tried and sent to jail. A mob, however, took him from the officers who had him in charge, and hanged him to an oak tree with a plow line till he was dead.

The Hinesville Gazette hears of considerable complaint about labor on the farms in Liberty county. It says: "Farmers find it difficult to contract for the year with hands to do regular farm work. The colored people are ambitions to secure farms of their own, or else they think that turpentine or mill men pay better prices. Others are engaged in timber, and it is useless to talk to them about farm work."

The Griffin Sun thinks that, in the absence of fractional paper currency, it would be a good idea for the government to issue, for transmission through the mail's, money postal cards, redeemable at all money order post offices at their face value, less one cent. The idea was suggested to the Sun because it wanted to send ten cents to a man to help him build a church, and it thinks an eleven cent postal card would just fill the bill.

The Carneville Register chronicles a sad accident, which happened to the two little children of Mr. John Miller, of Franklin county, last week. While playing around a pot of boiling water it was by some means turned over, and the two children were badly scalded. One of them, that paper learns, has died from the injuries received, and the other is seriously, if not fatally, burned, and hope for its recovery is said to be doubtful.

The Arlington Advance announces the death of Colonel F. L. Pepper, of that place. He was one of the first settlers of Arlington, was a genial highly esteemed and useful citizen, and had filled with great satisfaction many offices of public trust and honor. His funeral took place on Sunday, when he was buried with Masonic honors.

On Saturday morning last the train on the Selma, Rome and Dalton Railroad, coming north from Selma, jumped the track at Germania, Alabama. Three cars were thrown from the track and the road-bed was considerably torn up. No one was seriously hurt. The Rome Courier says: "When the new management of this road puts down its steel rails we hope these run-offs of freight trains will not be of such frequent occurrence."

Since Atlanta has been made a port of entry, Griffin wants to be one too, but the Pike County News thinks that Barnesville's claims for that honor are superior to those of either of the other cities.

With favorable weather the Gwinnett Herald hopes that Lawrenceville will greet her first railroad train in about three weeks. The Herald thinks that the arrival of that train will mark a new epoch in the history of the town.

The Pike County News rubs salt on a raw wound by saying Dr. W. H. Felton and General U. S. Grant will both be on the retired list after March 4th.

The Americus Recorder states that in Macon county, Mrs. Senter, an old lady over one hundred years of age, caught fire a few days ago, and was burned to death. She was so old and childish that her daughter, with whom she lived, had to tie her to keep her from the dames. It is supposed she fell, and her dress caught fire. The above facts are detailed by Dr. Jones, the family physician.

Doc. Wilson, a negro barber in Macon, shot through the heart and killed instantly Mr. James Tinley on Monday night. The murderer made his escape. His friends claim that Tinley drew a knife on him, but Mr. Tinley's friends state that he was a quiet, steady, peaceable man, and did not possess or carry a knife. Wilson comes from a bad stock and his family, according to the Telegraph and Messenger, has made itself conspicuous in that community during the past three years. One of the brothers was killed by Alex. Stone with an umbrella last year; another, Eugene, was tried for the burning of the Brown House, and a sister was suing for a divorce (Hays vs. Hays) when the main witness dropped dead in the court house last week. And now comes the only remaining brother in the connection just described.

Hinesville Gazette: "Mr. L. B. Norman, an energetic young farmer in this locality, who raised a quantity of the celebrated golden hull rice has sold out all he had on hand to General Lebuc, United States Commissioner of Agriculture. General LeDuc was so well pleased with the samples of the rice which he saw on his recent visit to this county that he at once engaged Mr. N.'s entire crop. His object is of course to distribute it over the country where rice is planted."

The Greinnett Herald mentions a narrow escape from a terrible death, as follows: "During the recent cold weather Mr. James Green, who lives near Centreville, in this country, had been out hunting, and, returned home, was building a fire in his residence. He had an old-fashioned powder horn containing about half a pound of powder. By some means, the stopper had come out, and, as he bent over to put the wood on the fire, the powder commenced pouring out into the blaze. The powder caught at once and rapidly run up to the horn, exploding it, badly burning him and one or two of his children. It was very令人震惊 that the explosion did no more damage."

The following remarkable deer tale is published by the Blackshear News. It says: "Mr. S. Wooll of this place, tells the following deer tale, and says it is perfectly true: Last Friday, as he was crossing the Alapsa river up at the Sweat bridge, he heard dogs trailing up the swamp as though they were running a deer. He hastened across, and before going many paces he heard the deer, as he supposed to swim it. Mr. S. hastened down to the drought to get ahead of the deer, which he did not succeed. The deer took no notice of Mr. Wooll it had fully obtained ground, when it turned upon Mr. S. for a combat, which came near being a serious one to him. However, he succeeded in getting it by the horns, being a seven snag buck, and held it until the hunters came up and cut its throat."

The matter has been kept secret, as it was feared any publicity might put the soundnels on guard. It seems that Caldwell was walking along the road in Forrestville, near the Rome Railroad shanties, when he set upon by three men, two of whom Caldwell, however, in the struggle, managed to take his knife, cutting two of his assailants, when they all released him and disappeared. The woman living in the neighborhood says that she men stopped at her house about that time who was bleeding at the hands. If true, as it appears this is one of the holdings of the country where rice is planted."

MACON, GA., February 10.—The Macon and Augu-ta railroad bridge over the Oemulgee river at this point was washed away yesterday—the second time within thirty days.

One hundred dollars reward is offered for the arrest of Doe. Wilson (colored), who murdered James Finley on Monday night. Finley entered his bar-room and was shot down by Wilson from behind the counter. Wilson is a light mulatto, with light-gray eyes; is of medium height, and about twenty years of age.

We announced yesterday that Mr. Frank J. Cohen, editor and proprietor of the Rome Bulletin, had decided to abandon the daily and issue only the Sunday Bulletin, because he did not believe that Rome could support three dailies. In Wednesday's issue of that paper Mr. Cohen announces that he has sold the paper to Mr. Andrew Moseley, who will continue the daily and weekly as heretofore.

A young Roman found himself in a very embarrassing predicament the other night. It was the time appointed for his marriage, and when the hour came he was laid up with a case of mumps. The Courier does not say whether the affair was postponed or not.

The Fort Gaines Tribune reports that the nice weather which prevailed in that section for ten days or more was interrupted by a rain Monday night, which continued through Tuesday, Tuesday night and Wednesday. The roads had just become passable, and farmers were busy preparing for another crop. The excessive wet weather, however, has given them a backset, and farm work of all kinds is at a standstill.

Work will be inaugurated on the Rome and Chattanooga Railroad within the next sixty days.

Robins are so thick in Burke county that on Sundays a negro man of Waynesboro amuses himself by catching them with fishing-hooks. He baits the hook and throws his line over the limb of the tree on which the birds most do congregate, and waits for them to bite. He caught twenty five in this way last Sunday.

On the 11th inst. Hon. A. H. Stephens was sixty-nine years old. The Harlem Advertiser hopes he may live to be exactly one hundred and thirty-eight.

We see it gravely stated that the "funeral directors" of Georgia will hold a convention in Atlanta on the 4th day of next May. All undertakers are solemnly invited to meet with them.

Dr. J. B. Hendrick, one of the oldest and best citizens of Covington, and for more than forty-five years a practising physician of that place, is dead.

Mrs. George J. Johnston, widow of the Atlanta bill poster who killed himself with opium a few nights since, announces her intention of removing from Montgomery, Alabama, to Atlanta, to carry on the business established by her late husband.

The recent high waters washed away about thirty feet of the dam of the City Mills of Columbus. This accident will cause the mills to cease operations for three or four months, and will involve the proprietors in serious loss, besides throwing several persons out of employment.

The Athens Banner is to be enlarged and improved in a few days.

According to the Marietta Journal the farmers of that section will have to buy largely of corn and bacon to run their farms for the coming season. It thinks this is certainly a bad way to farm.

Four hundred and fifty dollars reward has been offered for the arrest of Doc Wilson, the negro murderer of Mr. James Tinley in Macon. Of this the Mayor of Macon offers one hundred dollars, Mr. J. J. Tinley two hundred and fifty dollars, and Governor Colquitt one hundred dollars.

On Wednesday last Rev. Augustus Watson, colored, pastor of Mount Zion Church, Atlanta, was arrested on a warrant charging him with Beecherism. His congregation have always regarded him as above guile, and are greatly shocked at the developments.

The Covington Star says that "Mr. John Swann, of Henry county, was instantly killed on the 2d inst. by falling out of a tree. He was engaged in trimming up old field pines by climbing up and cutting off the limbs. After climbing up one about seventy-five or eighty feet, cutting off the limbs, and was coming down, he lost his hold in some way, and fell to the ground, a distance of about sixty feet, breaking his neck, back, arm and knee. He left a wife and two children."
Albany News and Advertiser: "We hear it rumored that a murder was committed in Lee county on the 10th, under the following circumstances: A Mr. Ledbetter went out fishing with another white man and a negro at a millpond about fifteen miles from Leesburg. All returned on time except Ledbetter. Foul play was suspected, and search was instituted without delay. Nothing could be heard of the missing man. Finally the pond was drained, when he was found with his throat cut. We learned no further particulars."

Says the Americus Sumter Republican: "Three years ago a young couple of Sumter county were engaged to be married. The day was set, license bought, the guests invited and a Justice of the Peace on hand to tie the knot, but true love sometimes has 'ketches and kinks' that mars the smoothness of its course It was so in this case. The bride elect smelt liquor on the breath of her lover, and broke with him then and there. To propitiate the assembled friends, two other lovers arose and were married. The young man rejected left the country and the State. A short while back he returned, found his loved one true to her old love, awaiting his return in a sober and manly condition, renewed his proposals, and the two were united at the Barlow House in this city on the tenth of this month."

Rome Courrier: "We had the pleasure of a call recently from Mr. J. W. Amberson, of Murphrey's Valley, Blount county, Ala. Mr. Amberson informs us that his father, Mr. J. D. Amberson, brought to Rome and sold the first bale of cotton ever sold in Rome as a market for the staple. He was then living at Spring Garden, Ala., and the cotton was taken at gin weight, there being no scales then in the little town for weighing cotton. The senior Mr. Amberson is still an active business man, being now one of the firm of Amberson & Son, at Murphrey's Valley. It is quite a commentary on the growth of the cotton trade of Rome that the gent eman who 'opened the market' is now living to see Rome's cotton receipts over a hundred thousand bales a year, with scales and balances and compresses all over town."

Says the Walker County Messenger: "The Messenger has lost a subscriber. On Wednesday of last week the wife of Tom Allen, a colored man in the town district, went to one of our citizens for whom Tom worked and got a dollar to buy some meat. When Tom came home at night and found what she had done he was very angry, and getting his gun, threatened to shoot her. A couple of colored men, who came in and stayed all night, kept the difficulty down. After they left in the house, the wife took the gun off from the house, and, after firing it off, bid it. This started matters afresh. Tom, in his rage, threw the chairs out of the house and began cutting them up with an axe. The Macon Herald tells of a romantic and sensational wedding which took place at Fort Valley on Sunday evening last, by which an expectant bridegroom found himself cut out of his bride-elect forever. "It seems." says that paper, "that one of the most beautiful and charming young ladies of Americus was engaged to be married to a certain young man of great wealth and high social standing, also of Americus, and all the preliminary arrangements for the happy event had been stilled and the affair was to have taken place this evening. The young lady, after having made her final visit to Macon for the purpose of completing her bridal outfit, stopped over at Fort Valley on her return to Americus, ostensibly for the purpose of visiting a young lady friend, but it turns out that before leaving Americus she had consented and arranged to give her heart and hand to another young man of equally good social standing and business qualifications, provide

Joseph Mize, Sheriff of Sumter county, lost $20 by an incendiary fire on Wednesday. His corn crib, its contents, and two stacks of fodder were consumed.

A large piece of a needle and a piece of thread were recently extracted from the foot of Dr. J. W. Ansley, of Buena Vista.

The Athens Banner says Andy Brown, colored in cutting up a turkey recently, found a dime in its glizzard.

The Pioneer Hook with Hope Company No. 1, are to hold a grand firemen's tournament in Athens May 18th and 19th. Funds for the display are now being raised.

In noticing Mr. Theodore J. Elmore's recent publication, the Christian Index, of Atlanta, says: "Family Memorials' is an e'egant volume of three hundred and fifty pages, printed on cream laid paper, and illustrated with a portrait of the a thor, and a picture of the old family homestead at St. Charles, Illinois. The binding is purple and gold, and the whole publication reflects the highest credit on the MORNING News Steam Printing Establishment, of Savannah.

The Darien Timber Gazette says: "The Southern Farmer's Monthly, Savannah, for February, came duly to hand. This is unquestionably the best publication of the kind published in this country.

Crowds gathered all along the line of the Atlantic and Western Railroad to catch a glimpse of the Bernhardt.

We learn from the Thomasville Times that Judge Hopkins, together with Mr. Mason of Philadelphia, and two gentlemen from Minnesota, recently bagged two hundred and fourteen quail in one day's shooting on the Monticello road. The Times states that the shooting has been and is remarkably enjoying fine, and many Northern visitors are enjoying it.

The State Agricultural Society will meet in Thomasville on Tuesday next. Col. Robert G. Mitchell, on behalf of the citizens, will deliver an address of we come. The Thomas County Stock Breeders' Association was formed on Tuesday. It is hoped that if it proves successful much capital diverted from the county will be retained there.

Friend Grubb thinks it is a shame that the port of Darien is always neglected in the matter of appropriations. He says that no port in America needs an appropriation as much as that one.

The Albany Advertiser says that farming operations have been unusually active in that section during the past week or two. The fine weather recently enjoyed has been most propitious for work of all kinds on the farm, and the absence of the farmers and laborers from Albany indicates that they have been improving each shining hour.

A special to the Columbus Times, from Newnan, states that on Thursday last a terrible accident occurred at Hogansville to W. H. Malone, a brakeman. He was between the cars coupling when he stepped into a stock gap. His left hand was cut off just above the joint. The train passed over his right arm, tearing it off. He is not expected to live.

Mr. D. B. Hack, a prominent citizen and manufacturer, of Augusta, is dead.

The Macon Telegraph understands that the friends of Doc. Wilson, the murderer of Mr. Tauley, say they would be willing to bring him to a trial six months hence, but not at the present time in the height of the excitement and prejudice against him. It is to be hoped the authorities will not consult Doc's friends in this matter, but will see that he is captured and brought to trial speedily, whether they are willing or not.

Judge Warner is still seriously sick. It is believed that his illness is the result of an attack of broken bone fever, which contracted some two months ago.

The Covington Enterprise states that last Friday night week at a negro frolic, in Newton county a general difficulty occurred among this fun-loving people. In the melee a colored baby was brained, and immediately gave up the ghost. The matter was brought before
The Swainsboro Herald says that the farmers of Emanuel county will probably be late in starting their crops, as the land is so boggy that they cannot plough. It will be some time yet before they can begin to break up corn ground.

The following are the Darlen Gazette's timber quotations for last week: Square—600 average, $6@6 75; 700 average, $7@7 75; 800 average, $7@8 90; 9.0 average, $9@10; 1,000 average, $10@11; 1,100 average, $11@12 25; 1,200 average, $12@13 25. Scab—300 average, $750@8; 400 average, $8@10; 500 average, $10@12 50; 600 average, $12@13 50.

Swainsboro Herald: "Cows and sheep continue to die. Emanuel probably has never sustained such a loss in live stock. Lambs are dying very rapidly, or rather they are nearly all dead."

From the Athens Banner we learn that work was begun on the University campus improvement on Wednesday. It will be plowed, barrowed and fertilized, and the dead and deformed trees will be removed. The improvement is due to the generosity of P. J. Berckmans, the August florist, who is superintending it.

In speaking of the new serial, "Vascoe," appearing in the WEEKLY NENS, the Thomasville Southern Enterprise says: "Cooner Estill deserves great credit for his uniting efforts to develop the native talent of the South and give to Southern readers a literature that has nothing of ridicule or abuse of the Southern people in t. May his efforts meet with even greater success than in the past."

The Thomasville Times states that the grocery store of J. C. Peters, and his wife's millinery store adjoining, on South Broad street, Thomasville, were destroyed by fire on Tuesday night. The firemen by desperate efforts confined the flames to the doomed buildings, and thus prevented a serious conflagration. The burned property was fully insured. The guests of the Mitchell House lined the verandahs and windows of the hotel, and watched with interest the labors of the firemen.

Atlanta Post Appeal: "The last issue of Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper contains a photograph of Col J. H. Estill, proprietor of the Savannah News, the photograph being furnished by Horace Brailey. The cut is said to be a strikingly appropriate likeness of Col Estill, and it is highly appropriate that Leslie should give the world the features of the proprietor of the best daily newspaper in the South. For the Savannah News is by far the best daily in the south."

Cochran Enterprise: "Mr. L. [Sirmion] attempted to cross the railroad track ahead of an engine near the depot on Tuesday, and was knocked some ten or twelve feet ahead by the cowcatcher, and was thrown across the switch bed sill, and was considerably and painfully scratched and bruised, and had a portion of the middle finger on his left hand cut off by a car wheel. It is wonderful that he was not killed. The amount of internal injury has not yet been determined. He blames himself altogether."

Atlanta Phonograph: "Yesterday morning at a dance of rather a questionable character, held at Wolf's beer garden, near this city, John Parks, of Atlanta, was shot by Henry Brown, of Nashville, who is in the city on a visit. Mr. Parks was shot with a pistol, the ball entering his face and coming out at the side. The wound, although quite painful, is not at all serious. Mr. Parks was on the streets yesterday attending to his business. Mr. Brown was arrested by Sneriff Perkerson, but was afterwards released at the request of Mr. Parks, who gave it as his opinion that the shooting was accidental. We have not been able to learn of the manner in which the shooting occurred, as no one acquainted with the particulars seemed willing to say much about it."

Darien Gazette: "During the past week about four hundred rafts came down, measuring eight million feet of scab and square timber. Scab is in good demand and bringing high prices. The reported rise in the river may curtail supplies for ten days. Timber has been coming down pretty freely during the past ten days, but we are sorry to state that a great deal of it was of poor manufacture and badly gotten out. Much of the square timber was

Georgia Affairs.
The *Faltimorean* of last week published the well known poem written by General Henry R. Jackson, of Savannah, during the Mexican war, entitled "My Wife and Child," and credited its authorship to Gen. Stonewall Jackson.

Mr. J. F. Cummings, of Atlanta, Vice-President of the Atlanta and Alabama Railroad, says he has the highest opinion of General Gordon, but doesn't believe he will be able to build the Georgia Western Road. He thinks the charter of that road has been bottled up by its sale to General Gordon.

On Monday morning last two freight trains on the Western and Atlantic Railroad came in collision near Tunnel Hill. We learn from the Atlanta Post-Appeal that the accident was occasioned by a failure of the train going North to obey instruction. Train No. 13, John Chester, engineer, was ordered to wait at Dalton until No. 12, John Webb, engineer, should pass. By some mistake, or cause unexplained, No. 13 failed to obey instructions and passed on. No. 12 had passed Tunnel Hill, and met No. 13 a short distance on. The two were close together before they discovered each other, when every effort was made to stop, but without avail. The two engines came together with a crash, and made a general wreck. William Jones, fireman on No. 12, was instantly killed. Ben Yancy, fireman on No 13, was mortally wounded.

While the Macon train was at Smithville last Sunday, suddenly the report of a pistol was heard, and a bullet came whizzing through the back of a seat occupied by a lady, narrowly missing her. The excitement was very great, and it was finally ascertained that the weapon had fallen from the pocket of a traveler, and the fall had caused the explosion. The passenger explained his possession of the pistol by saying that he frequently traveled with large sums of money about him, and the weapon was necessary to his proper self-protection.

We learn from the Macon Telegraph that Doc. Wilson, the slayer of Mr. Tinley, was captured by Sheriff Thebald, of Chattahoochee county, in the town of Apalachicola, Florida, just as he (Doc.) was on the eve of embarking on a lumber vessel bound for Boston. He was placed on a boat plying between Apalachicola and Columbus, Ga., heavily ironed and well guarded. When the boat touched at Bainbridge Mayor Corput was telegraphed the above and additional facts by the Mayor of Bainbridge and others. Sheriff Wescott, of Bibb, Chief of Police John Hurley, and Solicitor General Hardeman left Monday night for Columbus, and Doc. is now in their hands. He will be taken to Atlanta and confined in the jail of that town for safe keeping.

The Thomasville Enterprise reports two cases of severe, and perhaps fatal, burning of children this week. One was that of a young son of Mr. L. A. H. h., who was so badly burned that it was thought he could not survive more than two days. The other was that of a little colored child on Mr. Frank Winn's place, Thomas county, who was burned while all hands on the place were fighting fire. It is stated that the little one wandered out, and being too small to take care of itself, got surrounded by the fire, and was severely injured before succor came.

The Reidsville Enterprise says: "We passed though the lower portion of the county a few days ago, and found the farmers all busy at work preparing for the coming crop. Many have already planted corn, and are now preparing land for cotton, upland rice, etc. Rice is quite an important crop to many of the Tatnall county farmers."

The Milledgeville Recorder reports that Mr. Luke Robinson, an aged citizen of Faldwin county, was killed on Thursday last by an accident. The steers he was driving ran away, and the old man was thrown out of his wagon and killed.

Athens is greatly enthused over the approaching fireman's tournament in that city.

The Montezuma Weekly says a good many colored people in Dooy are on the high road to prosperity. It knows of ten in one vicinity who own nearly four thousand acres of land, all paid for.

The Montezima Weekly states that the farmers of that county have laid aside all despondent thoughts of the future and have gone to work in earnest. They intend to harvest a good crop this year if a favorable season is given them.

The Newnan Herald reports that as the outward bound freight and passenger train was moving out from Puckett's Station, six miles below Newnan, Wednesday night of last week, a rock was thrown into a window of the passenger car, crushing the glass and shutters. The Herald says: "It was a flint-rock, containing about thirty-two square inches, and, coming with the force it evidently did, would have certainly given the headache to the gentleman sitting by the next window had it chanced that way. The conductor was at a loss to account for the spiteful fling, as he knows of no one in the neighborhood who has any grudge against the road or its officials."

According to the Swainsboro Herald, a plan is being set on foot to set up a telegraph line from Swainsboro to Wadley. It is estimated that it will cost about six hundred dollars. That paper thinks that parties buying stock in this line will be making good investments.

Mr. Joseph S. Bean has retired from the editorship of the Augusta Sunday Mirror. He is succeeded by Mr. Tracy J. Hickman.

"H. W. G." writes from New York that he is willing to bet the next Gubernatorial race in Georgia will be between Felton and Blount, and that he knows that General Gordon could not be prevailed upon to accept the Governorship or any other office.

The Augusta Chronicle says peddling has become a nuisance in that city. It wants the practice put an end to. It thinks peddlers of all descriptions (including book agents, of course.) should be made to pay a license of at least one hundred dollars.

Augusta Chronicle: "Mr. George Cornwall, of New York, who went up to the Magruder Mine with Major George T. Jackson and party, last Thursday, and remained, after they left, for the purpose of examining the mine, returned yesterday afternoon. Mr. Cornwall is having been in Colorado four months in mining operations. He is a

The Augusta Chronicle and Constitutionalist chronicles the following sad occurrence in that city: "We learn that on Saturday morning last, Mrs. John Jones, living some eight miles west of Augusta, having occasion to come to the city, left her youngest child, aged about two years, in the care of a neighbor. After the mother left, it appears the child eluded the vigilance of the person in whose care it was placed, and wandered off in the woods. As soon as missed search was immediately instituted, but all efforts to find it were unavailing until Sunday morning, when it was found some distance from home in a small creek, in a sitting position, with its head resting on the bank of the creek, dead. It is supposed that the little thing died of exhaustion and exposure."

Newnan Herald: "Mention was made last week of a rock thrown into a car window on the Atlanta and West Point Road. A few days afterward Detective Hilderbrand was put on track of the criminal, and very soon caught up with Allen Hogan, a colored man, who proved to be the guilty party. Having been put off the train a short time before, while stealing a ride, he thought to take out a petty spite in the manner described. Having been arrested by the detective, he somehow managed to effect his escape, but was afterwards re-arrested, and is now in Coweta jail, awaiting his trial."

The Augusta News says: "The first engine that ever crossed over the Augusta canal made the trip yesterday on the Augusta and Knoxville Road. The new bridge, about four miles from town, is completed, and the track laid beyond the canal. A party composed of Mr. W. T. Wheless, Mr. H. P. Moore and other friends of the road, accompanied Captain Twiggs on the first trip across the canal yesterday. Quite a large party was on the programme, but several were left, not knowing the schedule."

The Dalton Citizen advises its farmer readers to "go slow on cotton and raise a surplus of hog and hominy." It says: "We greatly fear the cotton success in this and adjoining counties last year will operate to the disadvantage of our people—the farmers especially, many of whom have gone wild upon the subject of cotton planting and are preparing to put in more ground this year in the fleecy staple than ever before. It is well enough for our farmers to grow some cotton, but it will be ruinous to the farmer, especially the small planter, who fails to make a sufficiency of 'hog and hominy' for home consumption, just what many of them failed to do last year, judging from the quantity of meat, flour and other necessities of life that have been bought
hog and hominy' for home consumption, just what many of them failed to do last year, judging from the quantity of meat, flour and other necessities of life that have been bought in this market by the country people this winter for their own use. Cotton is a good thing to raise—there is ready money in it; but when it is grown to the neglect of the productions of wheat, corn, potatoes, etc., and the raising of cattle and hogs, it will react disastrously to the farmer sooner or later, who thus unwisely cultivates his land."

The Hawkinsville Dispatch mentions a case of attempted assassination as follows: "Tim Rowland, a young white man of this county, was brought up to Cochran on Saturday morning last by the up train on the Macon and Brunswick Railroad. Young Rowland was shot the night before near Graham station, No. 8, while walking along the railroad. Two men, concealed from view, arose immediately in front of him and both fired upon him with pistols. One ball pierced his clothing and the other ball struck him in the chest, and made a painful wound, and one which came near causing death. After receiving his wound, young Rowland walked to the station, and was brought up to Cochran next morning, and his wound was examined and dressed by Dr. Thomas D. Walker and Dr. S. L. Richardson. The wounded young man is a son of Mr. James Rowland, who lives a few miles below Cochran, in this county."

Macon Telegraph: "We understand that Doc. Wilson says he ran out the front door of Savage's barber shop on the night of the shooting and went across to the jail and rang the bell, for the purpose of giving himself up into the hands of the law, but receiving no response, and seeing the large and excited crowd gathering at the scene of the homicide, he became alarmed and concluded to seek safety. He went first to the house of his sweetheart, and finding that guarded by police, he then took himself to the cemetery. His subsequent course we have already described."

Atlanta Constitution: "By the Western and Atlantic passenger train there arrived in Atlanta last night W. Head, a prominent colored citizen of Americus. Head was a slave of Dr. Head, a rich Georgian, but when the war closed he began shifting for himself, and to-day is the owner of several thousand dollars worth of real estate. He is just back from an extended tour of the North, and last night stated to a Constitution reporter that he was thoroughly convinced that that section of the Union is no place for his race. He comes home thoroughly satisfied that the South is the colored man's home."

Says the Walton County News: "Two weeks since we noted the extraordinary size and height of a Murray county youth of the age of eighteen years. Murray challenged the production of a greater, and here are two. We have the figures and facts from the best authority, and we now in behalf of Walton challenge the State. There are two young men in this county, each of whom are eighteen years of age, whose combined height is 12 feet 11 inches—one being 6 feet 3 inches, and the other 6 feet 8 inches—and whose combined weight is 388 pounds—one weighing 196 pounds and the other 192. It certainly is a good county that can grow such boys."

"Some months ago," says the Warrenton Clipper, "Mr. Thomas Ivey's little boy, about two years of age, fell and one of his eye teeth was driven back into the gums, out of sight. The little fellow had a mouth full of teeth besides, and the parents thought the vacant place was made by the tooth being knocked out. The face became swollen, and the eye above became seriously affected. In a few weeks the eye tooth began to reappear, and has since come back in full, only it is some what shorter than the others. The eye is said by some who have examined it to be entirely sightless. Mr. Ivey lives in the neighborhood of Brier Creek Church, in this county, and is extensively connected throughout the county."

The Warrenton Clipper says all Georgians who wish to go to Texas should ponder this: "We know personally a young Baptist minister who went to T. with his family a year or so ago, and when in the State he purchased a horse. It turned out the horse was stolen, and being found in the hands of our young friend, and he not being able to prove himself clear of the theft, was convicted and sentenced for several years to the chain gang. A hotel proprietor and others, who deeply sympathized with the unfortunate young clergyman, and fully believing him innocent, immediately secured his services from the State to drum custom for his establishment. The young wife and children had to return with a downcast heart to Georgia. It does seem that the Baptists of Texas should look into this piece of severity on the part of their State's laws and see if something cannot be done. We believe he is in Houston, Texas, at this time and thus cruelly separated from his young family."

Reidsville Enterprise: "We have been informed by Dr. J. B. Rogers that Darkus Smith, a colored woman, living near his place, was terribly burned last Monday afternoon. From everything that can be gathered, the woman had evidently dropped asleep in front of the fire, and her clothing ignited and were burning rapidly when the flames, were discover ed. She made every effort to extinguish the flames, but a

Georgia Affairs.
The News is indebted to the Glynn County Agricultural Society, for a season ticket for the annual fair of the association.

The Augusta Chronicle states that the directors of the Sibley Manufacturing Company have fixed the capital stock of the company at $800,000. Of this all but $27,600 has been subscribed for, and this will undoubtedly be taken in a day or two, as several letters making inquiries in regard to the stock have been received from the North. More work was done on the buildings last month than during the entire winter, and the progress made last week was especially satisfactory.

Speaking of the prospects of the Georgia Western Railroad the Constitution quotes Mr. C. H. Phinizy, of the Georgia Road, as saying: "The road will certainly be built. I am myself interested largely in the road, and have been in New York with Mr. Gordon. I know the plans under which it is organized and do not hesitate to say that it will certainly be built."

The notorious Bill Taylor, while en route for Bufaula from Dawson, whence he was extra-fied, escaped from his custodian, and has thus far avoided recapture.

The dwelling on the plantation of Mr. W. O. Holden, at the fifty-three mile post on the Georgia Railroad, was destroyed by fire on Saturday. The fire was first discovered in the waterroom. The furniture, clothing and nearly all the provisions of the tenant occupying it were consumed.

The Sylvania Telephone reports that a negro in the lower part of Scriven county was bitten by a rattlesnake a few days since. Owing to the prompt attention of Dr. A. B. Lanier his life was saved. One of the fangs of the snake was broken of in the darkey's foot and had to be cut out.

The Rome Courier says that there are one hundred and fifty two thousand tons of fertilizers sold in Georgia every year. On this the farmers pay a tax of fifty cents per ton for inspection, amounting to $76,000. The Albany News and Advertiser reports that Charlotte Lonon, wife of Brown Lonon, and the mother of Ishmael Lonon, the colored member of the Legislature from this county, died very suddenly at her home, on the northern suburbs of the city, on Friday. The store house of Mr. J. T. Castleberry, in Monroe county, was broken into at night not long since, and goods to the amount of seventy-five dollars taken therefrom. Entrance was gained by boring into the shutters of a rear window. No clue, as yet, to the guilty parties.

He suffered untold to tears until Friday, when death came and relieved him of all pain.

Macon, November 25. — Editor Morning News: Winter has put in an appearance at last, and many confined their thanksgiving to this one topic on yesterday. We are commanded “in everything to give thanks,” and remember even in misfortune that it might have been worse. Many claim, however, that they have very little for which they can give thanks. The day was observed largely by business men in the front part of their establishments, while in the rear the employees were busily engaged. Many churches were opened, but comparatively few, even of church goers, were present. The exercises were impressive, and would have proved beneficial to the multitude who stayed away. Hundreds of turkeys were consumed by the fortunate, while the impeccable were content with sausage and spare rib. The day was bright, but the temperature was depressed and the wind searching. The rich moved about muffled in their great coats and wraps, while the poor supplied the lack of these things by a brisker walk and a more vigorous circulation. Altogether it was a good day.

Our Superior Court is taking a week’s holiday while Judge Simmons occupies a chair on the Supreme Court bench in Atlanta. It will reopen on Monday next and continue until Christmas. Doe Wilson, a rego barber, who killed young Tinley last winter and was captured in Florida as he was taking ship for Boston, will be tried for murder on December 12th. This murder has created more feeling in the community than any case now before the court. Several other murder cases will come up for trial.

Prof. B. M. Zettler, the Superintendent of our public schools, and once a teacher in the Savannah schools, tendered his resignation to the Board of Education, to take effect on January 1st, 1882. The board, however, declined to accept it, and induced him to withdraw it by increasing his salary $20. Financial support was the only cause assigned for his retirement. His retention is gratifying to the patrons of the schools. He has been a faithful, earnest worker, and with the material in hand he has worked the system admirably.

The boarding houses are gradually filling up with Northern visitors, and the hotels are well patronized by those who tarry only a short time and go further South. An immense travel is anticipated, and Macon hopes to attract her share of it.

The rush to Atlanta in consequence of the "one cent fare" seems unabated. In this blessing Macon is left out in the cold—at least left out until cold weather comes, when nobody will want to go. The authorities of the road, however, receive their blessings every day in consequence thereof, and this reminds us of the darky in a restaurant, who brought a fastidious boarder an outside cut of roast beef, who furiously resented the insult, when the darky, with arms akimbo, exclaimed: "Now, looky here, Boss, somebody's got to have the outside piece and it must as well be you as anybody." Somebody had to have the "cold run," and it might as well be Macon as anybody else. Nevertheless, many Maconites took advantage last week of the Southwestern excursion, and sent out ten or twelve miles and bought tickets, costing only about a quarter more than it will from Macon during the latter part of December. Even with all these advantages your correspondent has not been able to reach Atlanta yet.

I have recently paid a vif it to the farm of Mr. I. C. Plant, of which I spoke in my last. He only has been in possession this year, and what a wondrous change. He has placed a wire fence around the whole tract—140 acres. Most of this is cleared and under cultivation. Aside from his Bermuda grass meadow of 40 acres, he has raised a good crop of corn, interlaced with pumpkins and kershaws, almost covering the entire ground. Independent of all this he has one large two-story barn literally crammed with pea vine hay from top to bottom. His second barn is filled with Bermuda hay, with five or six stacks of 2,000 pounds each. He has a hay packer whereby he can prepare this provender for market in very quick time. He has now up some twenty or thirty acres of oats. He is experimenting with timothy, herd grass and swamp blue grass mixed, believing that it will be more luxurious in growth and more nutritious in quality than if grown separately. His success this past season has stimulated others, and lands in consequence have advanced from ten to twenty dollars per acre in that vicinity. This farm is located just two miles below Macon on the Oculgee river.

Mr. Plant tells me the reason that so much of the Southern hay is worthless is because it is ruined in curing. The northern method cannot be used in this section. After the grass is cut it should be exposed to the sun only about six hours, then removed to the shade and the curing process completed. If this rule is followed, our hay will compare with the best Northern production. Our Southern sun is too hot to allow the grass to lie any length of time exposed to its burning rays.

In curing his pea vine hay, he has slats extending across his barn every twelve or eighteen inches, and the vines are placed in layers on three or white surfaces.

Horrible Tragedy A Lady Waylaid, Outraged and Murdered.
SANTA BARBARA, April 4th. A LONDON
SANTA BARBARA, April 4th.—A Lompoc special to the Santa Barbara Press says: Mrs. Louisa Sargent of Santa Rita, near Lompoc, started alone on horseback to visit a neighbor on Saturday. Not returning in the evening, her husband started to meet her. He found her horse grazing by the roadside. Arousing the neighborhood, search was made until far into the night, without success. Yesterday morning the community turned out en masse, and succeeded in finding the body of Mrs. Sargent buried near a sheep camp. She had evidently been outraged and murdered, her head being crushed as if by the blow of a club. Suspicion rests upon a Mexican sheep-herder, who has been arrested. Intense feeling exists, and there is a probability that the man will be lynched.

Newmann, from the committee appointed to revise the rules, reported and moved the adoption of amendments. A debate ensued and the resolution was adopted. The amended rules do not change the hour of meeting. Recess and adjournment are fixed for the regular session. Two thousand copies of the Governor's message were ordered printed. Grove Johnson moved a reference to the Judiciary Committee of so much of the message as refers to alternative congressional apportionment. Adopted. Enos introduced a resolution requesting the Secretary of State to furnish the Senate with the official census of 1880, giving the population of California by wards, townships and counties. Baker moved to lay the resolution on the table.
Adjourned till to-morrow at 10 A. M.
Republican caucus announced for 2 o'clock this P. M.
The Assembly met at 11 o'clock.
On motion a committee was appointed to wait on the Governor and inform him that the Assembly is ready for business.
The following bill was introduced by McClure: An Act to divide the State into Senatorial and Assembly districts.
The Speaker suggested that the rules be suspended and the bill was read once before it went to the committee.
A discussion ensued, during which McClure charged the Democrats with obstruction. During the debate a message was received from the Governor transmitting his official message.
Camron hoped that the Democrats would not force the Republicans into a caucus. Some of them wished to pass a fair apportionment bill; but obstruction would drive them into caucus on the question.
Whipple said the minority was not here for obstruction, but they were not prepared to yield up their rights on a verbal promise of the majority that the rules would be suspended for every bill.

After further debate, the roll was called and the motion was lost. Ayes, 36; noes, 38.

the Lompoc Horror—The Suspected Sheepherd Struggle up and Makes a Disclosure.

SANTA BARBARA, April 5.—A Lompoc special to the Press says: A. Lansdell, Justice of the Peace, held an inquest on the body of Mrs. Sargent, murdered at Santa Rita. An Indian or Mexican sheepherder named Francisco Jimeno, who was found near the spot, denied all knowledge of the affair. He said he was lying asleep under a tree on the sheep ranch at the time. After the inquest was concluded, one hundred citizens took the sheepherder and hung him to a limb for some seconds. Upon being lowered, he stated that he had seen a man ravish and murder Mrs. Sargent, and as the body was near his cabin, he was fearful that suspicion might attach to him, and putting a rope around her neck, he had dragged her about 400 yards and buried her in a gulch. The marks of the rope were found on her neck, and the trail was plainly visible where the body had been dragged. His shoes fitted the footprints left near the place of concealment. His horses tracks corresponded in size with those made by the animal employed to drag the body, and blood and woman's blood were found in the same place.

The Santa Barbara County Tragedy
Swift Retribution.
Santa Lucia Oregon 48550 Santa Rita
SAN LUIS OBISPO, April 5th.—Santa Rita, near Lompoc, is terribly excited over the brutal murder by an Indian herder of the wife of John H. Sargent, a daughter of E. C. Kelley, on the Santa Rosa ranch, Saturday. The Indian, after being captured, said he saw an unknown Mexican kill her and ride off, and he buried her out of compassion, and hid her things to avoid suspicion. She was evidently dragged off her horse with a lariat, and her skull smashed. His shoes fitted the tracks exactly. The evidence was so conclusive that he was hanged to a tree near the spot, and left hanging, by a crowd of nearly 100 citizens.

MISTAKEN MURDERERS.
The Wrong Man Lynched by a California Crowd.
SAN FRANCISCO, April 7.—Dispatches received from Santa Barbara to-day indicate that a terrible mistake has been made by a maddened mob of lynchers. Francisco Jamino, the Mexican shepherd arrested on suspicion of ravishing and murdering Mrs. Sargent, was yesterday taken by the citizens after the inquest and hung by the neck for a few seconds.

On being taken down he said another man had committed the crime, but he saw it and as it was done near the cabin, to divert suspicion from himself, he put a rope round the neck of the deceased and dragged her to the place where found. He went over the ground with the citizens, also dug up the club with which the murder was committed, and produced some article taken from the murdered woman.

His stories as to the perpetrator were so conflicting that the citizens considered his guilt beyond doubt and hung him to a tree. Many citizens who were satisfied of Francisco's innocence protested strongly against his execution, but the mob, misled by his confused statements, insisted on his guilt and hanged him as stated.

Evidence has now accumulated showing that it was impossible for Francisco to commit the crime, but that his own brother, Ohienio Jamino, older than Francisco, was guilty of the terrible deed and maintained a sinful silence, while his innocent brother was murdered rather than betray him.

Doubly angered by this discovery, the excited citizens are now searching for Ohienio, provided with ropes, and are loud in their threats to hang him to the nearest tree when caught.

Francisco, the youth who was lynched yesterday, was only eighteen years old, and had never sustained a reputation that would justify his awful fate. Mrs. Sargent, the victim of the terrible crime, was a handsome young married lady, only twenty years of age, and the wife of a respectable and well-known citizen.

PAPERED April 9th A.
SANTA BARBARA, April 9th.—A Los Almos special to the Santa Barbara Press says that Euginio Jimeno, brother of the murderer of Mrs. Sargent at Santa Rita, Lompoe valley, proved an alibi by his employers, and was set at liberty. So frightened was he, however, by the treatment of the vigilantes, that he took to the brush and has not been seen since.
francisco-jimeno-lompoc-1881-04-05.A22:
PEKSONAL AND GENERAL.
ANDREW BROWN, white, and three colored men were scalded to death, and several others injured, by the explosion of a sawmill boiler at Berkley, Va.

The steamer Henry Frank arrived at New Orleans on the 2d with the largest cotton cargo ever brought to that port—9,226 bales, beside cotton seed and other freight. Only the smoke-stacks of the boat were visible.

Two brothers, Charles and John Miller, aged respectively 19 and 21, were shot and killed in a disreputable house at Evansville, Ind., on the night of the 3d. It is claimed the fatal shots were fired by a man named Knapke, a friend of the keeper of the house. He is under arrest.

WILLIAM HINSLEY was torn into fragments by the explosion of some dynamite cartridges, near Wilkesbarre, Pa. Wm. Williams, an engineer, was badly injured by the same explosion.

GUSTAV REICHFUS, a wealthy bachelor, was assassinated the other night, near Monroe, O. He was sitting with his brother's family reading a paper when he was shot at from outside a window.

GEORGE SCHMIDT, aged 2 years, died from hydrophobia at Evansville, Ind., on the 3d. He was bitten about four weeks previously.

The man who it is charged made the bomb that killed the Czar has been arrested and will be tried with the other conspirators. His name is Kibaltsenitisch.

A TELEGRAM from Athens, Greece, says a strong shock of earthquake at Chio, in the island of that name, destroyed many houses and seriously damaged nearly all left standing. There was considerable loss of life. Many neighboring villages were destroyed. Shocks were also felt in other islands, in Syria, Smyrna and at Tseme, where it is reported many people were killed.

The damage done by the recent overflow of Dakota rivers is said to be incalculable. Many lives have been lost, hundreds of buildings swept away, and thousands of head of stock drowned. Railroads are ruined, and all sorts of property damaged.

Seven lives were lost by the upsetting of a boat on the Ashley River, near Branchville, S. C., on the 5th.

RICHARD A. COWLING, a distinguished Louisville physician, died of rheumatism of the heart, aged 42.

A UKASE has been issued at St. Petersburg ordering an election for 228 members of a temporary Council to assist the Commandant of the city. All landlords and independent tenants may vote. The late Czar had projected the extension of this plan to the whole empire.

SECRETARY BLAINE is investigating the arrest of Boyton in Ireland, but he thinks all that this Government can do is to ask good treatment for the prisoner.

FRANCISCO TIMINO, a sheep herder, was lynched near Lompoc, Cal., for assaulting and murdering Mrs. Sargent.

VIRGINIA ponds were frozen over on the night of the 4th. It is feared the fruit crop is entirely ruined throughout a large portion of the State.

The workingmen of New York are demanding an increase of 50 cents a day in their wages. In many instances it has been already granted.

B. F. HARRINGTON, an outlaw, was shot and killed in Mount Princeton, Colo., while attempting to escape from the officers.

The Iowa State Brewers' Convention met at Dubuque on the 6th.

The Society of the Army of the Tennessee met at Pike's Opera-house, Cincinnati, on the 6th. Gen. Sherman presided, and read a sketch of the Battle of Pittsburg Landing, illustrated by maps and charts distributed among the members. After the day's session was concluded, the Society assisted at the unveiling of the McPherson statue in Fountain Square.

The Chilians threaten to levy $20,000 each on fifty Peruvians as a sort of war indemnity. The Peruvians protest, but it is not likely that their protest will have much effect.

In Russia-Poland the peasants refuse to swear allegiance in United Greek churches. They demand to be sworn before Catholic priests, and have driven away Greek priests. The Governor of the province declares they must take the oath in Russian churches.

The Khomnis and other Berber tribes threaten some of the French settlements in Algiers, and French troops have been dispatched to the frontier to act against them.

The Illinois and Mississippi Canal Commission has arranged for a Northwestern convention at Davenport on May 25, the delegates to be appointed by the Governors, Boards of Trade and Farmers' Clubs. The object of the gathering is to invoke the aid of Congress in creating a water route from the Mississippi to the lakes.

A FEARFUL accident occurred at Johnson's flouring mill, Monroe County, Ark., a few days since, resulting in the death of two men, Burrows and Jackson, and the probably fatal injury of several others, including Mr. Johnson, owner of the mill. The casualty was caused by the bursting of one of the millstones. The building was demolished by the force of the explosion.

The recent deaths from trichinosis at Hoboken, N. J., it is now alleged were due to eating sausage imported from Germany.

The Parkison Hotel at Orange, Fla., has been destroyed by fire. All the guests escaped. The loss is $12,000.

SELLING LIQUOR TO MINORS, Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. Avonora, Ill., Oct. 15.—Ole Olson, brother of Thomas Olson, who stabbed and killed Otto D. Freese, has made all day it that he and his brother obtained the liquor that intoxicated them on the night of the murder from the saloon kept by Daniel Freese, the father of the murdered boy. As both the Olsons are minors, the city authorities can prosecute a suit for unlawfully selling to minors. Active raids have already been commenced against the saloonkeepers for illegal practices, prompted by the recent horrors. Four have been indicted by the grand jury. A strong sight will be made on the trial of Thomas Olson. He has a con-
siderable amount of money in the hands of a guardian in La Salle County who promises to see that Olson is properly protected, and has employed the Hon. B. F. Parks, Jocelyn, and Willis. Daniel Freese has employed the Hon. A. J. Hopkins and Aldrich as prosecutors to aid the State's Attorney.

SHOT DEAD.
LITTLE Rock, Ark., Oct. 10.—Intelligence reached this city today of a terrible tragedy last Saturday at a sawmill near Grand Lake, Ark., a small town on the Mississippi River. William Brooks, proprietor of the sawmill, was beating on employe when a fellow workman named Willian Yountz interfered. Brooks, exasperated, turned upon Yountz, when the latter drew a revolver and fired, the ball striking Brooks in the head and killing him instantly. Yountz was arrested, and after a preliminary examination was discharged.

A DETECTIVE'S FATE.

St. Louis, Mo., Oct. 16.—The body of an unknown man was found yesterday hanging to a tree in thick woods four miles from Grain Valley Station, on the Chicago & Alton Railroad, some twenty miles from Kansas City. The body had apparently been hanging three days. The theory is that the man was a detective, and had been lynched by some one connected with the recent train robbery.

MURDERED FOR HIS MONEY.
Evansville, Ind., Oct. 16.—A colored man named Green was found dead in the suburbs of Henderson this morning, with his head split open with a cooper's adze. A man was arrested on suspicion and lodged in jail. The adze, covered with blood and hair, was found two squares from the body. It is supposed he was murdered for his money.

NOT GUILTY.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

EAST SAGINAW, Mich., Oct. 15.—The jury in the case of Shin Robinson, John Hughes, and James and John Wilson, charged with murder in the Chesonitry circus riot, brought in a verdict of "not guilty" today. There have been two convicted, five acquitted, and two parties yet to be tried in this case.

REWARD PAID.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., Oct. 15.—The Iron Mountain Railroad Company yesterday paid Clark Hall and the four men who assisted him in capturing the train-robbers $1,000 each. Moore and Huddlestone have not yet been paid. It is rumored they will sue the company.

ARREST OF COUNTERFEITERS.
EVANSVILLE, Ind., Oct. 16.—Two men giving the names of John Miller and E. C. Brobson were arrested a mile above the city today on a charge of counterfeiting. Spurious coin, molds, metals, etc., were found on them.

The Health of Chicago.
CHICAGO, October 16th.—Startling figures are given, showing a great and steady increase in scymatic disease, which, according to the State Board of Health, is due to the unclearly condition of the streets, and in a less degree to a large influx of the low classes of immigrants. Week before last there were 36 deaths from typhoid fever, and the number this week is still greater. In January there were 18 deaths from small-pox, in May 46, in August 116, in September 108, and so far in October 79. The entire mortality from small-pox in 1870 was 18. Unless there is a decided reform in the street cleaning methods, even greater mortality is probable.

Conkling's Health.
NEW YORK, October 16th.—A special from Utica says: Conkling, who has been unwell for some time, is reported unable to leave his room. His family physician has been frequently in attendance the past few days, and has enjoined absolute rest and the strictest quiet. It was known several days ago that he had been in bad health for some time, but it was not until within a day or two that serious illness was apprehended.

Business Portion of a Town Burned.
MEMPHIS, October 16th.—A fire at Humboldt, Tenn., destroyed twenty storehouses, including two squares on both sides of the main street; also the Humboldt furniture factory, postoffice and the West Tennessee Argus office. The entire business portion of the city is burned. Loss about $175,000; insurance, $16,000.

Body Found.
ST. LOUIS, October 16th.—The body of an unknown man was found yesterday hanging to a tree in the thick woods four miles from Grain Valley station, on the Chicago and Alton Railroad, some twenty miles from Kansas City. The body had apparently been hanging three days. The theory is that the man was a detective, and had been lynched by some one connected with the recent robbery.

Death of the Governor of Louisiana.
NEW ORLEANS, October 16th.—Governor Wiltz died at 12:30 this morning.

Criminal.
HENRY McDONALD was hanged at Silver City, Idaho, Oct. 18th, for the murder of George Mayers.

WHILE forcing his way into a hotel at Lancaster, Pa., William Gruzemer was shot dead by John Miller.

L. ROSENHEIMER, a merchant at Kewaskum, Wis., states that burglars obtained from his safe $2,000 in cash, and $6,000 in bonds.

THE schooner Triumph, in tow of the tug Success, wilfully crashed into the bridge at Chicago avenue, on the 13th inst., tearing away one hundred feet of railing.

A FRUID which has existed for years between C. S., Vincent and Samuel Cockrell, of Waverly, Iowa, closed last week by the killing of the latter in the street, in self-defense.

THE masked robbers who obtained $8,000 in gold from the farm house of Ezekiel Perrin were captured at Litchfield, Ill. Their discovery was due wholly to a drunken dispute over the division of the spoils.

CHARLES HOWLAND, a farmer residing near Paw Paw, Mich., went home intoxicated and struck his wife and stabbed his son, whereupon the latter drew a revolver and killed the brute.

EDWARD DENIG, bookkeeper for the contractors on the Indiana state-house forged warrants to the amounts of $1,500 and disappeared. Orders of his arrest have been sent to all the chief cities.

FRANK UTLEY, who was sentenced to the Wisconsin penitentiary for life, for the murder of his father, escaped from the guard October 14th, while digging potatoes on the prison farm.

JOHN ROBERTSON, formerly a clerk in the employ of the Lake Shore road at Chicago, has been arrested in Liverpool on a charge of forging checks for a large amount, and papers for his extradition will be asked.

FOUR masked robbers entered the farm-house of Allan Fairbank, at Wheaton, Ill., Tuesday morning, bound and gagged four members of the family, and secured from a mattress $2,600 in money and $10,-000 in registered bonds. Two Chicago detectives are at work on the case.

A duel between Captain Riddleberger and Hon. George D. Wise took place about ten miles from Richmond Oct. 18th. Four rounds were fired without injury to the combatants, when an amicable adjustment was reached.

A DRAMATIC journal of New York states that a separation has taken place between Edwin Booth and his wife, the latter having gone to reside with J. H. McVicker in Sixth avenue. The estrangement is said to be no new matter, and culminated in the discovery that Mrs. Booth had willed to her mother property in Chicago given her by her husband within a year.

PEOPLE near Independence, Mo., are greatly excited over the finding of a body hanging from a tree. It is believed that there has been a lynching by a vigilance committee for participation in the Glendale train-robbery. William Ryan was sentenced to twenty-five years in the penitentiary, which so unnerved him that he leaned on a chair for support.

JAMES VALIER was shot by his stepson, at Detroit, Mich., Oct. 18th, Marquis Lafayette Defoe, in a quarrel. Valier came home drunk, and began abusing his family, and threatened the life of his wife and Defoe. Hot words ensued, and Defoe was caught by the throat by Valier. The former drew a revolver and shot Valier in the bowels, from the effects of which he died at 11 o'clock. Defoe is under arrest, and claims to have done it in self-defense. Valier was 35 years of age. The same revolver accidentally shot Mrs. Valier's husband some years since.
gran-valley-station-gran-valley-station-.A9: On Saturday last, the body of a man was found hanging in a tree twenty miles from Independence, Missouri. The deceased is supposed to have been a detective who was engaged in searching for the train robbers, and having been captured by the gang, they strung him up to prevent his hunting them down. His remains have not been identified.

Four barrels of water from Salt Lake will yield one barrel of salt.
Dr. Holland offered "Timothy Titcomb" to three publishers before it was accepted.
The Right Rev. Henry Forester, D. D., Prince Bishop of Breslau, is dead.
It is estimated that Americans traveling in Europe spend nearly $100,000,000 annually.
The death is announced of Raffaelle Monti, the celebrated Italian sculptor at the age of 63 years.
A solution of common salt given immediately is said to be a successful remedy for strychnia poisoning.
That fish sleep has been well determined by observations conducted by Dr. Hermes and others in the Berlin aquarium.
The icebergs of the southern hemispheres are much larger than those of the northern, and frequently attain a height of 1,000 feet.
The Garfield monument at Lake View Cemetery, Cleveland, is to cost $200,000, of which Cleveland proposes to raise $50,000.
William H. Vanderbilt on Wednesay went from New York to Albany in his special car in three hours and twent-five minutes, or at the rate of about eighty-three miles an hour.

The Providence Journal says that the bodies of five persons have been taken from the Providence River inside of 18 months whose death has not been satisfactorily accounted for.

The Troy Times says that Mrs. Sarah M. Gould has paid a judgment of $500 and costs, in all about $1,000, obtained by a Lansingburg boy named Jocko, who was bitten by a dog owned by Mrs. Gould.

Miscellaneous Items.
St. Louis tobacco market (Oct. 22); Dark lugs, common to good, $5.00 to $6.25; bright smoking, common to good, $6.00 to $7.00; dark red leaf, $6.50 to $8.50; half-bright wrappers, common to medium, $10 to $18.

The St. Louis Republican, of a recent date, says: Mr. P. Van Frank, civil engineer of the St. Louis, Iron Mountain & Southern Railway, has returned from making the reconnoissance for a branch road through several important counties of Missouri. The projected line starts from Iron-dale in Iron County, and runs through Iron, Washington and Dent Counties to the southern line of Texas County, where it strikes the Kansas City, Springfield & Memphis Railroad. The length of the line will be about 110 miles, and will tap a fertile and richly-timbered country, giving St. Louis another valuable railroad tributary.

Curtis Goddard, an aged and blind wood-sawyer of St. Joseph, has received official notice of the allowance of a pension of $22 per month, with $9,700 in arrears. While in the army he contracted a disease which has not only wrecked him physically, but his eyes soon went out. For ten years he has made a very meager living by sawing wood.

It is understood that Allen Parmer, the brother-in-law of the James boys, has dismissed his suit for $40,000 against Superintendent Treat, of the United States Express Company, and ex-Marshal Liggett. Parmer sued for damages for false imprisonment. He was arrested in Texas for participation in the Glendale affair, but was never indicted. It is now stated that Parmer has been arrested for complicity in the Winston affair.

Reuben Grigsby, youngest son of Mr. A. W. Grigsby, an old and respected citizen and farmer of Mississippi County, committed suicide a few days ago by shooting himself in the center of the forehead with a rifle, which killed him instantly. It is said he had been very despondent during the week about what he termed a failure of his corn crop.

The St. Louis freight blockade still continues.

A very mysterious hanging is reported from Grain Valley, in the southwestern part of Jackson County. A farmer going through a dense woods was horrified to find the dead body of a man with a rope around his neck lying on the ground under a tree, while suspended from a limb above was another piece of the same rope. The farmer immediately gave the alarm, but all efforts at identifying the deceased proved a failure. One theory is that he was a detective and met his fate at the hands of the train robbers; another is that he was a horse-thief who met with summary punishment from the farmers of the vicinity. The third, and most reasonable proposition is, that the man committed suicide.

The twenty-seventh annual session of the Grand Lodge of I. O. G. T. of the State of Missouri convened at St. Louis on the 18th. Wm. F. Switzler, of Columbia, Grand Worthy Chief Templar, presided. The report of the Grand Worthy Chief Templar showed that the organization now numbers about 550 lodges, with an aggregate membership of 29,000 persons, and holds the position of banner Grand Lodge of the world.

A Monroe County man has trichinosis.

The Grand Jury at Independence have indicted John Bugler, John Land and Creed Chapman for participation in the Blue Cet train robbery on Sept. 7 last, and their trial has been fixed for the February term. Sam Chapman, captured at the same time, is held on an indictment for carrying concealed weapons, and he has made a statement in regard to the train robbery which will be used as testimony against the others. The Court of Appeals has refused to interfere in behalf of Kotovsky and Kring, the St. Louis murderers, now under sentence of death. In many orchards in Phelps County deach trees are in full bloom.
