From the Hub. A Horrible Crime.
On last Friday night, two negroes—Jim Taylor and Bob Green, went to the house of Col. Jas. Irwin during his absence and committed a horrible outrage upon the person of Mrs. Irwin. The negroes went to the house for the purpose of outraging a step-daughter of Col. Irwin, but she was absent at Reidsville with her step-father (Col. Irwin), and these two devils assaulted Mrs. Irwin, a lady nearly 50 years of age. Both of the negroes were arrested and carried to Reidsville, and during the trial confessed their guilt, and were committed to jail at Wentworth. A party was organized to lynch the rascals, but Sheriff Johnson took the negro Taylor, the negro who committed the outrage, and hurried to Kernersville, where he took the train and carried him to Greensboro and lodged him in jail at that place. During the night a party went to Wentworth and forced the jail, but when they found that Taylor was gone the left without molesting the other prisoner, and went in pursuit of the Sheriff and Taylor, but unfortunately failed to come up with them.

The victim of this outrage is a neice of our townsman, Maj. Ham Scales, and is also related to Capt. Grogan and Mr. Peter Dalton, and is a lady of great respectability and much loved in the community in which she lives. The courts should not be bothered with her outragers.
greensboro-greensboro-1881-06-06.A3:
The Horrible Outrage near Reidsville, N. C.
On Friday night last, near the town of Reidsville, Rockingham county, between the hours of 9 and 10 o'clock, two negroes, John Taylor and George Gunn, in the employ of Col. James Irwin, as farm hands, during the absence of their employer and his daughter, went to the house of Col. Irwin and finding Mrs. Irwin alone with her little son, entered the house. From what we are told it was a premeditated affair. The negroes went to Col. Irwin's not to assault or injure Mrs. Irwin, but the young lady who had accompanied her father to Reidsville. Bent on crime, however, Taylor then assaulted Mrs. Irwin. Notwithstanding the resistance made and the cries of the poor, unprotected victim, Taylor accomplished his purpose. Gunn, the other negro, it is said, made no assault upon Mrs. Irwin. He was present, however, and witnessed the hellish act. The negroes then left the premises and went over to Reidsville. Mrs. Irwin immediately went to a neighbor's house.

On Saturday about noon Taylor and Gunn were arrested and taken before a Justice at Reidsville, and during the trial confessed their guilt. The crowd which had assembled, became indignant and at one time lynching was freely talked of. The parties were committed to Jail at Wentworth. No effort was made to lynch them on the way to Jail, but on Saturday evening, it is reported, a number of gentlemen organized a lynching party. It appears that no attempt was made and Taylor and Gunn remained in Jail until Sunday night. During the afternoon of Sunday the Sheriff of Rockingham received information that another party had been organized and that an attempt would be made to take the negroes from the Jail Sunday night and hang them. Anticipating such an event, Sheriff Johnston took charge of John Taylor, the negro who actually committed the horrible deed, and moved off in the direction of Danville, Va. Gunn was left in the Jail at Wentworth. During the night a party of men went to Wentworth, and on reaching the Jail demanded the keys from the Jailor, but were refused. The next thing was to force the Jail doors, which was done, but when it was ascertained that Taylor was gone, the party left and went in pursuit of the fleeing Sheriff and his prisoner. Sheriff Johnston, in order to elude the pursuing party, changed his route and moved in the direction of Kernersville, in Forsythe county. Mr. O. C. Wheeler, the Jailor of Guilford county, met Sheriff Johnston at the depot, took charge of Taylor and conducted him to the county Jail, where he was confined in one of the cells.

Taylor is 22 years of age, weighs about 140 pounds, seems to be in excellent health, and although he is considerably excited, talks freely about the affair. He says, however, that Gunn is the guilty man; that he accompanied him to a point near the residence of Col. Irwin and then stopped. He heard the cries of Mrs. Irwin but was atraid to go to the house. He says that Gunn had frequently threatened to kill him.
but was afraid to go to the house. He says that Gunn had frequently threatened to kill him (Taylor.) He acknowledges the fact that he and Gunn were to go together and commit the crime with which they stand charged.

Mrs. Irwin is suffering considerably from the attack upon her. The good people of Reidsville seemed determined to mete out quick justice upon the guilty wretches. Rockingham Superior Court is now in session and it may be that these devils in human form can be tried this week. The people of this entire section sympathize with Col. Irwin and his estimable wife. No more worthy or highly esteemed citizens live in Rockingham county. Mrs. Irwin is said to be about 40 years of age, and is greatly beloved by the citizens of Reidsville and the immediate neighborhood, for her noble qualities.

In addition to the above the Raleigh Observer says: "A gentleman informs us that on Monday night a large party of armed men rode into Greensboro to take the negro fiend from the jail there, but he was taken away by the Sheriff and escaped death then."

It is said that Princess Dolgorouki, who was the morganatic wife of the late Czar, is instructing her financial agent to invest largely on her behalf in American securities, in which she has already placed between two and three million dollars.

VIRGINIA VIGILANTES
Break Open the Jail at Greensboro, Secure a Negro Prisoner and Hang Him.
DANVILLE, VA., June 12.—During the eclipse of the moon last night, John Taylor, a negro who had grossly assaulted a white woman, was taken from the Greensboro jail and hanged. A large number of persons visited the scene of the lynching to day. The lynchers numbered about two hundred, and upon the refusal of the jailer to deliver the keys of the jail they tore down the fence, broke open the jail doors and overpowering the guard, took the keys and entered. They unshackeled the negro and brought him to the buggy in waiting. The crowd then rode off at a swift gallop, and at a point seven miles south of Reidsville, Rockingham county, N. C., the negro was hanged. The afair was so unexpected and so quietly done that it was not generally known in Greensboro till all was over.
greensboro-greensboro-1881-06-06.A8: manner, outraged her, and left her insensible. The negroes were arrested, and confined under a strong guard. Gunn is reported as not having been guilty of participating in the assault, except so far as accompanying Taylor to the residence of Col. Irwin. On Saturday night a band of a hundred men assembled in Wentworth for the purpose of taking the prisoners from the jail and executing them forthwith, but the Sheriff getting information of it, took the most guilty man (Taylor) out of jail, and drove through the country to Kernersville, where he confined him that night, and on Monday morning he brought him to Greensboro, where he was lodged in jail. The prompt action of the Sheriff prevented the lynching at Wentworth, but only delayed the vengeance of an infuriated people, for on Monday night of last week, the Sheriff of Guilford was informed that an attempt would be made on that night by an armed mob to take the prisoner from the jail and hang him. To prevent violence the sheriff took the precaution to take Taylor under guard from his cell to a safe place near Greensboro, where he was kept until Tuesday morning and then returned to the jail. The excitement seemed to have subsided, until last Saturday night, when, during the eclipse of the moon, Taylor was taken from the jail by a large number of disguised men, who hanged him to a tree in the woods near town.

John Taylor, the African brute, who outraged an aged and honorable white lady, near Reidsville, Rockingham county, has been hanged until dead, and dumped into the soil at the foot of his gallows-tree.

It will be remembered that some ten days ago, Col. James Irwin, a well known citizen of Rockingham, carried his daughter, (a former pupil of the B. F. Seminary in Raleigh,) to attend a concert in Reidsville. Two negroes took the coach horses, and galloped back to the Irwin plantation; apparently unaware that Miss Irwin had come to town with her father. At least it is said they went to the house with hellish designs upon the daughter. The mother, a lady of near 50 years of age, suspecting no ill, sat at home until seized by the two villains. When she recovered consciousness she fled across the fields to the nearest neighbors giving the alarm; then fell fainting, and has been at death's door ever since, if not already dead at this writing.

The two brutes, John Taylor and Geo. Gunn, were soon in jail, and as the country aroused the sturdy farmers flocked in with fixed resolve to give that "short thrift" which is the only real deterrent in punishment. There being some doubt in the case of Gunn, he was allowed the benefit of a regular trial, and now lies in Rockingham jail, free from any danger of lynching. This is right. But there was no possibility of mistake in Taylor's case; therefore he should have gone to the gallows within twenty-four hours after his crime.

Unfortunately the Sheriff being a sworn officer, felt it his duty to save the prisoner for the formalities of the law; consequently took Taylor in his buggy, and fled through by-roads to Greensboro, 40 miles distant. Judge Lynch followed him, thither, but failing to find him, dispersed, until Saturday night last.

RETRIBUTION.

About 11 p. m on Saturday a body of 50 or 60 horsemen entered Greensboro, and being refused the jail keys, cut through three heavy doors, and found Taylor chained to the floor. In half an hour, the cavalcade marched out of town, in military order, carrying the mulatto tied to the back of a buggy. The latter realized his doom; but acted in sullen stolidness, as he has done from the first, refusing to affirm or deny his guilt. To a by-stander in Greensboro he said that all he wanted was to go to Heaven! (Every negro murderer adopts the same tune; and really seems to think he will have nothing to do but step off the gallows into the arms of the angels!)

Seven miles from Reidsville, the lynchers received word that Mrs. Irwin was too ill to permit of any commotion passing the house; therefore the procession halted by the road-side; and Taylor was placed upon the back of the horse he had ridden to do his crime. Being asked if he had anything to say,—he responded sullenly—"Get it over quick!" A sharp switch sent the horse from under him and he fell six feet, breaking his neck. This was about 4 a. m. on Sunday morning.

The news had gone abroad, and from far and near, came the country people, white and black, of all ages, to view the dangling ravisher. Towards evening the coroner appeared, and held inquest. Then the corpse was buried where it lay.

We have no regrets for the lynching,—May we commend it in all except two particulars: viz the delay, and the waving of handkerchiefs by women as the lynchers passed. Judge Lynch should always act calmly, quietly, even solemnly, as if fully conscious that he is usurping the office of the law, but not through passion, sudden feeling, or any other impulse than the grave necessity of Nature's Higher Law,—self-preservation. We repeat that we regret the delay, because the real object of Lynch Court is to set the seal of swift and sure retribution on certain foul crimes! Vengeance should follow within one hour after there is no longer a doubt of guilt. The lynchers should organize a jury and if any three or four intelligent gentlemen will assert doubts as to the prisoner's guilt, let him be remanded to jail to await formal trial. But where there is no possibility of mistake, the ravisher, whether white or black (and we should be more merciful to a negro than a white man, because he has fewer moral and educational influences to restrain his brutalusts)—the ravisher, we say, should be strapped, on his knees, to a stake; and the nearest male relative of the injured woman should be called upon to blow out his brains. Then a pile of stones and dirt should be heaped upon the godden corpse, and all men disperse to their homes.

Ah! have you ever thought what a "home" that must be, to which all eyes are turning as the scene of outrageous violence done to a gentle woman!

Conceive, if you can, a fate more horrible for a delicate and pure hearted girl, on the threshold of life, blushing with the rosy tints of maidenhood, per chance of "Love's Young Dream,"—suddenly, in one black hour, struck down and crushed like a trampled lily-lower, trampled and withered, and stained, through no fault of her own; zoomed to drag the lengthening chain of many weary years,—until the grave rings oblivion to the dreadful recollection—ever present, asleep and awake,—of that sudden assault, the vain cries or help, the fainting struggle against brutal strength, the wild alarm, the rocking of cruelly curious crowds, theaggerated details, the columns of newspaper reports, with her name hunted to the four corners of earth! Speedy Punishment.
The negro man who committed rape upon Mrs. Irwin last week near Reidsville, met with speedy punishment from the hands of the outraged people of Rockingham county. He was taken from the Jail at Greensboro on Saturday night last and hanged in Rockingham county on Sunday morning. The Greensboro "Battle Ground" gives the following short account of the affair:

"Saturday night at 10 o'clock a body of men met at a rendezvous about five miles north of Greensboro, and entered the city about 11 o'clock, and went direct to the city prison and demanded the person of John Taylor, the mulatto, who, about a week ago, outraged Mrs. Irwin, a highly respectable lady near Reidsville, in such a shocking and horrible manner. Mr Wheeler refused the keys, and as they had come prepared, they produced sledges and chisels and cut their way into the prison. They cut through three doors, each door having three heavy and massive locks. Taylor was also chained to the floor. At 11.20 they succeeded in getting into the cell, and he was tied hand and foot, and at 11.30 they emerged from the Jail, bringing him with them. He was placed in a buggy that was waiting at the gate. He was tied to the back of the buggy, and the crowd moved off in the direction of Reidsville. As they prepared to leave the city, the order was given by the leader to form in twos and be prepared for action in case they were fired into. They stated that they would hang him to a telegraph pole in Reidsville, provided they could arrive there before daylight; in case they were delayed, he would be hung to the first tree after they crossed the Guilford line. It was a determined set of men and the negro seemed to know his time had come and said he wanted to go to heaven. [Of course every negro criminal is led to believe that he is going to heaven if he is hanged.] Some one in the crowd told him that he now had a chance to say his last words, he replied that he had no statement to make. It is said that there were over two hundred men in the body.

It was evidently a pre-arranged affair, and must have occupied much of the time of the leaders who organized the movement. We are not prepared to say if any Greensboro men were in the party, but we think the general impression is that they were all citizens of Rockingham county."

When first arrested the negro confessed his guilt. It is stated that the colored people of that section express the opinion that Taylor got his just deserts.

[From the News and Observer.]
TAYLOR, THE NEGRO RAPE
FIEND, LYNCHED.
HANGED BY A BODY OF MASKED MEN—SPEEDY LETTIBUTION.

The notorious criminal, John Taylor, the negro who last week so brutally outraged Mrs Irwin, an elderly lady of Reidsville, on Sunday paid the penalty of his horrible crime, being hanged by a great party of lynchers, who took him from the jail at Greensboro Saturday night.

About fifty or sixty persons left Greensboro with Taylor, while a dozen ladies waved their handkerchiefs from the windows as the procession passed by. At 4 o'clock Sunday morning the party reached a point seven miles from Reidsville, when they stopped and swung up the prisoner to an oak limb. He (Taylor) was stubborn and sullen to the last, and he said little or nothing.

All day long the body swung there, until, the rope relaxing somewhat, the feet touched the ground. The scene was visited by very large and curious crowds of excursionists, both white and colored. These came from far and near, in every imaginable kind of vehicle, and on foot.

Late in the evening the coroner made his appearance and had the body cut down. A jury was empaneled and at once rendered a verdict that the deceased, John Taylor, had been hanged by unknown parties. The body was not molested. Taylor was hanged just as the law hangs criminals. He was assisted up to the limb of the tree by being mounted on the back of the same gray horse which he had ridden from Reidsville to the home of the lady, to commit the rape.

Jupe Billard, colored, was secured to inter the body, and placed it in a grave right at the foot of the oak on which it had swung. The county paid $4 for the interment. The county people agree that the lynching was right. T. C. E.

MISSISSIPPI MATTERS.
Moss Point has the measles.

DeKalb is to have a new courthouse.

N. I. Smith died near Senatobia last week.

Mrs. Ike S. Harvey, of Holmes county, is dead.

The Pioneer says Walthall needs a shoe-maker.

Mrs. Fannie Hudspeth died in Water Valley on Monday last.

The Baptist State Convention meets in Meridian on the 20th instant.

Dr. Morgan Adams, of Sardis, a dentist of ability, has removed to Jackson.

A half interest in the Homestead and Observer, at Meridian, is offered for sale.

Colonel J. J. Williams has again assumed the editorial chair of the Grenada New South.

The Democracy of Calhoun county have nominated R. N. Provine for the Legislature.

Hon. J. S. Montgomery, a prominent Republican of Adams county, has declared for Lowry.

Mr. M. A. Dees has sold his interest in the Democrat-Star to Messrs. M. B. Richmond and George W. Wilkes.

The State printing under Radical rule cost $100,000 annually; under Democratic rule it costs $25,000 annually.

William Allgood, an old and esteemed citizen, was found dead in his bed near Brookhaven, a few days since.

Hon. E. Henderson, of Harrison county, is the Democratic nominee for State Senator from the Seacoast District.

The Jackson Clarion is authority for the statement that Major Barksdale is not a candidate for the United States Senate.

Charles A. Hamilton, Esq., has purchased an interest in the Wesson Herald and taken control as editor and business manager of that paper.

ticket, and continue in the field till the close of the canvass. He is a fine speaker and ranks among the best lawyers in the State.

H. O. Eaton was shot and killed on Friday night last at Bunker Hill, Smith county, by Dan Hathorn. As soon as Hathorn shot Eaton, Dick Yawn shot Hathorn and killed him. Both Eaton and Hathorn died instantly.

The State tax in 1875, under Radical rule, was $9 25 on the thousand. The State tax under Democratic rule in 1881, is $3 on the thousand. The State tax under same rule in 1882 and 1883, may not exceed $2 on the thousand.

Five miles from Crystal Springs there was a boiler explosion last week, in which one white man and a colored man were killed, parts of the body of the colored man being carried 200 yards. Two others were badly wounded.

When the Republicans ruled the State, Kimball, Raymond & Co. charged fifty dollars for a six quire docket. J. L. Power does the work for twelve dollars—a difference in favor of Democratic rule of thirty-eight dollars on one book.

The tax levy in Hinds county in 1874, under Republican rule, was $224,731 27, and in addition, during a period of five years, a debt of $150,000 was created. The present tax levy of the county is $73,869 71, including the additional railroad tax.

Mississippi has provided handsomely for the education of her sons, both white and colored, in the liberal support annually given the University at Oxford, Alcorn University, the A. and M. College at Starkville, and the Normal school at Tugaloo.

Of the 760,000 square miles of timber lands in this country, the South owns 460,000, or nearly two-thirds. They will be mines of wealth in a few years. Mississippi, and especially the pine-wood counties, will come in for a large share of this wealth.

We learn from the Copiahian that Dan Coor's steam-mill, located in Copiah county, blew up on the 18th ultimo, killing two and severely wounding and scalding six other men. Dan Coor, the proprietor, was a young man of great energy and business capacity.

John Hicks, who some weeks ago eloped with the wife of Mr. G. W. Eggerton, who lives about twelve miles east of Shubuta, has been arrested and ledged in the jail at Quitman. They went to Monroe, Louisiana, where they were married and honey-mooned awhile.

Joe Thomas, the murderer, who was brought to Jackson from Arkansas, was taken to Vicksburg Saturday by Sheriff Joor, of Sharkey county. He was placed in the Vicksburg jail for safe keeping, there being a disposition on the part of citizens of Rolling Fork to lynch him.

The Kosciusko Star states that the gin-house of W. H. Stamfield, of Holmes county, was accidently set on fire last week by a lamp in the hands of an employee named Johnson. Johnson was in the lint-room, and before he could get out was so badly burned that he is not expected to live. The gin-house, with all its contents, was entirely consumed.

Last Saturday night an inoffensive and peaceable colored man named James Truss was killed at Desoto, by being stabbed in the neck. He only lived a few minutes after being stabbed. It is said that the following named persons were concerned in the matter: Burt McRee, Young Nealy, Cook Johnson and Cooper Morris, white, and Royal Evans, colored.

Alcorn, Jonestown; Green Clay, Bolivar Landing; General S. W. Ferguson, Greenville; Captain S. H. Parisot, Lee Richardson, George M. Klein, of Vicksburg, and John A. Dicks and J. W. Lambert, of Natchez.

The Jackson Clarion has come out very decidedly in favor of separating the judiciary from the executive department, whereupon the Free Press says: "It is about three-thirds right, but a little late in presenting its arguments. Several years ago would have worked as well, and would have been much better for the Democratic party. However, better late than never, and it is hoped the Clarion will have sufficient help."

Hon. Charles B. Howry has returned to his home in Oxford from the mountains of East Tennessee, but we regret to say with his health but slightly improved. He has entered actively upon the canvass and will strike telling blows for the Democratic cause."

Discussing German carp, the Columbus Enquirer-Sun says: "Some months ago a number of German carp were placed in various ponds near the city. This species of fish is very prolific, but they have proved extraordinarily so in the brick yard ponds. Here they are said to have greatly increased. A few, measuring five to six inches in length, have been caught in seines. They were not held in much estimation in ancient days, and were introduced in England about three hundred yars ago. Carp prefer quiet waters with soft or muddy bottoms, spawning in May or June, according to locality. The food consists of insects, worms and soft plants, though they eat almost any vegetable food in artificial ponds. They are very tenacious of life, and will pass long periods, especially in winter, without food. They afford but little sport to the angler, being very uncertain and are difficult to take in nets. The size varies from six inches to two and one-half feet, and their weight from one to eighteen pounds. They are in season from October to April, and are generally considered excellent for the table. The carp is in shap—something similar to the perch, although their body is longer and more slender. They are of a golden, olive-brown color above, yellowish beneath, and the fins dark brown. They live to a considerable age. An account of the death of a carp in France which was over four hundred years old has been going the rounds of the papers."

A COWARDLY CRIME.
Ten Respectable Citizens Charged With a Serious Offense.
Yesterday morning a Deputy United States Marshal arrived in the city by the train on the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway, having in custody ten respectable citizens of Montgomery county, who are charged with a very serious crime. It appears that on the night of the 2d of May last a party of disguised men visited the house of a colored man by the name of Jerry Hamilton, who in some manner had rendered himself obnoxious, and taking him therefrom carried him some distance and beat him so badly that he died from the effects of the injuries then received. This outrage occurred near Mount Vernon, the county site of Montgomery, and on the following day, when the news of the outrage was circulated, a large mass meeting of the citizens was called, at which resolutions were passed condemning in the strongest terms the cowardly crime, and pledging the assistance of the authorities to ferret out the perpetrators.

In the meanwhile, information was received in Savannah, and United States Commissioner Wade issued a warrant against a number of respectable citizens, charging them with a violation of the civil rights bill in connection with this crime, and a Deputy Marshal was instructed to execute the same. The names of the gentlemen who have thus been arrested, and who, we are informed, are among the most prominent and worthy citizens of Montgomery, the very last men to countenance such an outrage, are Messrs. Joseph Palmer, William Adams, Thomas Norris, Angus Norris, Algernon Brady, R. Brady, H. Brady, W. Darley and James Buckan. There appears to be no evidence against these parties, and they were arrested merely on suspicion. The offense with which they are charged does not, we understand, come under the civil rights bill.

They were arraigned yesterday morning before the Commissioner, who issued the warrant, but, the witnesses for the prosecution not being present, they would have been committed to jail but for the interposition of their attorneys, Messrs. Garrard & Melerim, who rendered ample bond for their appearance. Mr. P. W. Carswell, of Mount Vernon, is also associated with Messrs. Garrard & Meldrim for the defense. An examination in the case will be held to day at 12 o'clock.

FRATRICIDE.
FRATRICIDE.

SPRINGFIELD, Mass., June 8.—Dwlight Kidder, Jr., who fatally shot his half-brother, C. D. Kidder, was to-day held in default of $10,000 for examination. In an interview today the prisoner said: "It all came from carrying a pistol. I have carried one for six years; if I had a boy who carried one I would break his neck." The prisoner said his mother overheard the murdered man saying she wanted his father to die, so that she could get $5,000 insurance on his life. The prisoner asked him if he said so. He said he did. The prisoner threatened to kill him if the romark was repeated, and was put out of the house. The prisoner ran, and his brother ran after and struck him, and the prisoner then fired the fatal shot. The deceased was a prominent local Democratic politician, and the affair causes much excitement.

CRIMINAL NEGLIGENCE.

CRIMINAL NEGLIGENCE.

CEDAR RAPIDS, Ia., June 8.—The Coroner's jury, after a thorough investigation as to the cause of the railroad disaster Sabbath morning last on the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad, four miles west of this city, whereby Frank Horton and Thomas Hurley were killed, returned a verdict this afternoon, finding that the death of these two men was caused by the "culpable and criminal negligence of Charles B. Lewis, night operator at Cedar Rapids." The Coroner immediately issued a warrant for Lewis' arrest, and he was taken into custody. Information has been filed before Justice Anderson by W. F. Fitch, General Claim Agent of the Chicago & Northwestern, charging Lewis with the ering of manslaughter. The preliminary examination will be held to-morrow.

WINE, WOMEN, AND CARDS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Corvins's, O., June 8.—James S. Crane, the late defaulting Postmaster at London, O., was this morning sentenced by Judge Swing, of the United States Circuit Court, to imprisonment for one year in the Montgomery County Jail at Dayton. Many years ago Crane was left a large life estate, but, although now a comparatively young man, he has gone through it, wine, women, and cards being his constant companions for years. It is understood that he is also liable to prosecution on several counts for forging the

names of relatives. His sentence to-day is regarded as extremely light, considering his character and crime.

ATTEMPTED LYNCHING.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
EAST SAGINAW, Mich., June 8.—An attempt was made to-day at Chesaning to lynch four of the circus employés who are implicated in the murder of Monday night. They were escorted to the depot by a posse of twelve men, who kept the mob of fully 300 men back with loaded revolvers. The prisoners were finally put on the train and brought to Saginaw City. Their names are J. Hughes, John Quinn, Sim Robinson, and William Murray,—the last two colored. Murray halls from Chicago. The prisoners will all be brought into court to-morrow.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

NORTH MANCHESTER, Ind., June 8.—Last night the Chicago, Wabash & Michigan Railway ticket-office of this place was entered by burglars, who are following Van Amburgh's circus, but were scared away before getting anything. They entered other places, and were more successful. They are doing their stealing while the show is going on at night. Other towns have been visited by these crooks.

RAILROADED.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., June 8.—Last Saturday evening Charles Latour snatched Mrs. Meade's pocketbook, containing $25. He arrested on the charge, brought before the City Court, and placed under bond of $800 to answer in the Circuit Court. Yesterday he was indicted by the Grand Jury, and to-day he entered a plea of guilty, and the jury fixed his punishment at three years in the Penitentiary.

LYNCHING OF MURDERERS.

LITTLE Rock, Ark., June 8.—An old man named K. Hall, living near Locksburg, was robbed and afterwards murdered in Sevier County a few days ago by three negroes, who assisted him to cross a swollen creek. The fact becoming known by the citizens, they turned out in a body and captured the murderers, who confessed, and hanged them to a tree near the spot where they committed their dastardly crime.

NEW MEXICO DESPERADOES.

NEW MEXICO DESPERADOES.

Espnola, N. M., June 8.—Two desperadoes named Knowles and Connors attacked Voorhees' store, intending to rob it, and shot the proprietor twice, probably fatally. The latter returned the fire, and the desperadoes fled. A lynching party immediately organized and pursued. Knowles was shot dead. Connors was captured and returned to-day, and undoubtedly will be lynched to-night.

DISEMBOWELED.

Four Smith, Ark., June 8.—A difficulty occurred yesterday at Oak Bower, a small village near here, between Pres Ingraham and Andy Rhea about a well-anger, in the course of which Ingraham cut Rhea in the bowels, inflicting a fatal wound. Ingraham took to the woods and escaped.

SENTENCED.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa., June 8.—George W. Hubeley, a mall-route agent, convicted of stealing from the malls, was refused a new trial, and sentenced to pay a fine of $100, costs of prosecution, and undergo imprisonment one year in the Penitentiary.

INDICTMENT OF LAW-BREAKERS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

DECATUR, Ill., June 8.—To-day George Lander was indicted for the rape of Mrs. Mary Sturgess, aged 70 years, and Herman Myers and William Clark, of St. Louis, for robbery. All are in jail.

A DEPUTY-SHERIFF MURDERED.
DANVILLE, Va., June 8.—In Stokes County, North Carolina, on Thursday night, Frank Baker, a Deputy-Sheriff, was shot and killed by Jesse Smith, for whom he had a warrant of arrest. Smith escaped.

A BOLD ROBBERY.

A BOLD ROBBERY.

GALVESTON, Tex., June 8.—A single highwayman, masked, stopped the Fredericksburg stage, on board of which were four passengers with the driver, and riffled the mails and robbed the passengers.

A POSTMASTER.

Columbus, O., June 8.—James C. Crane, defaulting Postmaster at London, O., was to-day sentenced by Judge Swing to one year's imprisonment in the Montgomery County Jail.

CONVICT KILLED.

CONVICT KILLED.

THOMASTON, Mc., June 8.—Samuel E. Haines, serving a life sentence for the murder of a guard, was fatally shot to-day in making his third attempt to escape.

ATTEMPTED ESCAPE.

GALVESTON, Tex., June 8.—The News' special says Dr. Ball, in jail at Tyler for murder, and six other prisoners made a dash for liberty. Ball and three men were recaptured.

ROBBER SHOT AND KILLED.

SANTA FE, N. M., June 8.—Valentine Marquis was shot and killed by Fred Baxter while attempting to rob the latter's room.

GEN. HILLIARD.

He Announces His Intention of Retiring to Private Life—Col. Ellott to Succeed Him as Adjutant-General of the State.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

SPRINGFIELD, Ill., June 8.—Adjt.-Gen. Hillard to-day announced that he proposed to retire to private life next month. This news will be a surprise to the militia of the State. Gen. Hillard was first appointed to his present position by Gov. Beveridge in 1875, and was reappointed by Gov. Cullom under the new military code in 1877. He went into office when the State had but a few independent and struggling military companies, and has since rendered efficient service in systematizing and improving the service. Upon him has devolved the labor of perfecting the details of the organization, and in this work he has shown great zeal. In fact, Gen. Hillard was an enthusiast upon the subject of the State militia to such an extent that his will intended efforts have occasionally been misunderstood, and he has become unpopular in some quarters. But he will retire with the satisfaction of knowing that he has contributed largely to the advance made of late years in the organization and equipment of the Illinois National Guard, and that he has performed his duties faithfully. Gov. Cullom has decided to appoint Col. Isaiah H. Elliot, of Princeton, Bureau County, as his successor. Co

New Mexican Vigilants at Work.
SANTA FE, N. M., June 11.—The shooting scrape at Espanola night before last, in which Goodrich was wounded and Knowles was shot dead by Vigilants, had its sequel last night. Commons, who with Knowles, attacked Goodrich's store, and had escaped night before last, was yesterday forenoon captured six miles from Espanola and brought back there a prisoner. At 12 o'clock last night six masked men took him from the place of his confinement and hung him to a telegraph pole, where he was found dead this morning. The lynchers are not known. The violent death of these two men will doubtless have a salutary effect on the rough element in Espanola.
knowles-espanola-1881-06-08.A10:
Tragical Tales.
At Houston, Texas, on the 12th inst., Jack Dempsey, a wheelwright, was shot dead by W. A. Phillips, an express messenger, whom Dempsey attempted to kill at Henrietta.

John Taylor, a negro, who had grossly assaulted a white woman, was taken from Greenboro, N. C., jail and hanged on the night of the 12th, during the eclipse of the moon.

A stabbing affray occurred at Louisville, Ky., on the 11th inst., in which Mack Watson (colored) was killed.

Geo. C. Gattling, of San Francisco, stabbed his wife to death at a beer garden on the 10th inst.

Three masked men called J. E. Martin out of his house at Beiknap, Texas, on the 10th, and shot him dead.

Manly Ellis and Wight Newson, of Wilsom, N. C., both being in love with the same girl, quarreled on the 9th inst., when Ellis shot and killed Newson.

George Henderson, of McKeesport, Pa., while walking in the cemetary with a young lady, on the 7th inst., was set upon by a party of roughs and so badly beaten that he has since died.

Barry Corpenter shot and killed his brother, Lee Carpenter, fifteen miles west of New Albany, Ind., on the 9th inst. Barry, who is a low character, had been charged by Lee with seducing his own daughter.

At Soda Springs, five miles west of Leadville, Col., on the 9th inst., Otto Ballainx shot and killed a man named Andrews.

Louis Paxton, aged 19, was found in a field near St. Paul, Neb., on the 8th inst., with a rope around his neck and fastened to a plough handle, a bullet hole behind the right ear and the skull broken. His horses and wagon were gone. Vigilantes are in pursuit of the murderers.

Samuel D. Haines, serving a life sentence for murdering a guard, attempted to escape at Thomaston, Me., on the 8th inst., and was shot dead.

A difficulty occurred on the 8th inst., at Oak Bower, a small place near Fort Smith, Ark., between Thomas Ingraham and Andy Rhea, in the course of which Rhea was fatally wounded in the bowels.

An old man named Hull, living near Locksburg, Ark., was murdered in Sevier county, that state, by three negroes who were captured and hung by citizens. They confessed the deed before the final moment.

Two desperadoes named Knowles and Conners attacked Voorhees' store at Espanola, N. M., and shot the proprietor twice, probably fatally. A lynching party overtook the miscreants, shooting Knowles dead and lynching Conners.

Lewis Sweeden was assassinated while sitting on his porch in Van Buren county, Ark. It is whispered that he knew too much to suit certain "moonshiners."

In Stokes county, N. C., on the night of the 7th inst., Frank Baker, deputy sheriff, was shot and killed by Jesse Smith, for whom he had a warrant of arrest.

Charles D. Kidder, aged 35, traveling salesman for a Boston dry goods firm, was shot dead at Springfield, Mass., on the 6th inst., by his half-brother, D. Wright, aged 17.

A party of roughs attached to a circus attacked a dancing party at the village of Chesaning, Mich., on the night of the 7th. A policeman was pounded to death, and several persons were badly hurt.

A difficulty over a payment of 15 cents caused a man named Lee to stab fatally one Jennings, a negro, at Dolby Springs, Bowie county, Texas, on the 7th. Jenning's wife, who witnessed the fight, ran to her husband's aid, and with a hatchet fearfully mangled Lee. He is not expected to recover.

Wm. Murphy, the divorced husband of Mrs. N. McClarum, shot Mrs. McC. through the back, near Pittsburg, Pa., on the 7th, and then shot himself through the head. Mrs. McClarum will recover.

Capt. Costernaruff, a hero of the Crimean war, was shot and killed in the streets of Sebastapol by a retired colonel of the Russian army.

At a Joplin, Mo., variety theater on the 7th inst., a shooting affray was occasioned by a dispute in regard to terms of sale of the institution. C. F. Thompson, stage manager, and Thomas Carney, an employee, were killed.

GENERAL NEWS.
John Burroughs' experiment in introducing English skylarks into this country is not a success.

Twenty-three rioters have been sentenced at Cork to four months' imprisonment. The others were liberated.

A duel was fought in Clarendon, S. C. the other day, the pistols being loaded by friends of the combatants with cork bullets.

Gen. W. T. Sherman has accepted an invitation to attend the New England Fair at Worcester, September 7th.

A diabolical plot to blow up a stove foundry in Chicago, by loading a mould with powder, was discovered Saturday just as the workmen were about to turn in the red-hot iron. The plot was originated by strikers.

Bishop Fitzgerald thinks that if evictions are stopped until the land bill is passed there will be little further violence. He avers that the Skibbeen troubles are in no way connected with the land league.

Two New Mexican desperadoes attacked a store and shot the proprietor fatally. The latter returned the fire. The desperadoes fled. A lynching party pursued. One was shot dead and one captured.

A Nebraska village was entirely swept away by a cyclone last week.

Clara Folz, the San Francisco woman lawyer, being told by the opposing council in court that a woman's proper place was at home raising children, retorted: "A woman had better be engaged in almost any business than raising such men as you are, sir."

An army officer who professes to know, says that the viridict of the court of inquiry in the Whittaker case is that Whittaker mutilated himself.

Lightning killed a nephew of Secretary Robeson, in Kansas, the other day. The fluid never can be trained to strike in the right place.

Mr. Thomas F. Murphy of Augusta has become associate editor of the New Hampshire Daily Patriot.

Mr. Thomas F. Mur

Call Out the Troops.
Call Out the Troops.
San Antonio Express.
The people down about Larodo.
The people down about Laredo do not seem to like the idea of a colored inspector being appointed to keep an eye on them. A mulatto by the name of Samuel R. Hurst, from New Orleans, has recently assumed the duties of inspector, or river guard, and the people are rebellious. A gentleman just up from Laredo reports that Hurst was shot at three or four times the other night, and barely escaped being killed.
laredo-laredo-1881-09.A3:
CRIME.
In an affray at Lick Run, O., Richard Williamson shot James and Scott Tipton, the former fatally.

ALDERIAN PITTS, a wealthy farmer near Murfreesboro, Tenn., was assassinated in his melon-patch, evidently because he had commenced a divorce suit.

A negro river guard at Laredo, Texas, has several times been fired upon, it is believed by Mexicans, on account of his color.

The embezzlement of ex-Secretary Stuart, of the Brooklyn board of education, is now shown to be $107,500, and he has been rearrested.

ELLA St. CLAIRE, formerly a variety actress, in Mobile, married a negro, who was indicted for miscegenation, whereupon she sprang into the river and ended her career.

OTWAY B. ZANTZINGER, a young merchant of Baltimore, a nephew of Mrs. Admiral Farragut, has been arrested and sent to St. Louis for obtaining under false pretenses $7,000 worth of flour.

GEN. MORTON, the swindler, has reached Richmond, and the police are anxious to prevent a lynching. Miss Turpen, the victim of one of his bigamous marriages, lives in strict seclusion in that city with her widowed mother.

In the Jennie Cramer murder case, at New Haven, Henry C. Allen, a printer, has identified James Malley, Jr., as the person whom he saw riding with the murdered girl on the night of Aug. 5 which is considered a point of the greatest importance.

POLICE CAPTAIN HATHAWAY, of Chicago, went to Milwaukee in search of Nolan, who murdered a dock-laborer in a saloon on Michigan avenue. The man he sought resembled Nolan, but had lost no front teeth, which was positive proof of being on the wrong track.

GEN. MORTON, the bigamist and swindler, was taken from the train on the outskirts of Richmond, Va., and quietly placed in jail. His appearance has undergone a wonderful change in a few weeks, but the detectives say it is simulated. A showman offers $600 for the privilege of exhibiting him for one night.

A CLERGYMAN of Dayton, O., writes to the authorities of Richmond, Va., that he united in marriage an estimable lady and Morton, the bigamist, the latter giving the name of Lieutenant-Governor Miller, of Minnesota. This is the fifteenth matrimonial victim of the prisoner.

THOMAS H. LOWERRE, a compositor employed on the Chicago Tribune, was shot dead by his landlord, James B. Duncan, a photographer doing business on State street. The deed originated in charges of criminal intimacy between Lowerre and Mrs. Duncan. The killing was preceded by a furious fight, in which Duncan's shoulder-blade was broken.

Two men known to be robbers entered the train at Comstock's N. Y., and information was telegraphed to Albany and Saratoga officers. In an effort to capture them near Mechanicsville one of the thieves shot Deputy Sheriff Port, of Saratoga, in the neck. The fire was promptly returned, the robber being hit in the forehead. The accomplice undertook to run away, and was shot in the neck by a farmer.

linden-linden-1881-07-10.A1:
NEWS FROM OUR NEIGHBORS. TEXAS. Last Thursday Dr. H. J. Avinger, who resides on the East Line railroad, not far from Jefferson died of wounds received some days before at the hands of a negro, Hicks Ross, who disembowel him with a knife. The murderer was arrested and confined in Linden jail. FLORIDA. In the Gulf off Pensacola, at the red snapper banks, some days since, the water was so hot in the well of a fishing smack that about half a cargo of snappers died. The vessel returned to the banks, caught more fish and preserved them alive by some of the crew getting down into the well and keeping them constantly in motion. The fish seemed to become stupid and drowsy, evidently overcome by the heat, but their method of keeping them on the move enabled the fishermen to reach port with a profitable catch. They report like experience in years gone by, but not on so extensive a scale. ARKANSAS.
ARKANSAS.

During the past year two hundred houses have been built at Little Rock.

Near Ozark, last week, Fred Choate, a horse-thief, committed suicide to keep from being arrested.

A panther which has been preying on stock between Kensett and Searcy, has again made its appearance.

An oil-mill and cotton compress is to be erected at Fort Smith under the direction of Zeb Ward and E. Urquhart.

At Wiley's Grove, Van Buren county, a few days since a little daughter of M. Hatchett was tossed on the horns of a vicious cow and severely injured.

ALABAMA.

At Bridgeport last Friday an elopement was prevented by the indignant father and brother of the young lady, who intercepted the young couple at the depot, and presenting pistols at them, the bride was taken home by the father and the young man was ordered to leave.

On Thursday last, at Randolph, a negro entered the bedroom of Mrs. Hudgins, wife of the bridge foreman of the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia railroad, and attempted to outrage her person. She escaped from the room to the yard, where the negro caught her, and a desperate struggle ensued. Her cries brought assistance, and the villain fled and escaped. She received several blows on the head, and her throat and arms were severely bruised.

MISSISSIPPI.

The machinery for the Yocone cotton

MISSISSIPPI.

The machinery for the Yocona cotton mills has been received at Water Valley.

The storm of last week blew down nearly all the corn between Artesia and Columbus.

Anthony Fallelove, a negro who is under sentence of death, has again escaped from the Vaiden jail.

Near Fulton, several days since, Monroe Roberts committed suicide by shooting himself with a pistol. Cause, insanity.

At Water Valley last Sunday night a lamp broke in the Presbyterian church, setting the building on fire. The congregation extinguished the flames.

Last Wednesday night the residence of W. B. Saunders, four miles south of Grenada, was destroyed by fire. Cause, incendiarism. Nothing was saved from the building.

At Grenada, a few days since, J. W. Holland secured a judgment for $1000 damages against George W. Beard, Circuit Court Clerk, because the latter had issued a marriage license to Holland's daughter, she being under the age of eighteen. The case was appealed.

TENNESSEE.

Fine crops are reported from Haywood county.

At Chattanooga, last Friday, a man named Jones, from Ringgold, got into a row with Peyton Gray, a colored barber, and stabbed

Gray in the head twice with a knife and escaped.

Cashman, Bailey and Williams, the safecrobbers, are on trial at Brownsville.

A new Roman Catholic church is to be erected at Knoxville at a cost of $25,000.

Last week, in Wayne county, a yoke of oxen was killed while lttched to a tree during a thunderstorm.

Last week, near Lynnville, the residence of Joe P. Boyd was burned to the ground. Nothing was saved. No insurance.

At Chattanooga a general dog-killing progresses favorably. Dogs of both high and low degree unmuzzled become victims.

A gray eagle, seven feet ten inches from tip to tip, was recently killed near Rogersville. Its talons were covered with sheep's wool.

At Columbia last Saturday William Porter was shot dead in a saloon by Hugh and Sam Cook. Six or eight shots were fired. The Cooks were arrested.

Last week, near Brownsville, Gus Bolling, colored, was killed by the sides of a well caving in upon him. His cries for help were heard for several hours.

The Press and Times says the Courthouse at Rogersville has for years been a gambling hell, made so by disreputable parties who play cards therein at night.

Neal's State Gazette is out again, but in small size. It will soon be republished with new type and from new presses. Colonel Tom Neal is not the man to back down from a fire.

Near Columbia, at the Old Wellgrove, a debate is progressing between J. B. Martin, of the Church of Christ, and H. Bellap, o the Church of Latter-Day Saints, on the subject of Mormonism and divine inspiration as to the Mormon Bible and King James's version of the Scriptures.

Last week, at Knoxville, a dead white child was found in a vault on Methodist Hill. The jury of inquest discovered it to be the child of Harriet Kellar, a white girl. It was born alive, but no evidence of violence was found on its person. The girl was arrested on a charge of infanticide.

A recent shipment of 150,000 feet of Dyer county timber has been made direct to France. The logs were "squared up" in the woods, and the ends well oiled to keep the sun from cracking them. They were then rafted out of the Forked Deer to New Orleans, from which place ships took them to France.
linden-linden-1881-07-10.A2:
TEXAS TOPICS.
Waco had a splendid and most enjoyable celebration of the Fourth.

Genuine cotton worms have been found in some fields in Rusk county.

Mrs Jane Glow died suddenly Sunday morning in Sherman at the age of thirty-two years.

Mr. W. T. Lane and Miss Mollie E. Smith were married in Smith county last week.

James R. Seely, Esq., a prominent young lawyer of Mexia, died of black jaundice on the 4th.

Sue Allen, a colored woman at Waco, accidentally shot her hand off with a pistol on the Fourth.

The celebration of the Fourth at San Antonio is represented as having been a very tame affair.

There were fourteen deaths in Houston last week, one from drowning and five were children.

There is a great deal of sickness in Franklin county, but of a mild form being thermic fever generally.

There were seven marriages in Harris county last week and fourteen persons went to that matrimonial borne whence they will never return.

Fifteen thousand persons are said to have been present at the celebration at Denison on the Fourth.

The mortality among the children in Sherman and neighborhood during the past two months is alarming.

The condition of the corn crop in Walker county is deplorable and cotton is suffering because of the long dry spell.

Miss Georgie Johnson was thrown from a buggy at Bastrop Sunday, being painfully bruised and dislocating an ankle.

An excursion train of nine coaches filled with colored people from Houston went to San Antonio on the Fourth for a holiday.

The track of the International railroad is completed sixty miles west of San Antonio, and trains are running to a point fifty-four miles west.

D. P. Morrison has been appointed judge, and John D. Morrison district attorney, of the thirty sixth district. Both are residents of Aisscosa county.

Ed. Moore, one of the supposed Davis state police murderers of Hause and Gadbold at Tyler, eight years ago, was arrested at Jefferson on the 4th.

The corner stone of a new Episcopal church at Bastrop will be laid on August the 11th Bishop Gregg and other divines of that church will be present.

Rev. Dr. Kavanaugh, late of Houston, but now of Kentucky, and seventy-six years of age, married a buxom young widiw at Mt. Sterling, Kentucky, a few days ago.

A new street railroad company has organized at Houston and from the names to be seen among the officers and directors, it is evident an abundance of money is behind the enterprise.

Dysentery of a most malignant type is epidemic in some portions of Rusk county, and prevails to such an extent that there are not well people enough to wait on the sick or bury the dead.

The Lamar county horticultural society gave its third annual exhibition at Paris on the fourth. The display of vegetables was not so large as last year, but there was a vast attendance.

All the milk drinkers at a boarding house in Sherman were made sick by the milk they drank on the Fourth. A physician who was summoned, said the cows had been eating some poisonous weed.

The Good Hope western association of colored Baptists will convene at Marlin on the 14th inst. and remain in session several days. A Sunday school convention will be held at the same time.

The capitol commissioners have adopted the Herald's suggestion, and will invite each county in the state to contribute a representative stone, appropriately inscribed, to be placed in the new capitol.

The advertisement for bids for the erection of the new state house is to be published four times in the New York World, Chicago Times, St. Louis Republican, Dallas Herald, Galveston News, Houston Post, San Antonio Express, Jefferson Democrat and Austin Statesman.

The teachers' normal schools, now going on, are not supported by the state or in any wise under the control of the state authorities. They were inaugurated and supported out of the Peabody fund, and it was as an agent of this fund that Mr. Hollingsworth went north for the teachers.

A telegraph operator at the stone quarry of the Gulf Colorado & Santa Fe railroad near Brenham, was struck on the head by a man named Nicholson, Sunday, and painfully though not necessarily fatally hurt.

A majority of the city council of San Antonio will resign to keep from obeying the mandamus of the federal court at Austin to levy a special tax to pay a subsidy voted years ago, to a proposed railroad from Indianola to that city. In the meantime the case will be carried to the United States supreme court.

A correspondent of the Henderson Times, signing himself Suggs, announces that he discovered a comet in the heavens a few morning's ago, a while before daylight, as he happened to be gazing northward, and he hastens to inform a startled world of the fact. He ought to have that Rochester $200 by all means.

George WLynchwhose house and children in it, was burned near Hoxley some time ago, was convicted of murder in Leadville a few days ago. He always suspected a certain man of burning his house and children and swore he would kill him, and it is supposed this is the man he killed at Leadville.

Dr. H. J. Avinger, wounded by a negro some ten days ago, died on the 30th ultimo.
Dr. H. S. Avinger, wounded by a negro some ten days ago, died on the 30th ultimo. A post mortem examination revealed the fact that two of the intestines had been cut, and gangrene ensuing, death resulted. From accounts of the affair it was an unproycked and most malicious murder, yet the murderer was granted bail in $2,500, which he has been unable to give.

is parched and almost ruined for want of rain.
Dich Wood, a notorious character in Western Texas, was taken from the sheriff, who had him under arrest, by vigilantes, on the 26th, near Cariso, and shot to death. The vigilance committee, in that part of the State, has been previously unheard of.
On Saturday, the 25th ult., at Avenger Station, on the East Line railroad, Dr. H. J. Avenger engaged in a row with a negro, during which the latter slashed the doctor across the bowels with a razor, inflicting a mortal wound.
A report from Piedras Negras says that several American engineers were killed in the interior of Mexico recently, in consequence of a dispute regarding the right of way, but it is impossible to get any reliable particulars of the affair.
linden-linden-1881-07-10.A5:
Marshall.
Marshall, July 12.—The county of Harrison having been added to the third United States collection district, Mr Umbdenstock, the collector will continue to make his headquarters at Marshall.

The Dixon Car Work here are booming. A large force was added last week and more are expected this week. Those employed recently are skilled German workmen, who were brought from St. Louis and will add two hundred to the population of Marshall. The new importation will arrive Friday.

It is rumored, and pretty well confirmed, that the negro who killed Dr. Avenger, at Avenger station, in Cass county, was taken from the jail by a mob on Sunday and hanged. The rumors are confirmed by telegraph dispatches. The Linden jail is one of the strongest in the state and great violence must have been used.
linden-linden-1881-07-10.A6:
will hold their annual re-union at Corsicana, on the 3d proximo.

Bellville, on Tuesday, voted in favor of corporation for school purposes, by a majority of twenty eight votes.

Considerable sickness prevails at and around Marquez, in Leon county, and a number of deaths have resulted recently.

San Antonio has two clubs, one an anti-treating club, and the other a club to accept all treats offered but never to reciproscate.

Dr. M. C. McGregor, of Wesley, was shot through the leg, both bones being broken, on Sunday by the accidental discharge of a pistol.

The Tyler branch of the teachers' normal school was opened Tuesday morning. Prof J. R. Horne, of Alleytown, Pennsylvania, in charge.

Two hundred new hands, skilled Germans from St. Louis, have been added to the force of workmen in the Dixon car works at Marshall.

From almost every portion of southern, western and central Texas comes the glad tidings of heavy rains and rejoicings of the farmers.

A son of Mr. Kirkpatrick, living at Lampasas Springs, was thrown from his horse, Tuesday, and so seriously injured that he was not expected to live.

Some of the tooth doctors in the state are beginning to ask for a dental department in the state university. That is getting down to the root of the thing.

Dr. L. S. Rayfield, formerly a physician of Jefferson and then of Austin, died at Atlanta Georgia, on the 7th inst. and was buried at Jefferson on Sunday last.

The corn crop in Colorado county is fair and the cotton very fine. The boll worm has made its appearance in some localities, but Paris green is being freely used.

The case of the state against Reuben, Henry and Williford Laggins for murder, in Waller county, has been set for the 18th inst. at Bellville on change of venue.

The Gulf, Colorado & Santa Fe railroad seems to have benefitted Bellville very much, as the place is rapidly improving, with new brick buildings going up on every hand.

A man named Abe McCarty had a preliminary examination at Weatherford, Tuesday, on charge of assault with intent to rape Mrs. Watson and was admitted to bail in the sum of $1000.
A heavy rain and wind storm prevailed at Navasota and that vicinity Sunday, and the residence of Mr. Varnadoe, three miles from Navasota, was blown off its foundation. Nobody was hurt.

Two men in San Antonio claim to have seen an aerolite fall into the river back of their place of business a few nights ago. The spirits commonly used in San Antonio is calculated to make men see aerolites in fact a whole menagerie.

Miss L. M. Crunk, living at Gause, went to visit a neighbor, Mrs. R. S. Cox, Tuesday morning, and when near the house was attacked by a vicious dog belonging to Mrs. Cox. She was badly bitten on the arms and legs and Mrs. Cox in rescuing her was also bitten.

Additional testimony in favor of Wm. Burton, under sentence of death at Weatherford, was mailed to the governor on Tuesday, and it is hoped his sentence will be commuted to imprisonment. A belief in his innocence seems to be gaining ground, as some developments are slowly coming to light to establish that fact.

The Gulf, Colorado & Santa Fe railroad opened business at Belton on the 16th of last February, and up to July 1st, a little over four months, the tonnage received at that point was 10 833 042 pounds, and the amount forwarded 3 288 509 pounds. The tonnage shipped consisted of 2 315 bales of cotton and seventy-five car loads of grain with some sundries.

There seems to be little doubt of the lynching of the negro who murdered Dr. H. J. Avinger in Cass county recently. He was confined in the Linden jail, and when Dr. Avinger died of his wound public sentiment was so strong against the perpetrator of the heinous deed that it would not await the slow process of the law, with its delays and uncertainties.

Sheriff Brown, of Lee county, returned to Giddings on Monday with a man named George Keith, charged with the murder of a man named McFall several years ago. A man named Lasion was arrested at the time and trled for the murder, but was acquitted as he was innocent. Subsequent events led to the suspicion of Keith, and after several years he was traced to Sabine parish, Louisiana, where Sheriff Brown arrested him on requisition from the governor.

There is a camp meeting going on at Live Oak, in Hill county. Last Monday evening a young gentleman named Massey went to the meeting in company with two young lady friends and took his seat with them, as seems to be the custom now everywhere unless it is in remote country communities, but in a little while he was waited upon by two men who notified him that he must move his seat over among the men. This he declined to do, at the request of the ladies who were strangers. The men went off but soon returned reinforced with several others and without more ado they seized young Massey and unceremoniously hustled him off some distance from the meeting. Massey was not hurt, but his clothes were torn and he proposes to investigate the right of camp meeting committees to treat quiet and respectable people in such a manner.

A correspondent of the Coleman Telegram of June 30th, magnanimously informs an anxious public "that there are cases in the desert of monotonous life" but fails to state how life can be monotonous with an oasis here and there in its desrt. He then goes on to tell all about a barbecue and celebration that took place on the Fourth of July, at which three hundred to five hundred persons were present. There was an oration, of course, after the reading of the declaration of independence, and the youthful orator entered fully into the occasion. 10 EAST SAGINAW ITEMS. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. EAST SAGINAW, Mich., June 1.—W. B. Clark, convicted of horse-stealing, was sentenced to-day to State Prison for fifteen years. A charge for murder is also hanging over his head. Edward Brulette, an accomplice of Clark, was given three years. Thomas Powers, assault with intent to murder, three years in State Prison. ON TRIAL FOR MURDER. LITTLE Rock, Ark., June 1.—The trial of Jackson Green, charged with murdering his brother-in-law, Berry, at Bowling, in Lonoke County, a year ago, began here to-day. The case was tried last year but a new trial granted for the reason that the record did not show that the prisoner had been formally arraigned. The prisoner's mother and two sisters were present in court listening to the proceedings.
BENTENCE OF A COUNTERFEITER.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich., June 1.—Louis J. Kemp, alias Pete Conklin, one of the worst and most dangerous crooks in Western Michigan, arrested at Kalamazoo for showing a quantity of counterfeit coin, was to-day sentenced by Judge Withey, of the United States Court here to the Detroit House of Correction for two years. He pleaded guilty.

A HOSPITAL OFFICIAL IN TROUBLE
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
MILWAUKEE, June 1.—Dr. Marden, the Superintendent of the County Hospital, was suspended by the County Board to-day for alleged criminal intimacy with a weak-minded inmate and the attempted rape of another. It thought the charges are trumped up to displace Marden.

GILLESBURG, Ill., June 1.—A shooting atray occurred five miles southeast of here last evening between George Balloy and Luto Wallick. The ball entered Wallick on the left side near the nipple, and passed upwards. The round is considered dangerous. There was a woman at the bottom of it.

CHARGED WITH FORGERY.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Boston, June 1.—John Lyman Randall was arrested hero to-day on a charge of forging an assignment of a patent for asphalt block pavement. The patent is now owned by the International Paving Company of New York, who secured it from Robert Skinner and Bounet Bonnet, of San Francisco. Sales of the right have been made in several cities in Pennsylvania, in Detroit, and other places in the West, and many Eastern cities. The sales aggregate thousands of dollars. Randall claims that he is an agent for one Charles O'Connor, but will not say where or who he is, and has an alleged genuine power of attorney from him.

KILLED HER PARAMOUR.

KILLED HER PARAMOUR.
LEXINGTON, Ky., June 1.—Silas Payno (colored) was found dead last night in the house occupied by him and Josephine Smith. The neighbors heard them quarrelling. To-day an examination of the promises showed the washboard was split to pieces and that Payno's neck was broken by a downward blow. It is informed that the woman struck him with the washboard and thus killed him. The parties were not married, but have been living together a number of years.

SPRINGFIELD, Ill., June 1.—The Governor has pardoned George W. Strange, who was convicted of murder in May, 1874, by the Colos County Circuit Court and sentenced to the Penitentiary for twenty years. The pardon was granted on the recommendation of the Judge and State's Attorney.

FATAL AFFRY.

SEDALIA, Mo., June 1.—A farmer named Long, living near Fayette, got into a quarrel with a negro field hand named Sebree two or three days ago, during which Long was fatally beaten over the head with a hoo, and Sebree mortally wounded by a pistol-shot.

NEW ORLEANS, June 1.—T. J. Stephens brutally murdered an old German at Lake Providence. The murderer escaped.

PETTY LARCENY.

Stealing In a Toy Store.

A poor woman upon whose efforts depends the support of a half-score of small children, and perhaps a drunken husband, steals a loaf of bread—that's "larcony." A prominent man, surrounded by all the luxuries that wealth can buy and all the pliant associations that social distinction can confer, steals a few fancy articles for the toilet—that's "kleptomania." The woman pleads her poverty and the distress of children, and shows her worn and bony fingers in proof of the storm industry and frugality of her life. But the Justice before whom she is arraigned has heard so often the old, old story of starvation and manifold misery that his heart has become burdened, and without so much as a passing sigh he commits her with her scalding tears and wringing hands to the House of Correction, there to work out the full utonement of the injury done the baker from whom she stole the loaf. The prominent man makes a practice of helping himself generously to whatsoever pleases his fancy in the establishment of another, and the matter is hushed up so carefully that even the pilferer himself is not aware that the ones whom he has robbed are informed of his misdeeds. Kleptomania has an advantage over larcony. It is much more fashionable and utter to use the word "kleptomania" than that vulgar and altogether reprehensible term "thief." The fashionable shop-lifter, in case of discovery, has money to buy his freedom, and friends to quiet the wagging tongues of sound-loving people who do not believe in the conferring of distinctions in points of law and justice. And should a rumor become circulated to the effect that Mr. — was caught in the net of appropriating unto himself property which he does not intend to pay for, and which he thinks will not be missed, the charitable people of the community debate with themselves and finally conclude that a great abundance of the "occourtricity of genius," or an astonishing degree of long-drawn-out "absent-mindedness," is responsible for what ordinarily is called theft. A boy named Henry Stracke, stabbed his ten-year-old companion, Michael Hilberger to the heart, on the 3d inst., at Lancaster, O.

James Hogan, of Monticello, O., shot his divorced wife six times, inflicting dangerous injuries, and then with one shot killed himself on the 3d inst.

Elijah Sterling, proclaiming himself the son of God, attacked his wife and son with an axe on the 3d inst. at Crisfield, N. Y. The wife is fatally wounded, but young Sterling received only a flesh wound.

At Chicago, on the morning of the 3d inst., Thomas Burns shot and killed Charles Bell, his partner in the saloon business. They quarreled over money matters.

Melton and Baker, notorious horse thieves and burglars, were killed by a sheriff while resisting arrest in Hayes county, Texas, on the 3d.

Peter Morelli was fatally shot by Geo. Melasch, a restaurant keeper at San Francisco, Cal. They quarreled over a mining claim.

John Lynch ambushed and assassinated Charles Lyles about ten miles away from Leadville, Col., on the 1st inst. Cause, a long-standing quarrel over a mining claim.

Daniel McDonald was discharged from a Ludington, Mich., saw mill on the 31st ult., and on the night of the 1st was discovered cutting the belt in the mill by a boy named James Corwin. McDonald turned on his discoverer and kicked him to death.

E. D. Baldwin, of Forest City, Ark., on the 2d inst., by a man named Jones. Baldwin promptly shot his assailant dead and was acquitted by a jury.

A startling discovery was made on the Scofield farm in Woodruff county, Ark., on the 2d, being the mutilated body of a man. The trunk of the body lay in an outhouse, with the heart cut out, and one arm and the head severed. The heart was found in a neighboring field. No clue to the murder.

A number of convicts attempted to escape from a train near Bernham, Texas, on the 2d. Two were killed and four wounded, two mortally. One escaped.

Four young white men meddled with the cabin of Dennis Broteuni, a colored man, near Jefferson, Texas, on the night of the 1st inst. Broteuni opened fire on the party, killing Calvin Cope, and mortally wounding Israel La Grande. The survivors killed the negro and escaped.

At Senatobia, Miss., on the 2d inst., one McCracken engaged in a pistol fight with a barber named Blount. McCracken, who is chancery clerk of Tate county, died of wounds received, and Blount lingers in jail with mortal wounds.

I. J. Stephens brutally murdered an old German at Lake Providence, La., and escaped.

John Thomas, a farmer on the Red river, Texas, got into trouble on the 1st inst., and killed Deputy Sheriffs Krelht and Samuel and Charles Meredith.

A negro field hand named Sebree quarreled with his employer, named Long, near Fayette, Mo., and beat him with fatal effect, using a hoe. Sebree was mortally wounded by Long, before he succumbed.

A negro named Matt Butts crully murdered Maj. W. J. Bethea, in Early county, Ga., was captured near Arlington, on the 1st inst., by a mob of 200 men and hung.

Silas Payne, a Lexington, Ky., negro, was found dead in bed on the 31st ult., having been brutally murdered. Josephine Smith, his housekeeper, is charged with the crime.

Holney Hull was shot and instantly killed at Cynthiana, Ky., on the 31st ult., by his brother-in-law Alex. Odor.

M. Seguin, a correspondent of the Paris Telegraph, was killed by Arabs on the 28th ult., at Beja. The murderers were arrested and promptly shot.

E. L. Stickney, a mining man, entered a boarding house at Denver, Col., on the 31st ult., while the people were at dinner, and opened fire on one of the guests, M. F. Campan, a real estate agent, killing him and a Mrs. Devereaux. It is said Campan was improperly intimate with Stickney's wife. The shooting of Mrs. Devereaux was unintentional.

A quarrel arising from some trivial cause led to a duel with knives between two lads named Trent and Strickland, at Waldron, Ark. The latter will probably die, as the flesh on his arms was cut into shoestrings and portions of his legs were slashed off.

John Enrichs, an ex-policeman at Indianapolis, Ind., whose wife was seeking a divorce, shot his wife and her father on the 30th, and then shot himself. Enrichs is dead, but his wife and her father will probably recover.

In a quarrel about wages at North Middletown, Ky., William Cunningham shot and killed John Alexander.

Billy Meton, a notorious thief, was shot dead by Sheriff Martin, while attempting to escape Nankyles station, Texas, on the 30th.

John P. Nunley, near Charleston, S. C., challenged his nephew, George Nunley, aged 19, and killed him before he had chance to fire a shot. Family difficulties caused the murder.

A tramp named Mehan, stabbed a young man named Wm. Copeland, near Bridgeport, Ala., on the 29th ult., because he annoyed him while he was bathing. Copeiand died almost instantly. While the tramp was in prison, Sam Reese, a cousin of Copeland, stepped up and shot him dead. Reese escaped. Wm. Shock killed his brother-in-law Wm. Matthews, by striking him with a chair at Enola, Ark.. on the 30th.

THE ORIGIN OF DIXIE.
Dan Emmett, the old-time negro minstrel, is still performing in the West. He is the author of "Way Down South in Dixie," which was first a "walk round" chorus, written in 1859, for Bryant's Minstrels, then at Mechanic's Hall, Broadway. Emmett lately said to a Cincinnati Enquirer reporter: "I wish I was in Dixie' was a Northern circus expression, and not a Southern one, as many have supposed. I had traveled a great many years with circuses in my younger days, and 'the South' was then considered all that portion of the country below Mason and Dixon's line, called for short "Dixie," by showmen. In the early Fall of the year, when a frost would sometimes overtake a south-bound circus still in the North, the boys would think of the genial warmth of the section they were heading for, and many's the time on such an occasion have I heard them say, 'Well, I wish I was in Dixie's land now.' It was this that gave me the 'catch line' for my song." Two years afterward the rebellion broke out, and Emmett's air, which had become popular in the South, was made the representative tune of the rebels. The author says the work has paid him about $800.

The Mexican Government is paying a high premium for immigrants. It has just concluded a contract with Senior Rizzo, who binds himself to import Italian families to Mexico; he is to receive $60 for each immigrant, male or female, over twelve years, and $30 for each child under twelve years. Besides, a premium of $15 is promised on every imported Italian. The concessions made to the immigrants by the Government are not to be excelled.

Her brother-in-law, Mr. Fisher (both sisters having married brothers) conducts a truck farm and dairy at the place, and has employed several negro farm hands. During the absence in the afternoon of Mr. Fisher and the two Mrs. Fisher, the children, aged respectively seven to ten years, were left in the house, the parents coming to this city to attend to their usual market business. Late in the afternoon information was received that the children had been murdered, and the parents and relations returned to the house to find that the children—a boy and girl—had been cut to such an extent about the head that they probably died almost instantly. The girl, who was the elder, was mangled so badly as to be almost beyond recognition. By the side of the children lay an axe covered with blood and hair, showing conclusively that it was the weapon used to commit the deed. The next step taken was to notify the police, and inquiry revealed that one of the hands, a negro who had been in Mr. Fisher's employ some time, was missing. The news of the murder spread through the neighborhood with great rapidity and soon a crowd was congregaed about the scene. Parties were made up and the count. around was scoured, and with the assistance of the police the guilty party will no doubt be arrested soon. Mrs. Fisher has been very unfortunate since the death of her husband, as a few months ago one of her children was burned to death in the house. The murder has created considerable feeling in this city. Last night, at the K street market, where Mrs. Fisher has a large circle of friends, there was the wildest commotion, and butchers and hucksters were anxious to get away from the market in order, as they said, to take part in lynching the scoundrel if he were caught.
