Thomas Goff's mother, Mary Goff, a married daughter of Christina's, works in service at Ruppert's farm, about three miles from Fisher's, and visits her mother on an average of once a week. During the day Thomas minds cows at Lynch's place, near Brooks' Station, and at night sleeps at his grandmother's. The nearest neighbor to Fisher is a farmer named Kline; who visited the farm Saturday evening, shortly after the murder had been committed, and talked with the Taylors before the police, arrived, but learned nothing from them calculated to throw any light upon the matter.

Rose Taylor is not married, but has of late been receiving attentions from James Stokes, the negro who not a great while ago stood trial in the Criminal Court for butting a man to death. The Taylors have lived at Fisher's about three months, and have paid their rent promptly. In consequence of statements made Christina and Rose Taylor and the boy Thomas Goff were arrested, the first two Saturday night and the boy yesterday, it being considered necessary to hold the latter as a witness. At the inquest yesterday Thomas was confused and non-committal, and, though present during all the excitement Saturday night, swore positively that he had heard nothing of the murder.

An Important Clue.

The trio—mother, daughter and grandson—occupied separate cells at the Second Precinct Station to-day. A reporter of The Critic visited the women and conversed with them, but found them non-committal—still adhering to their original statements that they knew nothing of the murder. Rose Taylor was inclined to be sullen and impudent, but seemed somewhat uneasy at times that Mr. Kline, for whom she had sent last night, did not arrive. She refused to say what she wanted to see the gentleman for, except that she had something to tell him. The boy Thomas was taken into the office of Lieutenant Johnston and asked if he would not tell exactly what he knew about the movements of his grandmother and Aunt Rose Saturday afternoon. It was known that the latter went down to Lynch's and made him hurry home before he had finished his supper. After some hesitancy, Thomas made a statement which is worthy of consideration.

Statement of Thomas Goff.

The boy said: "My Aunt Rose came to Mr. Lynch's, where I was eating my supper, and said, 'Come on Tom; don't wait for nothing.' As we went along I asked her what was the matter, and she said that Mr. Fisher's two children was dead and that we would have to leave the place. When we got home she wanted me to go up to Ruppert's place, where my mother, Mary Goff, lived, to bring her to my grandmother's, so that we all could go away together. My grandmother told me to go up there also, but afterward told me not to go as it was too late. All this was before the police came. My aunt and grandmother acted like they were very much scared and kept on saying that we must leave the place. My aunt walked me very fast from Lynch's. When we got home Mr. Kline came over and asked about the murder. My grandmother said that she had seen somebody go across the field away from Mr. Fisher's house before the murder was discovered, but she didn't say what time it was, or who the person was."

Probably Another Clue.

During the search about Fisher's place yesterday the police found the skirt of an old dress in a brook near where the Taylors lived. When shown to Mr. Fisher and his wife they recognized it as one worn by Christina Taylor when they saw her Saturday morning. The old woman said yesterday that she had thrown it away several days prior to the murder. The police received information to-day, however, that a negro, James Thompson, a laborer employed by Mr. Kline, saw Christina change her dress Saturday afternoon and throw the old one into the brook. At an early hour to-day Detectives Miller and McElfresh went out to Kline's to find Thompson. In the meantime, Mr. Kline had failed to respond to the request of Rose Taylor to visit her at the station.

A Shrewd Policeman's Ideas.

While waiting for something new to be developed, THE CRITIC met Mounted Policeman West, the colored officer who was so active and successful in ferreting out the facts connected with the Hirth murder. Officer West is not engaged in the present case, but has watched it closely on his own account, and when asked what he thought about it, said that of course he was as liable to be mistaken as any one else, but the evidence thus far developed was not sufficient to convince him that the colored women under arrest were the guilty parties. "They are the most ignorant negroes I have ever seen," he said, "and under the circumstances it is natural enough that they should be confused and inclined to mix up statements having no knowledge of the law or its peculiar ways. I believe that the police will have to search further and deeper for the facts." Officer West has had a more varied experience among colored criminals perhaps than any man on the force, and is more perfectly acquainted with their ways, hence the importance which may be attached to his opinion.

What Policeman McNamara Learned.

Mounted Policeman McNamara was sent out to hunt up farmer Kline this morning to bring him in to see Rose Taylor. Mr. Kline was absent when the officer arrived at his farm. While waiting he conversed with people in the vicinity and learned some interesting particulars. In the first place he learned that the husband of the mother of the murdered infants had been dead several years. When he died he left three children. One of these, a girl, was burned to death on Joseph Fisher's farm while endeavoring to start a fire with coal-oil. Another child, born after the father's death, died later, also, from consumption. One of the parties seen by Officer McNamara said that the second child died quite suddenly, and created some talk in the neighborhood, but it was stated to the satisfaction of everybody that the babe died a natural death. This same person said, according to the officer's statement, that, notwithstanding Joseph Fisher's professed affection for his brother's children, he treated them rather harshly at times. queenstown-queenstown-1881-08.A4:
INNOCENTS BRUTALLY SLAUGHTERED.
The Mysterious Murder of Two Children in the County.
AN ADJOURNED INQUEST.
A murder, which seems the more horrible and atrocious when the deed is contrasted with the youth and innocence of the victims, was discovered in the county Saturday evening. At what time the murder was committed is still a mystery, as is also the manner of the crime, and the name and motive of the murderer. The murder occurred on the farm of Joseph Fisher, a market man, which stands on the Fort Bunker Hill road, about a mile north of Brooks' station, in the county. Here Fisher lived with his wife, and widowed sister-in-law, and the two children of the latter, Lizzie, aged six, and Joe, aged three years. Saturday the older members of the family came into the city to attend to their business, and left the children—as they were accustomed to do—alone in the house. Mr. Fisher returned to his home from the Northern Liberty market about six o'clock Saturday evening, drove his wagon through the grounds to the barn, noticing as he passed near the house the children lying on the ground near to trees.

THE MURDER DISCOVERED.

Having attended to his horse he walked to the house and thought he would wake the children, whom he believed were asleep. When he approached them the sight that met his eyes was horrible. They were beyond waking. Their clothing was stained with blood. The girl's skull was crushed in, and there was a terrible wound on the boy's forehead. Mr. Fisher at once gave the alarm. The police of the second precinct were notified, and an investigation of the murder was begun at once. Mr. Fisher returning to the city, took his wife home, who was at the market and the mother of the children, Mrs. Simon Fisher, who is employed as a domestic in the family of Mr. C. Horner, who keeps an eating house on 9th street, opposite the Center market.

ARRESTS MADE.

The first arrests made by the police were those of Mrs. Christina Taylor, and her daughter, Rose, two colored women, living in a stone house on Fisher's place, just at the gate leading from the main road to Mr. Fisher's house. Mrs. Taylor was arrested because she was seen to leave Fisher's house in the afternoon by the farm hands working near by. Yesterday Thomas Goff, grandson of Mrs. Taylor, was arrested. Coroner Patterson held an inquest yesterday morning, and as little light was thrown upon the murder after all the available witnesses were examined, adjourned it until Wednesday next.

SCENE OF THE TRAGEDY.

Fisher's house, which is a neat little cottage, stands among the trees on a little eminence off from the road. It faces south. The children were found at the northwest corner of the house, about thirty feet away, lying between two trees, a walnut and a cedar. Near them was an axe, which had been left in the morning at the wood pile northeast of the house. Some suppose that this weapon had been used by the murderer, though there were no marks upon it. The face of the little girl was placid and she appeared to have died without a struggle. The boy had one arm over his face, and seemed to have struggled. Ephraim Barnes and two colored men, who work on the place, were hoeing in a field southeast of the house in a hollow about 150 yards away. The house was exactly between them and the spot where the bodies were found. These men saw the old colored woman, Taylor, leave the house about four o'clock, their attention being attracted to her by her efforts to get rid of a dog which pursued her, barking furiously.

The Coroner's Inquest.

Yesterday the inquest was held at the house. The following jury was empaneled: James McNabb, jr., W. H. Harvey, John B. Lord, Elbert G. Benson, Lewis Behrens and Francis Oxraneter.

The first witness was Ephraim Barnes, who works on the place, boarding with the family. He testified that he was at work in the field near by with the colored men; that everything was quiet about the house till three or four o'clock in the afternoon, when the dogs made a racket, and looking up he saw an old colored woman coming away from the house; that one of the colored men told him that it was the old woman who lived at the gate; that Mr. Fisher returned home at six o'clock, and about ten minutes afterwards called, and witness ran to the house where he found the children dead; that the colored woman afterwards returned to the house, and he asked her what she had been to the house for, to which she replied that she came to return a washboard; that she had knocked at the front door about half an hour, and could neither see nor hear anyone; that about seven o'clock he saw her again west of the house, apparently looking about the bushes, he asked her what she wanted and she said: "I thought I heard somebody halloa;" he asked her what she had done with the washboard, and she said she took it into the house and set it down by the table in the back room; that she had got in and come out by the front door; that the washboard was found where she said she put it.

Thomas Ham, colored, one of the men working with Barnes, testified to seeing the old colored woman leaving the house.

Margaret Lynch, a neighbor living at Fort Bunker Hill, testified that Rose Taylor came to her house, apparently much excited, about a quarter after 7 o'clock, Saturday evening, and called her nephew, who worked there, saying that he must come at once.

THE UNCLE'S STORY.

Joseph Fisher, uncle of the two murdered children, testified that they were his brother's children, and had lived with him for two years; that he came home Saturday evening between 5 and 6 o'clock; put the horses in the stable, and as he returned to the house found the children dead; that the old colored woman Taylor had picked peas for him some time; he only knew of her coming to the house to borrow the washboard from his wife; the dog would generally bark at her when she came; there was no trouble with the mother of the children about them; she was willing to have the children at the house, and he and his wife liked to have them.

Dr. Hartigan, who made the autopsy, assisted by Dr. Wolhaufter, testified to having found a transverse wound, lacerated and elliptical shaped, ⅛ of an inch long, above the boy's left eye, and another of the same nature diagonally above and behind the left ear; besides several bruises of the scalp, indicating repeated blows by a blunt weapon. The skull was extensively fractured and crushed in two or three places. The examination of the little girl showed a wound of the scalp above the right ear, another below, and a smaller one three inches above the ear, and there were bruised spots on the same side of the head. The skull was extensively fractured, and the brains were exuding. These wounds, the doctor thought, were made with the same weapon as was used on the boy.

Thomas Goff, colored, grandson of Christina Taylor, testified that he was tending cows for Mr. Lynch on Saturday; that his Aunt Rose came for him while he was at supper, and said she wanted him at home; she said nothing about the children being killed and he did not know about it until that (Sunday) morning; he had not heard his grandmother say anything about the children; she did not seem excited, but her aunt did.

Peter Overton, colored, who lives at Major Goodloe's place, near by, testified that when passing the stone house Saturday evening, he asked the old woman (Christina Taylor) where her daughter was. She jumped up and said: "Go away man I don't want anything to give."

queenstown-queenstown-1881-08.A14:
THIRD EDITION
A MURDER CONFESSED.
The Deed "Inspired by the Devil"—Christiana Taylor, the Negress, Acknowledges Killing the Fisher Children.

WASHINGTON, August 11, 1881.

The mystery surrounding the tragedy at the village of Queenstown, reported in the Herald of Sunday last, was solved this afternoon. Christiana Taylor, an old negro woman who was arrested for the murder of the little boy and girl, aged three and six years respectively, on the farm of Joseph Fisher, on the Bunker Hill road, near this city, on Saturday last, confessed to-day that she committed the deed. She has heretofore denied all knowledge of the crime. This afternoon she sent for Captain Vernon, of the police, and Mr. Archibald White and to them made the following confession: "I was going along the path. It was not God Almighty, but it was the devil that put it in my head to kill them. I could not help killing them. I did it, not with the axe nor the washboard, but with a piece of wood, as big as my arm and about eighteen inches long. The children were running about the yard of the house. I struck the one with the long hair first, but I don't know how many times I hit her. I saw the axe in the woodpile after hitting them with the stick. What I killed them for I don't know; the devil got into me so that I could not help doing it. I picked the stick up in the road. I never told any one about it but you and Mr. Arch White. I believe it has worried me some. I have told the truth to you, white people. It is the truth from my heart. I threw the stick away down by the woodpile."

At the conclusion of the confession Christiana was removed to the jail. On the way down she seemed deeply depressed and talked but little. In reply to a question by Police Lieutenant Johnson she said:—"I could not help it. I hit the girl three times, when the boy caught me about my legs and screamed, and I then hit him on the head. I do not know how the Christmas tree came to be by the side of the dead children."

DISAPPEARANCE OF THE WEAPON.

A thorough search was made this afternoon for the stick of wood, but no traces of it could be obtained. It is supposed that if she did use a stick as her weapon it was used the night of the murder in the stove, as a hot fire was kept up in the stove all of Saturday night. It is claimed by some, particularly the colored people, that the woman is insane, and the testimony of Rose Taylor, her daughter, is liberally quoted. Rose in her testimony before the Coroner's jury yesterday said:—"Mother sometimes has giddy spells and behaves strangely. When she came back from Fisher's house Saturday she said, in a very excited manner, 'The Fisher children are dead and we must leave,' and directed me to go at once for my nephew, who works for Mrs. Lynch. Often when she has the spells she threatens to knock us down with a stick of wood." The colored people living in the vicinity of the house of Mr. Fisher have manifested considerable feeling concerning the murder, and have congregated nightly in the neighborhood of the police station where Christiana and Rose were confined. While they were not ready to believe that Christiana committed the deed, yet they were anxious that the perpetrator should be brought to justice. Rose will be detained as a witness to appear before the Grand Jury, which meets September 12. A singular fact in connection with this case is that there is not a living witness to her having committed the crime. When the Coroner's jury yesterday was ready to make up its verdict the testimony, although strongly circumstantial, was of such a character that the verdict had to be worded in the following language:—"The jury are unable to say positively by whose hand the deed was committed, but from the evidence adduced the suspicion points strongly to Christiana Taylor as the guilty party."

The Great Summer Danger.
The burning of a hotel at Beach Haven last Wednesday night will be very apt to make sojoiners at summer resorts nervous, and more afraid of fire than ever. And well may it have that effect. The danger from this source is greater than most persons suspect, unless they have carefully considered the subject and coolly calculated the probabilities of a fire, in the first place, and, secondly, the chances of escape in case one should occur. The fact is, that most of these summer hotels are merely vast tinder boxes, constructed with little reference to the prevention of a conflagration, and provided with few or no means or subduing one should it once get started. The chances are, therefore, at least ninety in a hundred that a fire breaking out in a watering place hotel will result in the total destruction of both building and contents; and we may add that if the inmates escape with their lives they may count themselves fortunate, indeed.

How can the matter be helped? It is hard to say. From the nature of the case, the situation is surrounded with difficulties, the number and character of which make it almost if not entirely impossible to provide complete security. Manifestly the expense of constructing a fire-proof building for a hotel to be occupied only two or three months in the year would be so great, and make the cost of staying in it so high, as to put that provision entirely out of the question. Neither is it possible to provide in all cases a supply of water sufficient to amount to anything in a fight with the flames. There seems to be left, then, nothing but vigilance and caution,—on the part of host and guest alike; and these ought to be exercised always, and in the extremest degree. No person should ever become an inmate of one of these mammoth establish-
uight to be exercised always, and in the extremest degree. No person should ever become an inmate of one of these mammoth establishments for a night—or of any hotel, for that matter,—without first becoming entirely familiar with all its stairways, passages and exits, and deliberately planning a route of escape in case of fire or any alarm of danger. These precautions should then be supplemented on the part of the guest with the greatest possible care in the use of matches, lights and fires. On the other side, the management of a hotel owes it both to itself and to its customers to use every means within reach to prevent the occurrence of a fire, as well as to keep the danger from it within the smallest limit possible. In this direction certainly nothing should be accepted as an effort in good faith which does not include the furnishing of reliable fire extinguishers, and also a plentiful supply of well-filled water-buckets in every hall of the house, together with a vigilant watchman on every floor, whose duty it should be to keep awake and constantly patrol all its passages the whole night through. These precautions ought to be required by law of every hotel situated remote from first class means of subduing a serious fire; but, law or no law, proprietors ought to take them, and the public should make it a point to studiously and firmly decline to patronize any house where they are not afforded.

The murder of the Fisher children is the most shocking crime that has been perpetrated in this vicinity for a long time. It was simply the act of a fiend. There is that in a little child which appeals to every sentiment of humanity. Its very innocence and helplessness inspire within the heart that is not devoid of every human sensibility a feeling of tenderness. It was evident that these two children, scarcely more than babes, had been killed without provocation of any kind. They were incapable of provoking an attack. Now, the mystery as to who perpetrated the act has been cleared up. The old negro woman, Christina Taylor, has confessed the inhuman, the monstrous deed; but the cause or motive for it remains unexplained. She does not pretend to assign any reason for the fendish act, which, it is easy to believe, must have been committed under some sudden and insane impulse. Still, that plea can hardly be successfully urged in her defence. The murderess was sane enough to conceal her guilt as best she could, and the welfare of society requires that she should be made to pay the extreme penalty provided by law for her offence.
queenstown-queenstown-1881-08.A19:
The Fisher Murder.—The negro woman, who was charged with the murder of the Fisher children (an account of which was given in the SENTINEL last week) near Brooke's Station, on the Metropolitan Branch R. R., has since made the following confession to Capt. Vernon, of the Washington police, which appeared in the Washington Post of the of the 12th instant:

I was going along the path; it was not God Almighty, but it was the devil that put it into my head to kill them. I could not help killing them. I did not do it with the ax, nor the washboard, but with a piece of wood as big as my arm, and about eighteen inches long. The children were running about the yard of the house. I struck the one with the long hair first; but I don't know how many times I hit her. I saw the ax in the woodpile after hitting them with the stick. What I killed them for I don't know. The devil got into me so that I could not help doing it. I picked the stick up in the road. I never told any one about it but you and Mr. Archie White. I believe it has worried me some. I have told the truth to you white people. It is the truth from my heart. I threw the stick away down by the woodpile.

The circumstances leading up to this confession are worthy of note. Without this statement or the discovery of some more direct evidence, it was the general opinion no case for even the Grand Jury could have been made against the woman. Lieut. Johnson, who has charge of the precinct in which the murder took place, determined to let nothing be left undone to unearth the criminal. The old woman had dropped hints about having something to tell. This Mr. Johnson wished to take every advantage of, but in such a way as not to vitiate the coming confession for use in court. On Wednesday, after the inquest, Christina said to Officer Rhodes, "If I tell, won't it be worse for me?" He replied that it would not.

The circumstances induced the delay in sending her to jail. Lieut. Johnson then decided to hunt up the people with whom the woman had formerly lived. She had mentioned Mr. White's name and he was seen and asked regarding her. Nothing of a dangerous tendency had shown itself in her conduct while with him. He came down, however, yesterday morning at Lieut. Johnson's suggestion to see if she would not talk to him. She at once intimated that if her children were there she would make her statement. Lieut. Johnson started for one of the girls. While he was away Capt. Vernon called to him and Mr. White. She after being cautioned, made her confession. After the statement was made she let fall other additional particulars. When she was beating the girl's head in the baby brother plead for his sister, clinging to her knees and crying. Neither of the children made any loud outcry.

As soon as Lieut. Johnson returned and learned what happened he determined to place the guilty wretch beyond the reach of certain parties whom he knew to be only awaiting her certain identification as the murderess to lynch her. He therefore procured a grocer's wagon, and drove rapidly off to jail. On the way she made the following additional statement:

The devil sent me up there. I tried to fight against him, but I couldn't. I struck the girl first; I struck two or three blows and she fell down. I struck them with a stick, not with the ax. Just as they fell I let them lay. I don't remember seeing the Christmas tree at all. I don't know how it got there.

On Saturday morning when picking vegetables for market the children found some white flowers and told Mrs. Fisher to give them to the Virgin Mary, the youngest adding, "hoping that she will make me a good boy, and keep the niggirs from killing me."

stearns-stearns-1881-12.A2:
The Alarming Reports
of lawlessness in the Kanawha mining regions, that have been lately telegraphad to the papers, led your correspondent to make a special visit to the scene of action. The facts may be summarized: At Coal Valley about 500 men employed in soft coal mines have been on a strike. They would not work themselves, and did all they could, short of violence, to dissuade others from doing so. The operators brought negroes from Virginia to take their places. The first batch were dissuaded from work by the striking miners. The troops were then called for. The peace was not broken nor was there any sign of trouble beyond the power of the civil authorities to control. The officers themselves admitted this, and I think the people generally regard the calling for troops as premature, and a serious mistake on the part of the Fayette authorities. The demand once made, the Governor could do nothing but comply.

The Question at Issue
between the miners and their employers is one not easily settled. The operators sell their coal to the railroad company, getting ninety-five cents per long ton, or less than three and a half cents per bushel. They pay the miner sixty-two and a half cents per ton; and to the land owner a royalty of fourteen cents per ton, besides ordinary running expenses, making the coal stand in the cars nearly what they get for it, and leaving them as margin nothing but the profits on the goods sold to the miners from the stores. To pay the increase of fifteen cents demanded by the miners is impossible unless the railroad should concede an advance on the price paid the operator. The miner, on the other hand, claims that he cannot live at sixty-two cents per ton. When employed he can make, one day with another, about one dollar and fifty cents per day net. Out of this he must pay six dollars a month house rent, and provide for his family. This he might do if the work were constant, but the railroad will not furnish cars to the operator more than half the time.

So the miner must live a year on the proceeds of six months' work. Lately there was an advance of fifty cents per ton in market, and the miners insist this advance should be divided between the railroad, the operator and the digger. The C. & O. railroad insists, however, upon taking all, on the ground as alleged that heretofore it has been carrying coal at a loss in order to keep the mines running and give the men work.

I think this railroad should be relieved from duty as a philanthropist. A law restricting railroads to their business as common carrier, preventing them from speculating in the industrial products along their line and requiring them to furnish cars for all freight that offers, would seem to be about the proper remedy. It would at any rate simplify matters by eliminating the railroad from the complication, allowing the operator to hunt his own market and make his own contracts, and leave him and his miners free to adopt a sliding scale adjusted with reference to the market price of coal. Such a scale is adopted at Campbell's Creek, where millions of bushels of coal are mined without a word of dispute and without a day's strike.

Policies.

You hear more of politics in this county than anywhere else in this section. In former years the Third district had no other interest save in politics, parties, conventions and candidates.

From every neighborhood the small fry politicians went out to disport themselves in the pool of which Charleston was the center, and the District the circumference. It is not so now.

At college the class in rhetoric used to have as an example of anti-climax the following poetical lines:
“Roll on, thon Connecticut, long hast thou ran,
Bringing shad to South Hadley and freedom to man.”

Still roll the Guyandotte and Kanawha as of old, from the solitude of sang-bearing wildernesses, and the sublime mysteries realms whence come forth vast Democratic majorities, dread, fathomless, inscrutable. But statesmanship now seldom troubles these blue waters with its canoes and keels.

“Shad to South Hadley and freedom to man,” no longer form the sole burden of the country’s business. The talk is of trade and telegraphs; mines and mills; timber and tobacco, and railroads and the restless elements of practical civilization. Here in Mason the idea that office-holding is the chief end of man still has its tenacious hold upon the public mind, but even here I can see something of an abatement of the popular passion. Time was when Mason county could furnish the material for both State tickets and have a surplus left for Congressional purposes.

Now, if she can have Barbee on the Independent ticket for Congress, with Hogg or Schon to oppose him as the Democratic nominee, with the understanding that some other Mason statesman is to succeed Davis in the Senate, and John English can have reserved for him a seat on the Supreme Bench, I think even Mason’s appetite would be sated.
stearns-stearns-1881-12.A3:
WEST VIRGINIA.
THE MINERS' TROUBLE IN THE KANDAWA VALLEY.
An Interview With the Prosecuting Attorney of Fayette County-The Cause of the Trouble and What is Needed to Remedy it.
A WHEELING AUTHOR'S TWO NOVELS.
Specia Correspondence of the Register.
WASHINGTON December 12, 1907

A WHEELING AUTHOR'S TWO NOVELS.

Specia Correspondence of the Register.

WASHINGTON, December 12.—I met Mr. J. W. St. Clair, the prosecuting attorney of Fayette county, here to-day, and had considerable talk with him concerning the recent miners troubles in the Kanawha section. He is a middle aged, muscular and plucky looking individual, and seems like the right sort of a man to hold his own in a rough community. He said he thought the troubles in his section of the State had been settled for the time being, and had been settled in the only way in which it was possible to settle them. "It had come to be a mere question," he said, "whether the coal operators in the coal valley should control their own property or not; and as the miner's association was so constructed and extended that trespassers could not be punished under the present laws, the only way to get along was to meet

Force With Force

when trespasses were attempted. I advised Wyant, one of the larger operators in the valley, whose employees were about to be interfered with, that if he posted his place and warned the strikers not to come on it, that he would have the right to keep them off, and, if necessary, shoot and drag them off. "Well," said Wyant, "if that is the law, I'll keep 'em off," and getting a box of shotguns he put them in the hands of trusted employees, and has been free from annoyance ever since.

The Faulkners, who have mines in the same neighborhood, pursued the same course and with the same success, and Eugene Dana, who manages the Campbell's creek mines, a little lower down, get along comfortably by exhibiting similar nerve when threatened.

As to the Recent Trouble

at Strain's, he said, the strike was ostensibly made against the railroad in the first instance, the men admitting that the operators could not pay the advance asked without an increase in the price paid for coal by the C. & O. agency. The mine owners used every effort to get an advance, and when they were unsuccessful offered their former miners a chance to go back to work at the old prices before trying the experiment of importing colored miners. The old hands refused to take hold or allow any one else, and got the first set of negroes imported to stop, by threatening their lives if they did not, and offering to take care of them if they did. It was in this part of the transaction that the women figured, assembling at the pitmouth with pans and sticks, their husbands and friends meanwhile congregating in the vicinity to the

Number of Several Hundred.

"You may not think a demonstration by women would amount to much," added St. Clair, "but when you come to tackle a crowd of square-built English and Welsh women, some of whom can whip an ordinary man in a fist-fight without any trouble, it is not so trifling a thing." Anyhow it was enough, aided by the backing at hand, to scare out the new hands, and some of them craw'ed out through the air-course in preference to facing the mob. The next lot brought on were negroes of the same class, and it was a mere question of protecting or abandoning the owners in their right to work them. The strikers, numbering about 400, were waiting for the negroes at the station, and the county officials

Were Powerless

to assert their authority and protect the new hands. The Sheriff, Tyree, is a man of good courage and equal good sense. He knew he could get no pass sufficient to bear him out in the immediate neighborhood. He had the right to call on the nearest organized military company or battalion for assistance without consulting the Governor, but he thought the authority of the Chief Executive would have weight, and the Governor promptly gave him permission to use such authority for the purpose of doing what he had a right to do without it. That was all there was of it. We got two companies on the ground and guarded the negroes from intrusion a couple of days until the strikers saw that they could not intimidate them into leaving and dispersed.

"Isn't there any other way to meet these troubles when they arise?"

"Not at present, and under similar circumstances. We have no proper legislation on the subject of trespass, and you can't very well go back to the common law proceeding on an information before a magistrate. Besides, with the influence of the Miner's Union against you, it is almost impossible to get testimony from witnesses who have full knowledge of facts. You have no idea of the class you have to deal with. There is not so much trouble with the Americans, Irish and negroes, but the English and Welsh contain a good many troublesome characters who work up most of the devilment. If I have received one anonymous letter

Threatening My Life,

I have had 20. The day I shot the negro who was endeavoring to escape, I was threatened by a mob, and at other times I have had to get out shooting irons in order to assert my right to stay where it was my plain duty to be. What is needed to put an end to this state of things, is legislation like that which stopped similar troubles in Pennsylvania. I know there will be some trouble in getting it, because there are always some members who will not act as they know they ought to act, for fear of losing a few votes, but the present Legislature is an exceptionally good one, and there have been, I think, enough exhibitions of the situation in our section to induce prompt and proper action by the two houses this winter.

Charlie Russell, whose industry helped to break up the Wheeling Standard, and who subsequently made considerable reputation as a historical novelist, lives here now, and he told me, yesterday, that he had a couple of brand new novels nearly ready for the press. The scene of one of them is laid in Wheeling, and the heroine, a fragile daughter of the southland, breaks one of her lower limbs in the second chapter. The hero, a young physician, is called in, but by an unfortunate mistake, "sets" the wrong limb. This naturally brings about an estrangement, but mutual explanations and corrections follow, and what might have been a fatal separation glides peacefully into a happy and enduring union. I do not know that I have reproduced the incidents exactly, but these will suffice to show what an inviting field the new Commonwealth is for the worker in moral fiction. Mr. Russell stated to me, what has been called to my attention by other novelists, that the absence of a proper international copyright law is gradually deterring many authors on this side of the waters from further attempts at works of fiction. Under the cheap system now in vogue of reproducing not only the standard but the best of the ephemeral foreign literature of the day in the cheap Seaside and Franklin Square editions, atten and twenty cents a volume, an American novel which is put upon the market at a dollar a volume stands very little chance of general circulation.

thomas-brayton-paoli-1881-07-31.A1:
BULLY FOR PAOLI.
A Case That Doesn't Need the Attention of the Governor.

On last Sunday night a gang of fourteen Orange County roughs on horseback and wearing masks, started out to mob a Negro living near Paoli, in that County. Apprised of their coming, he gathered three colored friends at his house, all armed, and awaited the appearance of the brave knights of the golden circle. The gang soon arrived and ordered the man to come out. He responded with a shot, and the roughs opened on the house with their revolvers in regular ku-klux style. The men in the house answered with their shot guns, and after the second round it was discovered that one of the roughs was badly wounded. The gang, panic-stricken, immediately retreated, taking the wounded villain with them. We have not yet learned the names of these men who so bravely defended their home, but they are certainly deserving of much credit for the good example they have set their more timid brethren. They are, however, men who will be hereafter respected in their community.
thomas-brayton-paoli-1881-07-31.A2:
HORACE WHITE, formerly editor of the Chicago Tribune, has been acting as confidential secretary of Henry Willard, and it is reported Horace is $500,000 in pocket from Henry's timely hints about investments. How glibly the blind pool magnates talk of the millions under their control.

Ohio papers are demanding the extermination of the Apache Indians, because some of that tribe horribly murdered Thomas K. Pugh, son of the late Senator Pugh of Cincinnati. There is nothing like an event of this character to change entirely the current of sympathy that is usually running in favor of the red man as against the white.

THE department of state at Washington declined to join European cabinets in advising Russia to treat with more justice the Jews, on the ground that such action would be simply meddling with what primarily concerns Russia alone. The "mind your own business" rule has become with nations in such cases as these, a law which the civilized world is bound to respect.

Among those mentioned as likely to succeed Justice Clifford are Chief Justice Gray, of Massachusetts; Judge Charles Devens, of Massachusetts, late attorney general of the Uuited States; Judge Hoar, of Massachusetts, and Senator Edmunds, of Vermont. There is a very warm feeling in favor of Judge Thurman, of Ohio,—not confined by any means to one political party—but it is probable that the question of locality will carry the appointment to the New England states.

THE London Standard, in an article on the harvest, says the general opinion in Mark Lane is that there is an average wheat crop in England, and the great majority of reports from different districts confirm that estimate. The barley crop cannot fail to be an average one. The root crop is less promising then they have been at this period for many years. Potatoes, however, are as good as the roots are bad. The prospects in Scotland are much less than in England. The most suspicious report of crops comes from Ireland.

THE members of the Minnesota railroad bond commission have adjourned until the 6th of September, for various reasons, among which are the following: that the arguments before the Supreme Court will not be concluded for some days, and after they are concluded judges and attorneys will naturally be tired, especially if the heat continues, and will need a week's rest. Then the supreme court justices will want a week, or perhaps two, to prepare and deliver their opinions upon the questions submitted, so that the date fixed—September 6th—will be none too far off.

THE New York Herald publishes a lengthy and interesting article showing that $100,000,000 has been subscribed in the last eighteen months in developing the resources of the south, or that portion lying east of the Mississippi and south of the Potomac. This money has been expended principally for the purchase or control of half a dozen or more railroads, the value of whose securities has been more than quadrupled by the operation. This is a large sum, but the New Orleans Picayune shows that it embraces less than half of the money which has flowed into the south during the past year to be invested in new industrial enterprises and means of transportation.

JUDGE ROBERTSON, the new collector of the port of New York, has assumed the duties of his office, and promises to conduct it on business principals, and to do every thing in his power to increase the efficiency of the service. Gen. Merritt, the late collector, was regarded as a model officer. His final report shows that for the fiscal year ending June 30, the revenues of the port reached a grand total of $140,000,-000, which were collected without the loss of a dollar to the Government. Of this vast revenue every one hundred dollars deposited in the treasury only cost the government $1.85 for collecting, or one and eight-tenths per cent. No other collector has ever made so satisfactory a showing.

MORE than seven thousand miles of railroad were built in the United States in 1880, or about twenty-five hundred more than in 1879. The total mileage of the country, now reaches nearly ninety-four thousand miles, which is thirty-three thousand more than were in operation ten years ago. The craze for building railroads seems to have reached the mania that prevailed previous to the revulsion of 1873, and the gift of prophecy is not required to determine what is likely to be the result. There are occasions where hindsight is not only equal, but a little better than foresight, and the old-fashioned lamp of experience a safer guide than the new fangled calcium and electric lights which often blind the wayfarer on his way.

The Chicago & Alton railroad, at a meeting of directors, declared a semi-animal dividend of 4½ per cent.

It is said it will not be a matter for surprise, if tickets from Chicago to Boston and vice versa, were sold at $1 each. The Grand Trunk is now going it at $5. The other roads had not come down to that, but the probabilities of the break are not far off.

Judge John Bowen, of Bismarck, has been appointed by Col. R. M. Newport, land agent of the Northern Pacific, town site agent, headquarters at Miles City. The judge is now at St. Paul, but within a few days will go to Miles City and commence operations.

The Chicago & Northwestern is now following the example set by Manager Merrill, of the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul, in establishing coal supply stations along its extreme western divisions. Superintendent Sanborn reports that the company propose putting in a supply of coal at all western stations sufficient to meet the demands of settlers during the coming winter and to avoid all danger of short supply by reason of blockades.

Jacob Eath, a workman at Wausau, Wis., shot himself to death.

Charles Schleifer, of St. Louis, blew out his brains on Monday last.

A five-year-old son of John Walters, living near the old soldier's orphan's home, Madison, Wis., threw himself into Lake Monona. He told his mother before hand that he was going away off, but nothing was thought of his remarks and his lifeless body was brought home.

The San Francisco Bulletin announces the receipt of information that the Oregon Navigation company is about to establish a line of steamers to China and Colombia, and that steamers will be put on at an early date. Nothing is reported of such an intention at the office of the company here.

At Indianapolis two men, named Thomas and John Comey, were shot and killed at the exposition grounds by a street car driver named W. H. Collier. They were attempting to rob him when he drew a revolver and shot both. After the shooting Collier drove his car back to the end of the route and gave himself up.

At Paoli, Ind., a mob sent word to Thomas Brayton, (colored) that he would be hanged. He barricaded his log house and had two female friends inside. When the mob, fifty strong, arrived, he fired, and with the assistance of the women to load, kept up the firing which was returned by the mob in a straggling way. The mob then dispered, carrying away five or six wounded comrades.

McKeesport, Pa., and the surrounding country are intensely excited over the murder of George McClure and the serious wounding of Constable Fleming, by a gang of eight thieves, while the former parties were in pursuit of the thieves, who had stolen goods from McClure to the amount of $3,000. A large force of armed men are scouring the country in search of the men. Six men, supposed to belong to the gang, have been arrested at West Newton, Pa. A reward of $7,000 has been offered for the capture of the thieves.

NEW HAVEN, Sept. 27.—At the Malley trial this afternoon, Frederick C. LAKEVIEW CEMETERY,

Where Rest the Remains of the Late President Garfield.

Chicago Times.

Lakeview Cemetery, where President Garfield.

Lakeview Cemetery, where President Garfield's remains will be laid to rest, embraces 300 acres on the south side of Euclid avenue, just beyond the east limit of Cleveland, five miles from the business center of the city. On the other side of the avenue is Wade Park, and in close proximity the site where the new Western Reserve University buildings are being erected. Nature seems to have designed this spot for the purpose to which it has been devoted, and all that art and money could do to enhance the natural beauties has been done. The grounds are owned by an incorporated association of Cleveland gentlemen of wealth and refinement, incorporated under the law, which requires "all gains or profits from the sales of lots or otherwise to be appropriated to perpetual adornment and repair to the cemetery." The land was purchased ten years ago and laid out by landscape designers and engineers selected for eminence in their professions. Wooded hills, grassy vales, secluded nooks, winding drives, sinuous walks, running brooks and quiet lakes are the conspicuous landmarks. The association adopted a plan different from any other cemetery, and expressed tersely in the original prospectus the following language: "A feeling is growing in the public mind that burials should be made where the quiet repose of the dead may be assured forever. The human heart clings to the grave of its departed hopes, and seeks consolation in rearing monuments and emblems of beauty over the remains of its departed loved ones. This can be fitly done, not in the tumultuous din of cities, but amid the quiet verdure, under the broad and cheerful light of heaven, where the harmonious and ever-changing face of nature reminds us by its resuscitating influence that to die is to

live again." With this sentiment prompting the plans, the cemetery has become in beauty and tasteful adornment the rival of the most celebrated cemeteries of the world, and the air of retired and restful loveliness of an inexpressible nearness to nature and withdrawal from the world is not found elsewhere. The great object of the association was to provide a resting place for the departed, free from the gloom of the tomb and from which should be banished everything suggestive of awfulness in death. No fence, either iron or wood, no coping or curbing of brick or stone, no hedge, wooden trellis, posts and chains, or anything to make an enclosure is permitted. Head and foot boards are prohibited, headstones not allowed to exceed fourteen inches in height. Thus the cemetery rather resembles a vast, well-kept park, with stately shafts and modest or ornate vaults in lieu of statuary and structures. President Garfield loved to stroll in this cemetery. It was his ideal of a final earthly resting place.

W. T. Bortzlen had a dispute with a Deputy Sheriff named Jere Ward at Scanlan's Landing, Ark., twenty miles below Memphis, Monday, about some business transaction. On Boteler returning to his home from Memphis Monday night, and just as he stepped off the steamer, he was shot dead by Ward.

Asiatic cholera has broken out in the districts of Djidah and Aden, Arabia. In the latter district there were forty-six deaths from the destructive contagion last week. All communication between Egypt and Arabia has been suspended so as to prevent the spread of the disease to the former country.

The ship Hatesburg, from New York to Oregon, with a cargo of railroad iron, struck at Hoviana beach, on the Californian coast, at midnight Monday, and went to pieces. Of a crew of twenty-four, nine men and the Captain were lost. A boy aged 13, who was on board, perished also. The bodies have not been recovered.

Messus, D. & J. Sadlier, the New York Catholic book publishers, who made an assignment about a month ago, have filed a schedule, which shows their liabilities to be $205,000 and their nominal assets to be $257,000. It is probable that the assets will not realize more than $190,000, however. The showing is rather creditable to the bankrupts.

Among the telegrams of sympathy and condolence with Mrs. Garfield received at the State Department yesterday was one from Christopher Columbus, Duke of Veragua, Spain, and descendant and representative of the great discoverer, on behalf of the American Congress now in session at Madrid. Secretary Hitt, in the absence of Secretary Blaine, suitably replied.

average about half a crop; cotton about two-thirds.

Fayetteville, since the building of the railroad, has taken a new lease of prosperity.

Hogs in Ouachita and Saline river bottoms are fat enough for meat as soon as the weather will serve to cure it.

Wur. Shelton Watson, of Scarce, ite county, was killed by an accidental fall from a second-story window last week.

KEOKY, Ia., Nov. 9.—The fiend who assaulted Mrs. Kenkel at Adrian, Ill., Monday, proves to be a young negro who had been employed on a farm in the neighborhood. He was arrested at Peoria today, confessed the crime, and was taken to Adrian by the officers. Upon reaching the scene of his crime a mob took the prisoner from the officers, and shot him three times. The officers rallied a force of men to their support, retook their prisoner, and conveyed him to Carthage, where he now lies in the county jail in a dying condition. Intense excitement prevails in Adrian and in towns through which the officers passed with their prisoner. He was taken to Carthage in a box-car, which was heavily guarded, and no one was permitted to see him.

The Trial of Lient. Flipper.

GALVESTON, Tex., Nov. 9.—In the Flipper case, the cross-examination of Col. Shafter occupied the court again yesterday. The question for the defense pointed to the attempt to prove Shafter overzealous in the service of the Government in stripping Flipper of all his personal effects. Shafter replied that the personal effects were taken at first, but subsequently tendered back. The balance was retained until some small debts were settled. Probably all have been offered but refused by Flipper, save through a civil process. The effects have been subject to his order since that time. The defense offered to prove that the enlisted men were so enraged at his confinement that propositions were made to relieve Flipper by force. The Judge Advocate declined the offer as improper.

Four DAVIS, Tex., Nov. 9.—The entire day was occupied offering evidence by the prosecution. The principal paper offered was a statement from the Treasury Department showing that Lient. Flipper was still accountable for $3,791.77 as Acting Commissary, and the attention of the Court was called to Sec. 5,494, Revised Statutes. Capt. Barber objected, on the ground that the paper was the only proper evidence in cases of contractor's embezzlement under Secs. 5,485 and 5,494, but it was not proper evidence when the charge was actual embezzlement under the Sixteenth Article of War. The question was argued at length and the objection overruled. The defense offered to formally except. Objected to by the Judge Advocate and overruled by the Court.

A Horrible Outrage Committed on a Newly-Married Woman by Two Scoundrels.

St. Louis, Mo., Nov. 9.—A Springfield, Mo., special gives an account of a most dulcous outrage perpetrated Monday night at Seymour, Webster County, a now railroad
bolleal outrago perpetrated Monday night at Seymour, Webster County, a now railroad town on the Kansas City, Springfield & Memphis line. It appears that a large number of people were gathered there, living in tents and huts awaiting the erection of houses. In one of the tents lived a newly-married man named Newton C. McLane. During Monday night Henry Carter and Frank Brown entered the tent, and while one of the ruffians hold a revolver at McLane's head the other ravished McLane's wife. They then changed places, and the other villain performed the same vile act upon the poor woman. The scoundrels then fled, but an alarm was given immediately and a large party started in pursuit. Brown was captured, and Carter will no doubt be taken. Judge Lynch is likely to settle the case.

LATEST TELEGRAMS CONDENSED.
Tuesday afternoon the residence of Mrs. Margaret Thiesing, on Brown street, Cincinnati, was burglariously entered during her absence and several valuable articles of jewelry and a watch and chain carried off. Entrance was effected through a rear window.

On Saturday night the police of San Francisco raided the gambling hells in that city, in furtherance of a plan to break up such business in that city. The result was a large number of prisoners found "fighting the tiger," who were pulled, and $4,000 in fines were realized to the city.

Some sneak thief broke the window of the jewelry store of J. S. Reynolds, at Hannibal, Missouri, a day or two since, and made off with several valuable watches and some jewelry. Reynolds was awakened by the noise and rushed down stairs, but the thieves were too quick for him, and made their escape.

An attempt was made a couple of days since to fire the large block on Main street, White Hall, Delaware, but the attempt was frustrated by the incendiary putting a cloth over the hole bored where the fire had been inserted, and thus preventing a disastrous conflagration, as the covering put out the flames.

An interesting but ridiculous libel suit is progressing at San Jose, California. A Miss Dixon was rather boisterous as a school girl, and the principal, Charles H. Allen, notified her mother she had better withdraw from school, as she was conducting herself badly. The libel suit was the result but the whole thing has a farcical air about it.

A special from Sonora, California, says the down stage from there was stopped at 4 o'clock Tuesday morning and Wells, Fargo & Co.'s treasure box was robbed of $3,200. One of the passengers was also robbed of $550, but no other passenger was robbed. The robbers were three medium-sized men and one large man masked in old sacks.

Under-Sheriff Irwin started to Jefferson City, Monday, with C. A. Malther, convicted in the circuit court of Carthage, Missouri, Saturday, of attempting to blackmail, and sentenced to two years' hard labor in the penitentiary. Malther is the man who wrote a letter to John C. Webb, of Webb City, asking that gentleman for $500, threatening death if he did not pay.

Joseph Abbott, living at Twelfth and Central avenues, Cincinnati, was knocked down by a regular Jack Sheppard, named Mike McCormick, Tuesday night, on Gilbert avenue, and robbed. McCormick was riding a horse, and dismounted, kicked the man
hue, and robbed. McCormick was riding a horse, and dismounted, kicked the man in the jaw, knocking him out of time, and then remounted and rode off. McCormick was captured to-day, and locked up on a charge of highway robbery.

Isaac and Richard Hill, two negroes, are now in jail at Vicksburg on a charge of killing young Daniel A. Cameron, of Bovina, at the Oakland place in that county, Monday morning. Cameron became engaged in a difficulty with the negroes when the latter drew their revolvers and fired with fatal results. In the meantime he fled, but was pursued and shot twice in the back. The negroes came near being mobbed.

Deputy Sheriff John Heckman went to the house of Moses Caten, in Geneva, Kentucky, a few days ago to serve a court paper. Caten resisted and the deputy sheriff shot him, the ball entering just below the right nipple and lodging under the skin back of the left shoulder. Caten, however, got in the house, procured his gun and shot at Heckman, the ball passing through his clothing. Caten is reported as dead.

A. Gattlab on Tuesday absconded with $2,000 of the Vicksburg Bank, given by that institution on a check purporting to have emanated from Mrs. A. P. Harris, of Edwards, Mississippi, for the endowment policy held by her late husband against the Knights of Honor. Gattlab clerked for a while in the house of L. A. Moss, and for six months was engaged in hunting a place. The thief, after forging the check and obtaining the money, left for parts unknown.

John Crawford and John H. Burchell, convicts in prison for burglary, scaled the walls Monday afternoon, of the Jeffersonville, Indiana, penitentiary, between two armed guards in the tower. Both got across the road. Guard Scantlin called to them to halt, but Crawford kept on running. After a second call, McRae fired, killing Crawford instantly. The ball entered the back of the head, coming out at the front. Burchell was captured and returned to prison.

Information received Friday at Keokuk, Iowa, from Ferris, tells of the attempted outrage of a farmer's wife, named Kenkel. The assault was made by a tramp while Mrs. Kenkel was alone at her home. The wretch threw a blanket over her head and tried to force her to the floor. The woman was plucky and resisted him, biting him badly in the scuffle, and the rascal, finding that he could accomplish nothing, took to the cornfield and fled. He is being pursued, and if caught will be roughly dealt with.

Last July, A. L. Hunt, a Richmond drummer, and Ed. Calloway, the Kimball house clerk at Atlanta, exchanged shots in the Kimball house bar-room, and the latter received a severe wound in the cheek. Hun was indicted for assault with intent to commit murder, but readily gave bond. Efforts to compromise failed and Calloway was also indicted. But Monday morning when the cases were called, it was announced a compromise had been effected and both parties plead guilty to carrying concealed weapons, and each was fined $100 and the costs by the judge.

GILFILLAN'S NOTICE.

Washington, November 12.—Gilfillan, Treasurer of the United States, has orpered that no bonds deposited as security for the circulation of public deposits, shall hereafter be surrendered or be allowed to pass from the custody of the Treasurer's office, except upon the surrender of circulating notes deposite of lawful money deposited upon other bonds in the name of the Treasury of the United States in trust or in care of the depository bank upon order of the Secretary of the Treasury.

ONE HUNDREDTH AND FIFTH CALL.

At the close of business to-day there had been $9,846,950 of United States bonds received at the Treasury under the 105th call.

Transoceanic.

EVIL EFFECT OF THE READJUSTER SUCCESS.

London, November 12.—The Economist says that Virginia funded bonds have fallen six per cent. because of the success of the Readjuster party in the recent election.

LAND COURT PROCEEDINGS.

Dublin, November 12.—Among the applications for fixing judicial rent recorded are 130. On the estate of Sir George Calhuast of Cork, and others on the estate of the Endowed School Commissioners, and of the Marquis of Ely, Fermaugh county, and 170 on the estate of McNamara mines, where tenants have long refused to pay rent. The land Commissioners have resolved in all cases where notices have been served on or before to-day it will not refuse application, even if it sit until midnight. This greatly increases tenants' facilities.

SNOW.

London, Nov. 12.—A dispatch from Odessa says the railway traffic in Central Russia is greatly impeded by snow which has prevented the sowing of winter wheat, especially in the government of Kharkoff.

Fiend Finished.

Keokuk, Iowa, November 12.—The fiend who assaulted and ravished Mrs. Kenkel, at Adrian, Ill., on Monday, proved to be a young negro who had been employed on a farm in the neighborhood. He was arrested at Peoria today, and confessed the crime, and was taken to Adrian by the officers. Upon reaching the scene of his crime, a mob took the prisoner from the officers and shot him three times. The officers rallied a force of men to their support, retook their prisoner and conveyed him to Carthage, where he now lies in the county jail in a dying condition. Intense excitement prevails in Adrian and in the towns through which the officers passed with their prisoner. He was taken to Carthage in a box-car, which was heavily guarded, and no one was permitted to see him.

Cowboy Canard.

Cowboy Canada.

Wellington, Kans., Nov. 12.—A source of relief pervaded this city Tuesday evening. Sheriff Thralls took Chastain and Carter, the cowboys out on the 4 o'clock train this afternoon, en route for the penitentiary at Leavenworth. No demonstrations were made by the cows last night looking to the release of Chastain and Carter, although it was claimed that quite a party of them were camping in the brush about two miles out with that intention. The jail was placed under a heavy guard and the streets patrolled the entire night, that the town might not be taken by surprise. The night passed quietly, however, and no cowboys appeared, other than a few stray ones who could have walked the streets at any other time without attracting any attention.

A Black Man Attempts a Black Deed.

Louisville, Ky. Nov. 12.—A Frankfort special to the Courier-Journal says: A negro man named William Russell went to the residence of Mrs. Hutchinson, near the Kentucky Military Institute, this evening, and assaulted her with intent to commit rape. He knocked her down with a shovel and broke her arm. He afterwards shot her in the shoulder. He than ran but was afterward captured and brought to this city and lodged in jail. To-night great excitement prevails in the neighborhood, and threats of lynching are freely indulged in.

French Visitors in Porkopolis.

Cincinnati, Nov. 12.—The French visitors were called on this morning by Mayor Means and informally welcomed to the city. Afterwards, at his invitation, they appeared on change where they were warmly received by the merchants. This afternoon they spent in visiting places of interest in the city and suburbs.

LORD LORNE has sailed for England. The bank of Walker & Co., at Zurich, Switzerland, is reported to have been robbed of 75,000 francs and all negotiable securities and its books burned. The bank has suspended. Unpleasant surmises regarding the affair are current.
THE cotton statistics for the present season show a falling off in the receipts at every Southern port, except New Orleans, from last year, the decrease in some cases being considerable. The estimates of the total crop made by members of the New York Cotton Exchange vary from 5,175,000 to 6,500,000 bales. Bradstreet's reports would indicate the smaller estimate as being the nearer correct.

A WASHINGTON special says: "The bill providing for the admission of Dakota as a State has been already prepared, and some Senators and Congressmen have prepared speeches in support of the admission. The bill will be pushed vigorously. Senator David Davis will support it, which insures its becoming a law and the admission of the Territory as a State, with probably two Republican Senators."

The annual report of the Pension Bureau shows that on the 30th of June, 1881, there were 268,830 pensioners; net increase during the year, 18,028; aggregate annual value of all pensions, $28,769,967. The annual disbursements of the office, however, largely exceed this sum. For instance, the total amount paid for pensions during the year (exclusive of certain arrears in claims allowed prior to January 25, 1879), was $49,-723,147, the difference being accounted for in arrears of pensions, or "accrued pensions," covering a period dating back to the discharge, in each case, of soldiers still living and soldiers' deaths in the claims of widows or minor children.

INVESTIGATION into the affairs of the Mechanics' National Bank of Newark, N. J., so hopelessly wrecked by Cashier Baldwin, discloses the fact that some two years ago Henry P. Marchbank, at that time engaged as corresponding clerk of the bank, got away with $50,000 of its funds, which has never been recovered. Marchbank was retired, but the matter was not made public, it is supposed on account of the clerk's too intimate knowledge of the Cashier's own and much more extensive defalcation. Marchbank has now been arrested. He is a man of some property, and like Baldwin, has heretofore been esteemed as an estimable and upright gentleman.

In an election riot between whites and blacks at Marion Station, five miles north of Meridian, Miss., A. T. Harvey, Assessor, Joseph Barnett, Jeff. Seegars and Vincent Seegars were killed and Levi More and James Hodges wounded. All these were white men. They are said to have been unarmed and unprepared for an attack. The negroes were led by Ad. Vance, a white man. After the shooting they retired to Vance's house, and an attempt to arrest them by the Sheriff's posse resulted in further bloodshed, John Vance, a son of Ed., being killed, as was also A. H. Warren, of Meridian, one of the Sheriff's posse. The negroes were finally driven to the woods, but at last accounts had not laid down their arms.

THE State elections held on Tuesday, the 8th, as indicated by the earlier returns, resulted as follows: In New York the Democrats seem to have elected their State officers with the exception of Secretary of State. Gen. Carr, the Republican candidate, runs ahead of the balance of his ticket and is probably elected. The Legislature will be close, but the Democrats have probably secured a majority on joint ballot. Wm. W. Astor, the Republican candidate for Congress in the Eleventh District, is beaten by Flower, Democrat; and in the Ninth District, Hardy, Democrat, defeats Thomas Murphy, Republican. In Pennsylvania the Republicans seem to have elected Bailey State Treasurer, although the Democrats do not yet concede this result. In Virginia the Readjusters have probably elected Cameron for Governor and secured a working majority in the Legislature. In Wisconsin the Democrats have made large gains, owing somewhat to the Probibition vote, but the Republican State ticket is probably elected, by an estimated plurality of some 5,000 or 6,000. In New Jersey the Legislature remains Republican by a reduced majority, and the same is true of Connecti-
future remains Republican by a reduced majority, and the same is true of Connecticut. The Democratic majority in Mississippi is estimated at from 20,000 to 30,000. In Massachusetts, Minnesota and Nebraska the Republican tickets were elected by the usual majorities on a light vote. In Maryland the Republicans have made some gains in the Legislature, but not enough to be made effective.

LATE Irish news: Despite suppression, the Land League of several local branches continue to meet secretly. A circular has been issued to the police instructing them to immediately report any meeting supposed to be held for League purposes though held ostensibly for another. The object is with a view to the arrest of participants. The Executive is considering what to do in regard to the Ladies' League. A curious plan has been adopted in some parts of the west of Ireland with a view of keeping the "no-rent" manifesto before the tenants. It takes the form of a promissory note, which has been circulated among the farmers attending fairs. The note is a promise to pay rent on the day Parnell, Davitt and other suspects are released. It is intended the note shall be signed by the tenants and sent to the landlords. It is stated that the Land League leaders have changed their front and directed tenant farmers to send in their claims under the land act, with a view of swamping the commission. A tenant farmer named Doherty was shot dead recently while entering his house, at Carrigan, Galway, it is believed because he had paid his rent. He had been boycotted for some time. Two persons were arrested..... Up to the 6th of November 16,000 tenants had appealed to the Land Commission to fix a fair rent.....The military authorities have inaugurated a system of alarm drills to train the troops to fall into a defensive position in case of attack. This is a revival of the practice which prevailed during the repeal movement in '48.

CHARLES MADDER shot and killed Miss Phoebe Bernard at Tiffin, O., because she would not marry him. Both were young people of the best standing in the community. The murderer was arrested, and there were strong threats made of lynching him.

SMALL-POX is epidemic in Stearns County, Minn., and the physicians of the State Board of Health are bending all their energies to confine it to districts now infected and to eventually root it out altogether. They encounter considerable difficulty on account of the ignorance of the inhabitants, who look on the disease as a visitation of Providence.

A MOVEMENT is on foot among the leading millers of the country to shut down all operations for thirty days. It is claimed that wheat is now held at speculative prices, and also that the supply of flour on hand largely exceeds the demand, both of which wrongs, in the view of the millers, can be righted by the temporary suspension of milling operations.

GOVERNOR CHURCHILL, of Arkansas, granted a reprieve in the cases of two colored murderers, Jackson and Hill, sentenced to be hanged at Hamburg, Jackson County, on the 22d ult. All preparations had been made for the execution, and a crowd of several thousand persons

CRIME.
JOHN SHEA escaped from a bailiff in St. Louis, and a few hours later killed Police Officer Doran, who caught him committing a burglary.
ALBERT MADDEN, a mail agent on the Rock Island road, was arrested at Des Moines for purlining eight hundred lettars, and gave bail in $2,000.

The police of Cincinnati have locked up a Hebrew with three different names, who perpetrated bankrupt frauds in that city, Chicago, and Davenport, sovering the past ten years.

The other morning a dozen masked men broke into the jail at Shakespeare, Arizona, and lynched two cow-boys confined for stealing stock.

The sheriff at Meridian, Miss., states that Edward Vance, the colored man who led in the election tragedy, had in his house three kegs of powder and large quantities of buckshot.

W. J. FULLER, a moonshiner in Habersham county, Georgia, killed Taylor Love for furnishing information to the revenue officers. Commissioner Raum has ordered the utmost vigilance in securing the arrest of the murderer.

The man captured at Grand Island, Neb., and believed to be Edward Maxwell, alias Edward Williams, has been identified by Deputy Sheriff Knight, of Pepin county, Wisconsin, and two brothers of the murdered Sheriff Coleman, who have applied to Governor Vance for requisition papers.

A NEGRG who committed an outrage on Mrs. Kunkel, near Adrian, Ill., confessed his guilt, and was ordered taken to jail at Carthage. Neighbors of the unfortunate woman endeavored to take the prisoner from the officers and lynch him, falling in whihah, sevelots were fired at him, fatal wounds being inflicted. A large posse got the bleeding brute into a box-car and conveyed him to jail.

DR. J. CLAY MADDOX, of Baltimore, while repelling an attack on the election inspectors, was shot dead by some person in the crowd behind him. As a surgeon in the confederate service he quarreled with General Beauregard, he had a street affray with a journalist in Richmond, killed a physician of Alexandria in a duel, and had been tried for committing an abortion.

DETECTIVES in the employ of the Wisconsin Central railway have captured three more passenger conductors for complicity in the frauds recently discovered on that road. T, H. Rhoades and L. F. Mead were veteran employees, and were arrested at Stevens Point, and S. S. Weller was apprehended at Green Bay. Each gave bail at Milwaukee in the sum of $500.

JOHN TATE, of Chicago, was seen the other evening to lower a bundle of goods from the upper floor of the store of J. V. Farwell & Co. A special policeman took the plumber, valued at $500, and notified the watchman. The store was surrounded by officers, and the thief was captured in the basement, after the whole building had been ransacked for him. He confessed hat he hid in the store in the afternoon. He is 23 years of age, and the son of respectable people.

AT Tiffin, O., a theological student, named Charles E. Madder, killed Miss Phoebe Bernard on the street because she declined his attentions. While a mob was arranging to lynch the murderer, Sheriff Lease was informed of the plan, and made ample preparations to hold his prisoner. The police attempted the arrest of Andy Moore, leader of the mob, and three officers were badly wounded. Dennis Hallahan was captured with a rope in his possession. Sixty men guarded the jail the next evening, and there was a general belief that another attempt to lynch Madder would be made before daylight, which the sheriff defeated by sending the prisoner in a buggy to Fremont, to be placed behind the bars at Toledo.
